abstract: Computing the inverse dynamics of a robot ann is an active area of research in the control literature. We hope to learn the inverse dynamics by training a neural network on the measured response of a physical ann. The input to the network is a temporal window of measured positions; output is a vector of torques. We train the network on data measured from the first two joints of the CMU Direct-Drive Arm II as it moves through a randomly-generated sample of "pick-and-place" trajectories. We then test generalization with a new trajectory and compare its output with the torque measured at the physical arm. The network is shown to generalize with a root mean square error/standard deviation (RMSS) of 0.10. We interpreted the weights of the network in tenns of the velocity and acceleration filters used in conventional control theory.

paragraphs: The paper studies whether a neural network can learn a robot arm's inverse dynamics from measurements of the physical arm. The task is to infer the torques associated with a movement. The network receives a window of measured joint positions over time and produces a vector of torques, connecting recent motion history to the required mechanical output.

Training data come from the first two joints of the CMU Direct-Drive Arm II during randomly generated pick-and-place trajectories. After training, the authors evaluate the network on a new trajectory. They compare its torque predictions with measurements from the real arm, directly testing whether the learned relationship extends to a movement outside the training sample.

The reported root mean square error divided by standard deviation is 0.10 on this generalization test. The authors also interpret learned weights in terms of velocity and acceleration filters used in conventional control theory. This interpretation connects learning from position windows to familiar motion quantities, helping explain what the trained network extracts from its temporal inputs.
summary.tldr: A network learns robot-arm torque predictions from position histories and generalizes to a new trajectory with a reported normalized error of 0.10.

title: Using Backpropagation with Temporal Windows to Learn the Dynamics of the CMU Direct-Drive Arm II

paragraphs: This paper connects rhythmic neural activity to the physical chewing movements of a lobster's gastric mill, a system of three teeth in its stomach. Although the controlling stomatogastric ganglion is well characterized, understanding its neural rhythms alone does not fully explain feeding behavior. The mechanics of the body being controlled also matter.

The authors construct a computer model of the gastric mill's muscles and skeletal components. They use Hill's muscle model and a quasi-static approximation for skeletal dynamics. These modeling choices provide a way to translate patterns recorded from an isolated ganglion into predicted motor patterns, linking neural observations to a physical interpretation.

The model can simulate changes in chewing patterns caused by neuromodulators. This connects changes in neural rhythmic activity with changes in the movements those rhythms produce. The contribution is a behavioral interpretation of isolated circuit activity through an explicit model of the controlled musculoskeletal system, with the quasi-static treatment forming a stated approximation in that interpretation.
summary.tldr: A musculoskeletal model translates lobster gastric neural rhythms into predicted chewing movements, including changes induced by neuromodulators.

title: Mapping Between Neural and Physical Activities of the Lobster Gastric Mill

abstract: We present a new learning architecture: the Decision Directed Acyclic Graph (DDAG), which is used to combine many two-class classifiers into a multiclass classifier. For an N -class problem, the DDAG con(cid:173) tains N(N - 1)/2 classifiers, one for each pair of classes. We present a VC analysis of the case when the node classifiers are hyperplanes; the re(cid:173) sulting bound on the test error depends on N and on the margin achieved at the nodes, but not on the dimension of the space. This motivates an algorithm, DAGSVM, which operates in a kernel-induced feature space and uses two-class maximal margin hyperplanes at each decision-node of the DDAG. The DAGSVM is substantially faster to train and evalu(cid:173) ate than either the standard algorithm or Max Wins, while maintaining comparable accuracy to both of these algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a Decision Directed Acyclic Graph, or DDAG, for turning binary classifiers into a multiclass classifier. For a problem with N classes, the architecture contains N(N − 1)/2 classifiers, covering every pair of classes. The graph provides a structure for combining their two-class decisions into a final classification.

For nodes that use separating hyperplanes, the authors derive a bound on test error using VC analysis. The bound depends on the number of classes and the margins achieved at the nodes, but not on the dimension of the input space. This motivates using classifiers that seek large margins within the graph.

The resulting algorithm, DAGSVM, uses maximum-margin binary hyperplanes in a feature space defined by a kernel. The paper reports substantially faster training and evaluation than the standard algorithm and Max Wins, with comparable accuracy. The theoretical result explains the emphasis on margins, while the reported comparison shows that the graph architecture can offer computational benefits without an observed loss of accuracy in those comparisons.
summary.tldr: DAGSVM organizes pairwise maximum-margin classifiers in a directed acyclic graph, achieving reported speed gains with comparable accuracy.

title: Large Margin DAGs for Multiclass Classification

originalAbstract: In this paper we will treat input selection for a radial basis function (RBF) like classifier within a Bayesian framework. We approximate the a-posteriori distribution over both model coefficients and input subsets by samples drawn with Gibbs updates and reversible jump moves. These datasets are also used to infer the a-posteriori probabilities of dif(cid:173) ferent input subsets.

paragraphs: The paper treats input selection for a classifier resembling a radial basis function model as a Bayesian inference problem. The goal involves deciding which inputs to use while also estimating the model's coefficients. Both choices are represented through a posterior distribution, so uncertainty about the input subset becomes part of the learning problem.

The authors approximate this joint posterior using samples generated by Gibbs updates and reversible jump moves. Together, these operations explore model coefficients and alternative input subsets. Sampling supports an assessment of multiple candidate subsets and their posterior probabilities, linking the selection of inputs to uncertainty about the fitted model.

The method is evaluated on public datasets, with classification accuracy compared against a conventional automatic relevance determination scheme. The same datasets are used to infer posterior probabilities for different input subsets. The contribution thus includes both predictive evaluation and probabilistic input assessment: it examines classification performance while also estimating how strongly the data support particular choices of inputs.
summary.tldr: Bayesian sampling jointly estimates classifier coefficients and input subsets, yielding posterior probabilities for alternative feature selections.

title: On Input Selection with Reversible Jump Markov Chain Monte Carlo Sampling

abstract: We examine eight different techniques for developing visual rep(cid:173) resentations in machine vision tasks. In particular we compare different versions of principal component and independent com(cid:173) ponent analysis in combination with stepwise regression methods for variable selection. We found that local methods, based on the statistics of image patches, consistently outperformed global meth(cid:173) ods based on the statistics of entire images. This result is consistent with previous work on emotion and facial expression recognition. In addition, the use of a stepwise regression technique for selecting variables and regions of interest substantially boosted performance.

We found that local methods, based on the statistics of image patches, consistently outperformed global meth(cid:173) ods based on the statistics of entire images. This result is consistent with previous work on emotion and facial expression recognition. In addition, the use of a stepwise regression technique for selecting variables and regions of interest substantially boosted performance.

paragraphs: This paper compares eight ways of turning images into representations for visual speech recognition. The central question is which image information should be retained before recognition takes place. The methods include different versions of principal component analysis and independent component analysis, combined with stepwise regression to select variables.

A key distinction is whether a representation uses statistics from small image patches or from an entire image. In the reported comparison, patch-based methods consistently performed better than methods based on whole images. This gives a concrete reason to examine local visual structure when designing these representations. The authors also describe the result as consistent with earlier findings on emotion and facial expression recognition.

The selection stage mattered as well: stepwise regression substantially improved performance by choosing variables and regions of interest. Together, the findings connect recognition quality to both the spatial scale used to construct features and the subsequent choice of which features to retain.
summary.tldr: Local image representations and stepwise feature selection improved performance in a comparison of visual speech recognition techniques.

title: A Comparison of Image Processing Techniques for Visual Speech Recognition Applications

abstract: A nonlinear supervised learning model, the Specialized Mappings Architecture (SMA), is described and applied to the estimation of human body pose from monocular images. The SMA consists of several specialized forward mapping functions and an inverse map(cid:173) ping function. Each specialized function maps certain domains of the input space (image features) onto the output space (body pose parameters). The key algorithmic problems faced are those of learning the specialized domains and mapping functions in an op(cid:173) timal way, as well as performing inference given inputs and knowl(cid:173) edge of the inverse function. Solutions to these problems employ the EM algorithm and alternating choices of conditional indepen(cid:173) dence assumptions. Performance of the approach is evaluated with synthetic and real video sequences of human motion.

paragraphs: This paper estimates human body pose from monocular images using a nonlinear supervised model called the Specialized Mappings Architecture. The model contains several forward mappings, each responsible for particular regions of the image-feature space, together with an inverse mapping. Its structure allows different parts of the input space to receive specialized treatment.

Each forward function converts image features into body-pose parameters within its assigned domain. Learning must determine both those domains and the functions operating on them. Inference presents a related challenge: the system must estimate pose from an input while incorporating knowledge supplied by the inverse function. The architecture therefore couples specialization with reasoning in both mapping directions.

The authors address these problems using EM and alternating choices of conditional-independence assumptions. They evaluate the approach on synthetic and real video sequences of human motion. The stated contribution is an architecture and learning procedure for coordinating specialized pose estimators, with evaluation spanning generated and recorded motion sequences rather than a reported quantitative advantage in the abstract.
summary.tldr: A supervised architecture learns specialized image-to-pose mappings and combines them with an inverse mapping for monocular body-pose estimation.

title: Learning Body Pose via Specialized Maps

abstract: We describe a new algorithmic framework for learning multiclass catego- rization problems. In this framework a multiclass predictor is composed of a pair of embeddings that map both instances and labels into a common space. In this space each instance is assigned the label it is nearest to. We outline and analyze an algorithm, termed Bunching, for learning the pair of embeddings from labeled data. A key construction in the analysis of the algorithm is the notion of probabilistic output codes, a generaliza- tion of error correcting output codes (ECOC). Furthermore, the method of multiclass categorization using ECOC is shown to be an instance of Bunching. We demonstrate the advantage of Bunching over ECOC by comparing their performance on numerous categorization problems.

In this framework a multiclass predictor is composed of a pair of embeddings that map both instances and labels into a common space. In this space each instance is assigned the label it is nearest to. We outline and analyze an algorithm, termed Bunching, for learning the pair of embeddings from labeled data. A key construction in the analysis of the algorithm is the notion of probabilistic output codes, a generaliza- tion of error correcting output codes (ECOC). Furthermore, the method of multiclass categorization using ECOC is shown to be an instance of Bunching. We demonstrate the advantage of Bunching over ECOC by comparing their performance on numerous categorization problems.

paragraphs: This paper approaches multiclass classification by learning representations for both examples and class labels. Two embeddings place them in a common space, and an example receives the label located nearest to it. Classification therefore depends on the geometry of the learned representations and on how the two mappings fit together.

The authors introduce and analyze Bunching, an algorithm that learns this pair of embeddings from labeled data. A central element of the analysis is probabilistic output codes, which generalize error-correcting output codes. This construction broadens the coding framework while retaining a connection to an established approach to multiclass learning.

The paper shows that multiclass categorization with error-correcting output codes is a special case of Bunching. Comparisons across numerous categorization problems demonstrate an advantage for Bunching over that method. The findings support learning within the broader framework on the problems studied, while the special-case relationship explains precisely how the new approach encompasses an existing one.
summary.tldr: Bunching learns a shared space for examples and labels, generalizing error-correcting output codes and outperforming them in reported comparisons.

title: Multiclass Learning by Probabilistic Embeddings

abstract: Given a set of hidden variables with an a-priori Markov structure, we derive an online algorithm which approximately updates the posterior as pairwise measurements between the hidden variables become available. The update is performed using Assumed Density Filtering: to incorporate each pairwise measurement, we compute the optimal Markov structure which represents the true posterior and use it as a prior for incorporating the next measurement. We demonstrate the resulting algorithm by cal- culating globally consistent trajectories of a robot as it navigates along a 2D trajectory. To update a trajectory of length t, the update takes O(t). When all conditional distributions are linear-Gaussian, the algorithm can be thought of as a Kalman Filter which simpliﬁes the state covariance matrix after incorporating each measurement.

The update is performed using Assumed Density Filtering: to incorporate each pairwise measurement, we compute the optimal Markov structure which represents the true posterior and use it as a prior for incorporating the next measurement. We demonstrate the resulting algorithm by cal- culating globally consistent trajectories of a robot as it navigates along a 2D trajectory. To update a trajectory of length t, the update takes O(t). paragraphs: The paper develops an online method for updating beliefs about hidden variables as pairwise measurements arrive. It begins with a prior Markov structure among those variables. Each new measurement changes the posterior, and the algorithm approximately updates that distribution while maintaining a structured representation.

The update uses Assumed Density Filtering. After incorporating a pairwise measurement, the method computes an optimal Markov representation of the posterior and uses that representation as the prior for the next measurement. This repeated approximation allows measurements to be processed sequentially rather than requiring a new unrestricted posterior representation at every step.

The authors demonstrate the algorithm by estimating globally consistent trajectories for a robot moving in two dimensions. Updating a trajectory of length t takes O(t) time, so the stated update cost grows linearly with trajectory length. When all conditional distributions are linear-Gaussian, the method can be interpreted as a Kalman filter that simplifies its state covariance matrix after each measurement. This provides a familiar interpretation of the approximation in that special case.
summary.tldr: An online filtering method maintains an approximate Markov posterior from pairwise measurements and demonstrates linear-time updates for robot trajectories.

title: Location Estimation with a Differential Update Network

abstract: Accurate representation of articulated motion is a challenging problem for machine perception. Several successful tracking algorithms have been developed that model human body as an articulated tree. We pro- pose a learning-based method for creating such articulated models from observations of multiple rigid motions. This paper is concerned with recovering topology of the articulated model, when the rigid motion of constituent segments is known. Our approach is based on ﬁnding the Maximum Likelihood tree shaped factorization of the joint probability density function (PDF) of rigid segment motions. The topology of graph- ical model formed from this factorization corresponds to topology of the underlying articulated body. We demonstrate the performance of our al- gorithm on both synthetic and real motion capture data.

We pro- pose a learning-based method for creating such articulated models from observations of multiple rigid motions. This paper is concerned with recovering topology of the articulated model, when the rigid motion of constituent segments is known. paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover the connection structure of an articulated body from observations of its moving parts. Such structures are often represented as trees in human-body tracking. Here, the rigid motion of each constituent segment is assumed to be known; the task is to learn how those segments are connected.

The authors search for a maximum-likelihood tree-shaped factorization of the joint probability distribution of segment motions. In plain terms, they choose a tree-structured statistical description that best accounts for the observed motions under their model. The topology of the resulting graphical model corresponds to the topology of the articulated body.

The method is demonstrated on both synthetic data and real motion-capture data. Its contribution is a learning-based route from observed segment motions to an articulated connection structure. The known-motion assumption is essential to understanding the scope: the method addresses recovery of the tree topology once segment motions are available, rather than presenting the entire process of extracting and tracking those segments from raw observations.
summary.tldr: Given known rigid-segment motions, the method learns an articulated body's topology through a maximum-likelihood tree factorization.

title: Recovering Articulated Model Topology from Observed Rigid Motion

abstract: We consider the task of depth estimation from a single monocular image. We take a supervised learning approach to this problem, in which we begin by collecting a training set of monocular images (of unstructured outdoor environments which include forests, trees, buildings, etc.) and their corresponding ground-truth depthmaps. Then, we apply supervised learning to predict the depthmap as a function of the image. Depth estimation is a challenging problem, since local features alone are insufficient to estimate depth at a point, and one needs to consider the global context of the image. Our model uses a discriminatively-trained Markov Random Field (MRF) that incorporates multiscale local- and global-image features, and models both depths at individual points as well as the relation between depths at different points. We show that, even on unstructured scenes, our algorithm is frequently able to recover fairly accurate depthmaps.

paragraphs: The paper learns to estimate scene depth from a single image. Its training data pair monocular photographs with corresponding ground-truth depth maps, covering unstructured outdoor environments such as forests, trees, and buildings. Supervised learning then connects the appearance of an image to the depth values the model should predict.

The authors emphasize that local image features alone do not provide enough information to estimate depth at a point. Their discriminatively trained Markov random field therefore incorporates image features at multiple scales, including both local evidence and global context. It models individual depth values together with relationships between depths at different image locations.

This combination matters because depth predictions at separate points need to be interpreted in the context of the wider scene. The reported results show that the algorithm frequently recovers fairly accurate depth maps, even for unstructured scenes. The finding supports the usefulness of learning contextual and relational information for monocular depth estimation, with the stated success remaining frequent and approximate rather than universal or exact.
summary.tldr: A supervised Markov random field combines multiscale image context and depth relationships to frequently recover fairly accurate depth maps from single outdoor images.

title: Learning Depth from Single Monocular Images

abstract: We focus on the problem of estimating the graph structure associated with a discrete Markov random ﬁeld. We describe a method based on 1- regularized logistic regression, in which the neighborhood of any given node is estimated by performing logistic regression subject to an 1-constraint. Our framework applies to the high-dimensional setting, in which both the number of nodes p and maximum neighborhood sizes d are allowed to grow as a function of the number of observations n. Our main result is to estab- lish suﬃcient conditions on the triple (n, p, d) for the method to succeed in consistently estimating the neighborhood of every node in the graph simul- taneously. Under certain mutual incoherence conditions analogous to those imposed in previous work on linear regression, we prove that consistent neighborhood selection can be obtained as long as the number of observa- tions n grows more quickly than 6d6 log d + 2d5 log p, thereby establishing that logarithmic growth in the number of samples n relative to graph size p is suﬃcient to achieve neighborhood consistency. Keywords: Graphical models; Markov random ﬁelds; structure learning; `1-regularization; model selection; convex risk minimization; high-dimensional asymptotics; concentration.

Keywords: Graphical models; Markov random ﬁelds; structure learning; `1-regularization; model selection; convex risk minimization; high-dimensional asymptotics; concentration.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to recover the graph of a discrete Markov random field from observations. It estimates each node's neighborhood using logistic regression with an l1 constraint. The neighborhood estimates identify which other nodes are connected to each node, turning graph recovery into a collection of constrained regression problems.

The analysis allows both the number of nodes, p, and the largest neighborhood size, d, to increase with the number of observations, n. Its main result gives sufficient conditions for consistently recovering every neighborhood simultaneously. This addresses an entire growing graph, rather than guaranteeing accuracy only for one selected node.

Under mutual incoherence conditions, the authors show consistency when n grows faster than 6 d^6 log d + 2 d^5 log p. The logarithmic dependence on p is favorable, but the expression also has a substantial dependence on neighborhood size. Thus, the result establishes conditional sample sufficiency, with graph size and connectivity playing distinct roles. It does not establish that this observation count is necessary.
summary.tldr: Constrained logistic regressions can consistently recover a growing graph under stated incoherence and sample-growth conditions.

title: High-Dimensional Graphical Model Selection Using $\ell_1$-Regularized Logistic Regression

abstract: Many tasks (e.g., clustering) in machine learning only require the lα distances in- stead of the original data. For dimension reductions in the lα norm (0 < α ≤ 2), the method of stable random projections can efﬁciently compute the lα distances in massive datasets (e.g., the Web or massive data streams) in one pass of the data. The estimation task for stable random projections has been an interesting topic. We propose a simple estimator based on the fractional power of the samples (pro- jected data), which is surprisingly near-optimal in terms of the asymptotic vari- ance. In fact, it achieves the Cram´er-Rao bound when α = 2 and α = 0+. This new result will be useful when applying stable random projections to distance- based clustering, classiﬁcations, kernels, massive data streams etc.

paragraphs: Many learning tasks need distances between observations rather than the original observations themselves. This paper studies how to estimate those distances after stable random projections compress the data. The setting covers l-alpha distances for alpha greater than zero and at most two, with massive datasets and data streams motivating the need for efficient processing.

Stable random projections can support distance computation in a single pass through the data. The paper's contribution concerns the estimation step: how to turn projected samples into an accurate distance estimate. It proposes a simple estimator based on fractional powers of those samples, providing one approach across the stated range of alpha.

The reported near-optimality concerns asymptotic variance, which describes estimation variability in the large-sample regime. At alpha equal to two and in the limit as alpha approaches zero from above, the estimator reaches the Cramér–Rao bound. These findings support its use in distance-based clustering, classification, kernels, and streaming applications; the stated optimality is tied to that statistical criterion and those particular endpoint cases.
summary.tldr: A fractional-power estimator recovers distances from stable random projections with near-optimal asymptotic variance.

title: A Unified Near-Optimal Estimator For Dimension Reduction in $l_\alpha$ ($0<\alpha\leq 2$) Using Stable Random Projections

abstract: Social tags are user-generated keywords associated with some resource on the Web. In the case of music, social tags have become an important component of Web2.0" recommender systems, allowing users to generate playlists based on use-dependent terms such as "chill" or "jogging" that have been applied to particular songs. In this paper, we propose a method for predicting these social tags directly from MP3 files. Using a set of boosted classifiers, we map audio features onto social tags collected from the Web. The resulting automatic tags (or "autotags") furnish information about music that is otherwise untagged or poorly tagged, allowing for insertion of previously unheard music into a social recommender. This avoids the ''cold-start problem'' common in such systems. Autotags can also be used to smooth the tag space from which similarities and recommendations are made by providing a set of comparable baseline tags for all tracks in a recommender system."

Autotags can also be used to smooth the tag space from which similarities and recommendations are made by providing a set of comparable baseline tags for all tracks in a recommender system."

paragraphs: Music recommendation systems can use listener-supplied tags to organize songs around activities or moods. But tracks with few or no tags are difficult to place within that system. This paper proposes predicting social tags directly from MP3 audio, giving otherwise poorly described music an entry point into a tag-based recommender.

The method uses boosted classifiers to map audio features to tags gathered from the Web. Its output is a set of automatic tags, or autotags, describing a track in the vocabulary already used by the social recommendation system. The connection between sound and user-created descriptions lets the system supply tag information before listeners have provided it.

The authors describe two uses for these predictions. Autotags allow previously unheard music to enter the recommender, addressing the cold-start problem caused by missing tags. They can also provide comparable baseline descriptions across all tracks, smoothing the tag space used to compute similarities and recommendations. This second use concerns consistency across the catalog, including music that already has some human annotations.
summary.tldr: Boosted classifiers predict social music tags from audio to introduce untagged songs into recommenders and provide consistent catalog descriptions.

title: Automatic Generation of Social Tags for Music Recommendation

abstract: Current object recognition systems can only recognize a limited number of object categories; scaling up to many categories is the next challenge. We seek to build a system to recognize and localize many different object categories in complex scenes. We achieve this through a simple approach: by matching the input im- age, in an appropriate representation, to images in a large training set of labeled images. Due to regularities in object identities across similar scenes, the retrieved matches provide hypotheses for object identities and locations. We build a prob- abilistic model to transfer the labels from the retrieval set to the input image. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach and study algorithm component contributions using held-out test sets from the LabelMe database.

paragraphs: Recognizing many object categories in complex scenes requires deciding both what objects are present and where they are located. This paper approaches that task by comparing an input image with a large collection of labeled training images. The comparison uses an image representation chosen to support matching between scenes.

The approach relies on regularities across similar scenes: retrieved images can suggest plausible object identities and locations in the new image. A probabilistic model then transfers labels from the retrieved set to the input. Retrieval therefore supplies candidate explanations, while the probabilistic transfer stage turns those examples into recognition and localization predictions.

The authors demonstrate effectiveness on held-out test sets from the LabelMe database and examine the contributions of individual algorithm components. These evaluations support scene alignment as a practical route toward recognizing many categories. The core idea is to make previously labeled scenes useful as structured evidence: their object arrangements provide information that can be transferred when the system encounters a similar new scene.
summary.tldr: Matching a new image to labeled scenes and probabilistically transferring their labels supports recognition and localization across many object categories.

title: Object Recognition by Scene Alignment

abstract: Hierarchical penalization is a generic framework for incorporating prior informa- tion in the ﬁtting of statistical models, when the explicative variables are organized in a hierarchical structure. The penalizer is a convex functional that performs soft selection at the group level, and shrinks variables within each group. This favors solutions with few leading terms in the ﬁnal combination. The framework, orig- inally derived for taking prior knowledge into account, is shown to be useful in linear regression, when several parameters are used to model the inﬂuence of one feature, or in kernel regression, for learning multiple kernels. Keywords – Optimization: constrained and convex optimization. Supervised learning: regression, kernel methods, sparsity and feature selection.

paragraphs: Statistical models often use explanatory variables that have a meaningful hierarchical organization. The paper introduces a general way to incorporate that organization into model fitting. Prior information enters through a penalty, allowing the relationship among variables to influence which parts of the model receive substantial weight.

The proposed penalty is convex and operates at two connected levels. It performs soft selection among groups while shrinking the variables within each group. This favors solutions with only a few leading terms in the final combination, making the hierarchy relevant both to group importance and to the contributions of individual variables.

The authors show the framework's usefulness in linear regression when several parameters together describe the influence of one feature. They also apply it to kernel regression for learning multiple kernels. These applications illustrate why grouping matters: the meaningful unit of explanation can span several parameters. Hierarchical penalization provides a common fitting framework for using that structure, while its convex formulation connects the statistical objective to a tractable class of optimization problems.
summary.tldr: A convex hierarchical penalty uses prior variable groupings to softly select groups and shrink their members in regression models.

title: Hierarchical Penalization

abstract: Applications of multi-class classification, such as document categorization, often appear in cost-sensitive settings. Recent work has significantly improved the state of the art by moving beyond ``flat'' classification through incorporation of class hierarchies [Cai and Hoffman 04]. We present a novel algorithm that goes beyond hierarchical classification and estimates the latent semantic space that underlies the class hierarchy. In this space, each class is represented by a prototype and classification is done with the simple nearest neighbor rule. The optimization of the semantic space incorporates large margin constraints that ensure that for each instance the correct class prototype is closer than any other. We show that our optimization is convex and can be solved efficiently for large data sets. Experiments on the OHSUMED medical journal data base yield state-of-the-art results on topic categorization.

paragraphs: Document categorization often involves classes arranged in a hierarchy and settings where different mistakes carry different costs. This paper uses the hierarchy to estimate an underlying semantic space. The aim is to learn a representation that supports classification while reflecting relationships among the categories.

Each class is represented by a prototype in the learned space, and a document is classified using the nearest prototype. Large-margin constraints require the correct class prototype to be closer to each training instance than competing prototypes. This connects the geometry of the representation directly to the classification decision: distances are learned to separate the correct category from alternatives.

The authors show that the optimization is convex and can be solved efficiently on large datasets. Experiments on the OHSUMED medical journal database achieve state-of-the-art topic categorization results. The contribution combines a learned semantic representation, a simple nearest-neighbor decision rule, and a tractable optimization formulation. The reported results support this combination for the evaluated medical-document categorization task.
summary.tldr: A convex large-margin method embeds document categories as semantic prototypes and classifies documents by their nearest prototype.

title: Large Margin Taxonomy Embedding for Document Categorization

abstract: Sequential decision-making with multiple agents and imperfect information is commonly modeled as an extensive game. One efficient method for computing Nash equilibria in large, zero-sum, imperfect information games is counterfactual regret minimization (CFR). In the domain of poker, CFR has proven effective, particularly when using a domain-specific augmentation involving chance outcome sampling. In this paper, we describe a general family of domain independent CFR sample-based algorithms called Monte Carlo counterfactual regret minimization (MCCFR) of which the original and poker-specific versions are special cases. We start by showing that MCCFR performs the same regret updates as CFR on expectation. Then, we introduce two sampling schemes: {\it outcome sampling} and {\it external sampling}, showing that both have bounded overall regret with high probability. Thus, they can compute an approximate equilibrium using self-play. Finally, we prove a new tighter bound on the regret for the original CFR algorithm and relate this new bound to MCCFRs bounds. We show empirically that, although the sample-based algorithms require more iterations, their lower cost per iteration can lead to dramatically faster convergence in various games.

This paper develops a general sampling-based family, MCCFR, encompassing both original CFR and a poker-specific sampling approach.

The contribution combines a domain-independent sampling framework with theoretical guarantees and evidence that cheaper updates can outweigh the need for additional iterations.
summary.tldr: Monte Carlo CFR uses cheaper sampled regret updates with high-probability guarantees and can reach approximate equilibria much faster.

title: Monte Carlo Sampling for Regret Minimization in Extensive Games

abstract: We introduce a new type of Deep Belief Net and evaluate it on a 3D object recognition task. The top-level model is a third-order Boltzmann machine, trained using a hybrid algorithm that combines both generative and discriminative gradients. Performance is evaluated on the NORB database(normalized-uniform version), which contains stereo-pair images of objects under different lighting conditions and viewpoints. Our model achieves 6.5% error on the test set, which is close to the best published result for NORB (5.9%) using a convolutional neural net that has built-in knowledge of translation invariance. It substantially outperforms shallow models such as SVMs (11.6%). DBNs are especially suited for semi-supervised learning, and to demonstrate this we consider a modified version of the NORB recognition task in which additional unlabeled images are created by applying small translations to the images in the database. With the extra unlabeled data (and the same amount of labeled data as before), our model achieves 5.2% error, making it the current best result for NORB.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a deep belief network for recognizing three-dimensional objects from images. Its highest layer uses a third-order Boltzmann machine, and training combines generative and discriminative gradients. This joins learning about the image data with learning to distinguish object classes within the same training approach.

The authors evaluate the model on the normalized-uniform NORB dataset, containing stereo image pairs with varying viewpoints and lighting. The model records 6.5% test error, compared with 11.6% for the cited shallow SVM models. Its result approaches the cited 5.9% convolutional-network result, whose architecture incorporates knowledge of translation invariance.

The authors also modify the task by adding unlabeled images generated through small translations of existing images. Keeping the amount of labeled data fixed, they obtain 5.2% error, reported as the best NORB result at the time. The distinction between these evaluations matters: the lower error uses additional unlabeled data. Together, the results demonstrate the proposed architecture's recognition performance and its ability to benefit from that semi-supervised training setup.
summary.tldr: A deep belief network recognizes NORB objects effectively and improves further when trained with additional translated, unlabeled images.

title: 3D Object Recognition with Deep Belief Nets

abstract: Several key problems in machine learning, such as feature selection and active learning, can be formulated as submodular set function maximization. We present herein a novel algorithm for maximizing a submodular set function under a cardinality constraint --- the algorithm is based on a cutting-plane method and is implemented as an iterative small-scale binary-integer linear programming procedure. It is well known that this problem is NP-hard, and the approximation factor achieved by the greedy algorithm is the theoretical limit for polynomial time. As for (non-polynomial time) exact algorithms that perform reasonably in practice, there has been very little in the literature although the problem is quite important for many applications. Our algorithm is guaranteed to find the exact solution in finite iterations, and it converges fast in practice due to the efficiency of the cutting-plane mechanism. Moreover, we also provide a method that produces successively decreasing upper-bounds of the optimal solution, while our algorithm provides successively increasing lower-bounds. Thus, the accuracy of the current solution can be estimated at any point, and the algorithm can be stopped early once a desired degree of tolerance is met. We evaluate our algorithm on sensor placement and feature selection applications showing good performance.

paragraphs: The paper addresses maximizing a submodular set function while limiting how many items can be selected. This formulation appears in applications such as feature selection and active learning. The optimization problem is NP-hard, motivating methods that can pursue exact solutions while also reporting how good an unfinished solution is.

The proposed algorithm uses a cutting-plane approach implemented through repeated small binary-integer linear programs. It is guaranteed to reach an exact solution after finitely many iterations, and the authors report fast convergence in practice. This is an exact optimization method whose finite-termination guarantee does not amount to a polynomial-time guarantee.

A complementary procedure supplies decreasing upper bounds on the optimal objective value, while the main algorithm supplies increasing lower bounds. The gap between them indicates the remaining uncertainty about solution quality. This allows computation to stop once a desired tolerance is met, rather than always waiting for exact completion. Evaluations on sensor placement and feature selection show good performance, illustrating the value of combining exact search with usable progress certificates.
summary.tldr: A cutting-plane algorithm exactly solves cardinality-constrained submodular maximization and provides bounds that support early stopping at a chosen tolerance.

title: Submodularity Cuts and Applications

abstract: Metric constraints are known to be highly discriminative for many objects, but if training is limited to data captured from a particular 3-D sensor the quantity of training data may be severly limited. In this paper, we show how a crucial aspect of 3-D information–object and feature absolute size–can be added to models learned from commonly available online imagery, without use of any 3-D sensing or re- construction at training time. Such models can be utilized at test time together with explicit 3-D sensing to perform robust search. Our model uses a “2.1D” local feature, which combines traditional appearance gradient statistics with an estimate of average absolute depth within the local window. We show how category size information can be obtained from online images by exploiting relatively unbiquitous metadata fields specifying camera intrinstics. We develop an efficient metric branch-and-bound algorithm for our search task, imposing 3-D size constraints as part of an optimal search for a set of features which indicate the presence of a category. Experiments on test scenes captured with a traditional stereo rig are shown, exploiting training data from from purely monocular sources with associated EXIF metadata.

paragraphs: This paper asks how object recognition can use absolute physical size without requiring training images from a specialized three-dimensional sensor. Size can help distinguish objects, but restricting training to such sensors can limit the available examples. The authors instead obtain category size information from ordinary online images with camera-intrinsic metadata.

The model uses a local feature described as 2.1D, combining appearance-gradient statistics with an estimate of average absolute depth in the feature window. Training uses monocular imagery and associated EXIF metadata, without three-dimensional sensing or reconstruction. At test time, the learned model is paired with explicit three-dimensional sensing so that physical size can constrain the search.

The authors develop an efficient metric branch-and-bound algorithm that incorporates three-dimensional size constraints while optimally searching for a set of category-indicating features. Experiments use test scenes captured with a conventional stereo rig. The contribution connects readily available training imagery with metric information at deployment, allowing size-sensitive search without requiring the training collection itself to come from a three-dimensional sensor.
summary.tldr: Camera metadata adds absolute-size information to models trained on monocular images for size-constrained visual search with three-dimensional sensing at test time.

title: Size Matters: Metric Visual Search Constraints from Monocular Metadata

abstract: We present a dynamic nonlinear generative model for visual motion based on a latent representation of binary-gated Gaussian variables. Trained on sequences of images, the model learns to represent different movement directions in different variables. We use an online approximate-inference scheme that can be mapped to the dynamics of networks of neurons. Probed with drifting grating stimuli and moving bars of light, neurons in the model show patterns of responses analogous to those of direction-selective simple cells in primary visual cortex. Most model neurons also show speed tuning and respond equally well to a range of motion directions and speeds aligned to the constraint line of their respective preferred speed. We show how these computations are enabled by a specific pattern of recurrent connections learned by the model.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a dynamic nonlinear generative model that learns visual motion from image sequences. Its hidden representation uses Gaussian variables controlled by binary gates. Through training, different variables come to represent different directions of movement, linking the model's internal organization to structure in the visual input.

The authors use an online approximate-inference procedure that can be expressed through the dynamics of a neural network. When tested with drifting gratings and moving bars of light, model neurons show response patterns analogous to direction-selective simple cells in primary visual cortex. This is a comparison of response behavior between the model and those biological cells.

Most model neurons also exhibit speed tuning. They respond comparably across combinations of motion direction and speed lying along the constraint line associated with their preferred speed. The paper connects these computations to a particular pattern of recurrent connections learned during training, explaining how the network's learned interactions support its observed motion responses.
summary.tldr: A recurrent generative model learns motion representations and develops direction- and speed-sensitive responses resembling those of visual cortical cells.

title: Learning visual motion in recurrent neural networks

abstract: The Lovasz $\theta$ function of a graph, is a fundamental tool in combinatorial optimization and approximation algorithms. Computing $\theta$ involves solving a SDP and is extremely expensive even for moderately sized graphs. In this paper we establish that the Lovasz $\theta$ function is equivalent to a kernel learning problem related to one class SVM. This interesting connection opens up many opportunities bridging graph theoretic algorithms and machine learning. We show that there exist graphs, which we call $SVM-\theta$ graphs, on which the Lovasz $\theta$ function can be approximated well by a one-class SVM. This leads to a novel use of SVM techniques to solve algorithmic problems in large graphs e.g. identifying a planted clique of size $\Theta({\sqrt{n}})$ in a random graph $G(n,\frac{1}{2})$. A classic approach for this problem involves computing the $\theta$ function, however it is not scalable due to SDP computation. We show that the random graph with a planted clique is an example of $SVM-\theta$ graph, and as a consequence a SVM based approach easily identifies the clique in large graphs and is competitive with the state-of-the-art. Further, we introduce the notion of a ''common orthogonal labeling'' which extends the notion of a ''orthogonal labelling of a single graph (used in defining the $\theta$ function) to multiple graphs. The problem of finding the optimal common orthogonal labelling is cast as a Multiple Kernel Learning problem and is used to identify a large common dense region in multiple graphs. The proposed algorithm achieves an order of magnitude scalability compared to the state of the art.

paragraphs: The Lovász theta function is useful in graph optimization, but computing it through semidefinite programming can be expensive even for moderately sized graphs. The paper establishes an equivalence between this function and a kernel-learning problem related to one-class support vector machines, creating a connection between graph algorithms and machine learning.

The authors identify a class of graphs, called SVM-theta graphs, on which a one-class SVM can approximate theta well. A random graph with a planted clique of size proportional to the square root of the vertex count belongs to this class. Their SVM approach identifies the clique in large graphs and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods.

Finding the optimal shared labeling becomes a multiple-kernel-learning problem used to locate a large dense region common to several graphs. The authors report an order-of-magnitude scalability improvement for the proposed algorithm, illustrating how these mathematical connections can enable larger graph analyses.
summary.tldr: Connections between the Lovász theta function and kernel learning enable scalable SVM approaches to planted cliques and shared dense graph regions.

title: The Lovász ϑ function, SVMs and finding large dense subgraphs

abstract: Memristive devices have recently been proposed as efficient implementations of plastic synapses in neuromorphic systems. The plasticity in these memristive devices, i.e. their resistance change, is defined by the applied waveforms. This behavior resembles biological synapses, whose plasticity is also triggered by mechanisms that are determined by local waveforms. However, learning in memristive devices has so far been approached mostly on a pragmatic technological level. The focus seems to be on finding any waveform that achieves spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), without regard to the biological veracity of said waveforms or to further important forms of plasticity. Bridging this gap, we make use of a plasticity model driven by neuron waveforms that explains a large number of experimental observations and adapt it to the characteristics of the recently introduced BiFeO$_3$ memristive material. Based on this approach, we show STDP for the first time for this material, with learning window replication superior to previous memristor-based STDP implementations. We also demonstrate in measurements that it is possible to overlay short and long term plasticity at a memristive device in the form of the well-known triplet plasticity. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first implementations of triplet plasticity on any physical memristive device.

Many implementations had focused on finding waveforms that produce spike-timing-dependent plasticity, without closely matching biological waveforms or addressing other forms of plasticity. This paper uses a biologically motivated model to guide the device behavior.

The authors adapt a neuron-waveform-driven plasticity model to BiFeO3 memristive material. The model had explained a broad range of experimental observations. The contribution connects a biologically grounded waveform model to measured device behavior, showing that the hardware can express more than one relevant form of synaptic change.
summary.tldr: A biologically motivated waveform model enables timing-dependent and triplet plasticity in BiFeO3 memristive devices.

title: Waveform Driven Plasticity in BiFeO3 Memristive Devices: Model and Implementation

abstract: What if there is a teacher who knows the learning goal and wants to design good training data for a machine learner? We propose an optimal teaching framework aimed at learners who employ Bayesian models. Our framework is expressed as an optimization problem over teaching examples that balance the future loss of the learner and the effort of the teacher. This optimization problem is in general hard. In the case where the learner employs conjugate exponential family models, we present an approximate algorithm for finding the optimal teaching set. Our algorithm optimizes the aggregate sufficient statistics, then unpacks them into actual teaching examples. We give several examples to illustrate our framework.

We propose an optimal teaching framework aimed at learners who employ Bayesian models. Our framework is expressed as an optimization problem over teaching examples that balance the future loss of the learner and the effort of the teacher. This optimization problem is in general hard. In the case where the learner employs conjugate exponential family models, we present an approximate algorithm for finding the optimal teaching set. Our algorithm optimizes the aggregate sufficient statistics, then unpacks them into actual teaching examples. We give several examples to illustrate our framework.

paragraphs: This paper considers learning from the teacher's perspective. A teacher knows the intended learning goal and can design training examples for a Bayesian learner. The question is which examples to provide when both the learner's eventual errors and the effort required to teach matter. The authors express this tradeoff as an optimization problem over teaching data.

The general optimization problem is difficult. For learners using conjugate exponential-family models, the paper develops an approximate algorithm that first works with aggregate sufficient statistics. These statistics summarize the information from examples that is relevant to the model. Optimizing the summary provides an intermediate representation of the teaching set.

The algorithm then unpacks the optimized statistics into actual examples that can be shown to the learner. Several examples illustrate the framework. Its contribution is a concrete way to connect a desired learning outcome to deliberately constructed training data, while accounting for teaching effort. The approximate solution applies to the specified model family rather than solving the general teaching problem exactly.
summary.tldr: An optimal-teaching framework balances Bayesian learner error and teaching effort, with an approximate algorithm based on sufficient statistics for conjugate exponential-family models.

title: Machine Teaching for Bayesian Learners in the Exponential Family

abstract: Multitask learning can be effective when features useful in one task are also useful for other tasks, and the group lasso is a standard method for selecting a common subset of features. In this paper, we are interested in a less restrictive form of multitask learning, wherein (1) the available features can be organized into subsets according to a notion of similarity and (2) features useful in one task are similar, but not necessarily identical, to the features best suited for other tasks. The main contribution of this paper is a new procedure called {\em Sparse Overlapping Sets (SOS) lasso}, a convex optimization that automatically selects similar features for related learning tasks. Error bounds are derived for SOSlasso and its consistency is established for squared error loss. In particular, SOSlasso is motivated by multi-subject fMRI studies in which functional activity is classified using brain voxels as features. Experiments with real and synthetic data demonstrate the advantages of SOSlasso compared to the lasso and group lasso.

This paper considers a setting where features can be grouped by similarity and related tasks may need similar, rather than identical, features.

Sparse Overlapping Sets lasso turns that idea into a convex optimization procedure that automatically selects related features across tasks. Its motivating application is multi-subject fMRI analysis, where brain voxels serve as features for classifying functional activity. The formulation allows useful features to differ between tasks while still exploiting their organization into similar sets.

The authors derive error bounds and establish consistency for squared-error loss. Experiments on real and synthetic data show advantages over lasso and group lasso. The contribution is a less restrictive form of feature sharing with both statistical analysis and empirical support: tasks can benefit from common structure without requiring their selected features to coincide exactly.
summary.tldr: SOS lasso uses convex optimization to share similar features across tasks, with error guarantees and advantages in fMRI-motivated experiments.

title: Sparse Overlapping Sets Lasso for Multitask Learning and its Application to fMRI Analysis

abstract: Sparse Subspace Clustering (SSC) and Low-Rank Representation (LRR) are both considered as the state-of-the-art methods for {\em subspace clustering}. The two methods are fundamentally similar in that both are convex optimizations exploiting the intuition of Self-Expressiveness''. The main difference is that SSC minimizes the vector $\ell_1$ norm of the representation matrix to induce sparsity while LRR minimizes nuclear norm (aka trace norm) to promote a low-rank structure. Because the representation matrix is often simultaneously sparse and low-rank, we propose a new algorithm, termed Low-Rank Sparse Subspace Clustering (LRSSC), by combining SSC and LRR, and develops theoretical guarantees of when the algorithm succeeds. The results reveal interesting insights into the strength and weakness of SSC and LRR and demonstrate how LRSSC can take the advantages of both methods in preserving the "Self-Expressiveness Property'' and "Graph Connectivity'' at the same time."

paragraphs: Sparse Subspace Clustering and Low-Rank Representation approach clustering through a shared idea: data points can be represented using other points. They encourage different properties in the resulting representation matrix. The former promotes sparsity through an L1 penalty, while the latter promotes low rank through a nuclear-norm penalty.

This paper observes that a representation matrix can possess both properties at once. It proposes Low-Rank Sparse Subspace Clustering, which combines the two approaches, and develops theoretical guarantees describing when the combined algorithm succeeds. The motivation is to use complementary structural preferences within a single clustering method.

The analysis clarifies strengths and weaknesses of the original methods, particularly around preserving self-expressiveness and graph connectivity. A useful representation must support the intended subspace relationships while also connecting points in a way that supports clustering. The results show how the combined approach can obtain advantages from both methods with respect to these properties. Its success is characterized by theoretical conditions, rather than asserted for every possible dataset.
summary.tldr: Low-Rank Sparse Subspace Clustering combines sparsity and low-rank penalties, with guarantees explaining when it preserves useful representation and connectivity properties.

title: Provable Subspace Clustering: When LRR meets SSC

abstract: We investigate a general framework of multiplicative multitask feature learning which decomposes each task's model parameters into a multiplication of two components. One of the components is used across all tasks and the other component is task-specific. Several previous methods have been proposed as special cases of our framework. We study the theoretical properties of this framework when different regularization conditions are applied to the two decomposed components. We prove that this framework is mathematically equivalent to the widely used multitask feature learning methods that are based on a joint regularization of all model parameters, but with a more general form of regularizers. Further, an analytical formula is derived for the across-task component as related to the task-specific component for all these regularizers, leading to a better understanding of the shrinkage effect. Study of this framework motivates new multitask learning algorithms. We propose two new learning formulations by varying the parameters in the proposed framework. Empirical studies have revealed the relative advantages of the two new formulations by comparing with the state of the art, which provides instructive insights into the feature learning problem with multiple tasks.

paragraphs: Multitask feature learning seeks useful representations across related prediction tasks. This paper studies a framework that expresses each task's model parameters as the product of a shared component and a task-specific component. Several earlier methods fit within this formulation, making it a common basis for examining how sharing and individual task behavior interact.

The authors analyze different regularization choices for the two components. They prove an equivalence with approaches that jointly regularize all task parameters, while allowing a more general family of regularizers. They also derive an analytical relationship between the shared and task-specific components, clarifying how regularization shrinks parameters within the multiplicative representation.

The analysis motivates two new learning formulations obtained by varying the framework's parameters. Empirical comparisons with state-of-the-art methods reveal relative advantages of these formulations. The paper's contribution is therefore both explanatory and constructive: it connects existing approaches through a mathematical framework and uses that connection to develop further choices for learning features across multiple tasks.
summary.tldr: A multiplicative framework connects shared and task-specific feature learning to joint regularization and motivates two new formulations.

title: On Multiplicative Multitask Feature Learning

abstract: In a multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem a gambler needs to choose at each round of play one of K arms, each characterized by an unknown reward distribution. Reward realizations are only observed when an arm is selected, and the gambler's objective is to maximize his cumulative expected earnings over some given horizon of play T. To do this, the gambler needs to acquire information about arms (exploration) while simultaneously optimizing immediate rewards (exploitation); the price paid due to this trade off is often referred to as the regret, and the main question is how small can this price be as a function of the horizon length T. This problem has been studied extensively when the reward distributions do not change over time; an assumption that supports a sharp characterization of the regret, yet is often violated in practical settings. In this paper, we focus on a MAB formulation which allows for a broad range of temporal uncertainties in the rewards, while still maintaining mathematical tractability. We fully characterize the (regret) complexity of this class of MAB problems by establishing a direct link between the extent of allowable reward variation" and the minimal achievable regret, and by establishing a connection between the adversarial and the stochastic MAB frameworks."

We fully characterize the (regret) complexity of this class of MAB problems by establishing a direct link between the extent of allowable reward variation" and the minimal achievable regret, and by establishing a connection between the adversarial and the stochastic MAB frameworks."

paragraphs: In a multi-armed bandit problem, a decision-maker repeatedly chooses among options with unknown rewards and observes a reward only for the chosen option. Learning which options are promising competes with earning rewards immediately. This paper studies that tradeoff when reward distributions can change over time, rather than remaining fixed throughout play.

The authors introduce a formulation that accommodates a broad range of temporal uncertainty while remaining mathematically tractable. The central quantity is the amount of reward variation the setting permits. This makes environmental change part of the problem’s complexity, alongside the challenge of learning from feedback available only for selected actions.

The paper fully characterizes regret complexity for the class it studies by linking allowable reward variation to the smallest achievable regret. It also establishes a connection between stochastic and adversarial bandit frameworks. The result gives a theoretical account of how changing rewards affect the best possible learning performance, replacing the fixed-distribution assumption with an explicit relationship between variation and achievable regret.
summary.tldr: A non-stationary bandit formulation characterizes how allowable reward variation determines minimal achievable regret and connects stochastic and adversarial settings.

title: Stochastic Multi-Armed-Bandit Problem with Non-stationary Rewards

abstract: Dynamics-based sampling methods, such as Hybrid Monte Carlo (HMC) and Langevin dynamics (LD), are commonly used to sample target distributions. Recently, such approaches have been combined with stochastic gradient techniques to increase sampling efficiency when dealing with large datasets. An outstanding problem with this approach is that the stochastic gradient introduces an unknown amount of noise which can prevent proper sampling after discretization. To remedy this problem, we show that one can leverage a small number of additional variables in order to stabilize momentum fluctuations induced by the unknown noise. Our method is inspired by the idea of a thermostat in statistical physics and is justified by a general theory.

Recently, such approaches have been combined with stochastic gradient techniques to increase sampling efficiency when dealing with large datasets. An outstanding problem with this approach is that the stochastic gradient introduces an unknown amount of noise which can prevent proper sampling after discretization. To remedy this problem, we show that one can leverage a small number of additional variables in order to stabilize momentum fluctuations induced by the unknown noise. Our method is inspired by the idea of a thermostat in statistical physics and is justified by a general theory.

paragraphs: Dynamics-based methods generate samples by evolving a system whose behavior is designed around a target probability distribution. Combining these methods with stochastic gradients can make sampling more efficient on large datasets. However, the gradients introduce an unknown amount of noise, creating a problem for whether the resulting procedure samples the intended distribution.

The paper focuses on the disruption this noise can cause after the dynamics are discretized into computational steps. Its solution adds a small number of variables that stabilize the momentum fluctuations caused by the unknown noise. The design takes inspiration from thermostats in statistical physics, using additional dynamical quantities to regulate the sampling process.

The authors justify the method through a general theory. The contribution is a mechanism for addressing stochastic-gradient noise within dynamics-based Bayesian sampling, connecting a large-data computational strategy with a physical idea for controlling fluctuations. The central claim is that these extra variables can stabilize the noise-induced momentum changes, helping remedy the sampling problem identified by the paper.
summary.tldr: Thermostat-inspired auxiliary variables stabilize momentum fluctuations caused by unknown stochastic-gradient noise in Bayesian sampling.

title: Bayesian Sampling Using Stochastic Gradient Thermostats

abstract: Partial monitoring is a general model for sequential learning with limited feedback formalized as a game between two players. In this game, the learner chooses an action and at the same time the opponent chooses an outcome, then the learner suffers a loss and receives a feedback signal. The goal of the learner is to minimize the total loss. In this paper, we study partial monitoring with finite actions and stochastic outcomes. We derive a logarithmic distribution-dependent regret lower bound that defines the hardness of the problem. Inspired by the DMED algorithm (Honda and Takemura, 2010) for the multi-armed bandit problem, we propose PM-DMED, an algorithm that minimizes the distribution-dependent regret. PM-DMED significantly outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in numerical experiments. To show the optimality of PM-DMED with respect to the regret bound, we slightly modify the algorithm by introducing a hinge function (PM-DMED-Hinge). Then, we derive an asymptotical optimal regret upper bound of PM-DMED-Hinge that matches the lower bound.
