paragraphs: Partial monitoring models repeated decisions when the learner receives limited feedback about what happened. Each round pairs a chosen action with an outcome, producing both a loss and a feedback signal. This paper studies finite action sets and stochastic outcomes, with the aim of controlling accumulated regret.

The authors derive a logarithmic regret lower bound that depends on the outcome distribution. This describes problem difficulty more specifically than a single worst-case rate. They then introduce PM-DMED, inspired by a bandit algorithm, to pursue low distribution-dependent regret. Numerical experiments show substantial improvements over state-of-the-art methods.

For the matching theoretical guarantee, the authors modify PM-DMED using a hinge function. This variant, PM-DMED-Hinge, has an asymptotically optimal upper bound matching the lower bound. The distinction matters: the empirical performance claim concerns PM-DMED, while the stated optimality proof uses the modified algorithm. Together, the results supply a distribution-sensitive benchmark and an algorithm that asymptotically attains it.
summary.tldr: A distribution-dependent regret lower bound guides PM-DMED, whose hinge-modified variant asymptotically matches the bound.

title: Regret Lower Bound and Optimal Algorithm in Finite Stochastic Partial Monitoring

abstract: We introduce convolutional DRAW, a homogeneous deep generative model achieving state-of-the-art performance in latent variable image modeling. The algorithm naturally stratifies information into higher and lower level details, creating abstract features and as such addressing one of the fundamentally desired properties of representation learning. Furthermore, the hierarchical ordering of its latents creates the opportunity to selectively store global information about an image, yielding a high quality 'conceptual compression' framework.
originalAbstract: We introduce convolutional DRAW, a homogeneous deep generative model achieving state-of-the-art performance in latent variable image modeling. The algorithm naturally stratifies information into higher and lower level details, creating abstract features and as such addressing one of the fundamentally desired properties of representation learning. Furthermore, the hierarchical ordering of its latents creates the opportunity to selectively store global information about an image, yielding a high quality 'conceptual compression' framework.

paragraphs: This paper introduces convolutional DRAW, a homogeneous deep generative model for images. It reports leading performance in latent-variable image modeling. Beyond modeling performance, the work focuses on the organization of the learned representation: whether the model separates broad image information from lower-level detail in a useful hierarchy.

The algorithm naturally distributes information across higher and lower levels, producing abstract features. That organization matters because representation learning seeks more than a collection of hidden numbers; it seeks features that capture meaningful structure. Here, the stated contribution is a hierarchy in which different levels carry different kinds of image information, linking the generative model’s internal representation to abstraction.

The hierarchy creates an opportunity for conceptual compression by selectively storing global information about an image. Rather than treating all latent information as equally necessary to preserve, this framework uses the ordering of the latent variables to prioritize broad content. The paper describes the resulting compression framework as high quality. Its central idea is that a structured generative representation can support selective storage of image concepts.
summary.tldr: Convolutional DRAW organizes image information hierarchically, enabling conceptual compression through selective storage of global image content.

title: Towards Conceptual Compression

abstract: We present a general framework for classification of sparse and irregularly-sampled time series. The properties of such time series can result in substantial uncertainty about the values of the underlying temporal processes, while making the data difficult to deal with using standard classification methods that assume fixed-dimensional feature spaces. To address these challenges, we propose an uncertainty-aware classification framework based on a special computational layer we refer to as the Gaussian process adapter that can connect irregularly sampled time series data to any black-box classifier learnable using gradient descent. We show how to scale up the required computations based on combining the structured kernel interpolation framework and the Lanczos approximation method, and how to discriminatively train the Gaussian process adapter in combination with a number of classifiers end-to-end using backpropagation.
originalAbstract: We present a general framework for classification of sparse and irregularly-sampled time series. The properties of such time series can result in substantial uncertainty about the values of the underlying temporal processes, while making the data difficult to deal with using standard classification methods that assume fixed-dimensional feature spaces. To address these challenges, we propose an uncertainty-aware classification framework based on a special computational layer we refer to as the Gaussian process adapter that can connect irregularly sampled time series data to any black-box classifier learnable using gradient descent. We show how to scale up the required computations based on combining the structured kernel interpolation framework and the Lanczos approximation method, and how to discriminatively train the Gaussian process adapter in combination with a number of classifiers end-to-end using backpropagation.

paragraphs: Classifying a time series becomes difficult when measurements are sparse and arrive at uneven intervals. The gaps create uncertainty about the underlying process, and different observation schedules do not naturally fit classifiers that expect inputs with a fixed number of features. This paper develops a framework that addresses both issues together.

Its central component is a Gaussian process adapter: a computational layer connecting irregular observations to a classifier while accounting for uncertainty about the temporal process. The framework can work with any black-box classifier that can be learned through gradient descent. This makes the adapter a general interface between the observation format and the prediction model.

The authors combine structured kernel interpolation with the Lanczos approximation method to make the required computations scalable. They also show how backpropagation can train the adapter and classifier jointly. Consequently, the adapter can be adjusted for the classification objective as part of the complete system, bringing uncertainty-aware processing into an end-to-end learning framework.
summary.tldr: A scalable Gaussian process adapter connects sparse, irregular time series to gradient-trained classifiers while accounting for uncertainty.

title: A scalable end-to-end Gaussian process adapter for irregularly sampled time series classification

abstract: In neuroscience, the similarity matrix of neural activity patterns in response to different sensory stimuli or under different cognitive states reflects the structure of neural representational space. Existing methods derive point estimations of neural activity patterns from noisy neural imaging data, and the similarity is calculated from these point estimations. We show that this approach translates structured noise from estimated patterns into spurious bias structure in the resulting similarity matrix, which is especially severe when signal-to-noise ratio is low and experimental conditions cannot be fully randomized in a cognitive task. We propose an alternative Bayesian framework for computing representational similarity in which we treat the covariance structure of neural activity patterns as a hyper-parameter in a generative model of the neural data, and directly estimate this covariance structure from imaging data while marginalizing over the unknown activity patterns. Converting the estimated covariance structure into a correlation matrix offers a much less biased estimate of neural representational similarity. Our method can also simultaneously estimate a signal-to-noise map that informs where the learned representational structure is supported more strongly, and the learned covariance matrix can be used as a structured prior to constrain Bayesian estimation of neural activity patterns. Our code is freely available in Brain Imaging Analysis Kit (Brainiak) (https://github.com/IntelPNI/brainiak), a python toolkit for brain imaging analysis.

paragraphs: Researchers use similarities between brain activity patterns to study how the brain represents stimuli or cognitive states. A common procedure first estimates each activity pattern from imaging data and then compares those estimates. This paper shows that structured noise in the estimated patterns can create misleading structure in the resulting similarity matrix.

The problem is especially severe when signals are weak relative to noise and experimental conditions cannot be fully randomized. The proposed Bayesian approach instead places the covariance between activity patterns inside a model of the imaging data. It estimates that covariance directly while averaging over uncertainty about the unknown activity patterns, then converts it into correlations.

The authors report that this produces substantially less biased representational similarities. The method can also estimate a signal-to-noise map indicating where the inferred structure receives stronger support. Its learned covariance can subsequently guide Bayesian estimates of activity patterns. Together, these outputs connect the representation being studied with uncertainty about the measurements supporting it.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian model estimates neural similarities directly from imaging data while accounting for uncertain activity patterns, reducing noise-induced bias.

title: A Bayesian method for reducing bias in neural representational similarity analysis

abstract: It is commonly assumed that language refers to high-level visual concepts while leaving low-level visual processing unaffected. This view dominates the current literature in computational models for language-vision tasks, where visual and linguistic inputs are mostly processed independently before being fused into a single representation. In this paper, we deviate from this classic pipeline and propose to modulate the \emph{entire visual processing} by a linguistic input. Specifically, we introduce Conditional Batch Normalization (CBN) as an efficient mechanism to modulate convolutional feature maps by a linguistic embedding. We apply CBN to a pre-trained Residual Network (ResNet), leading to the MODulatEd ResNet (\MRN) architecture, and show that this significantly improves strong baselines on two visual question answering tasks. Our ablation study confirms that modulating from the early stages of the visual processing is beneficial.
originalAbstract: It is commonly assumed that language refers to high-level visual concepts while leaving low-level visual processing unaffected. This view dominates the current literature in computational models for language-vision tasks, where visual and linguistic inputs are mostly processed independently before being fused into a single representation. In this paper, we deviate from this classic pipeline and propose to modulate the \emph{entire visual processing} by a linguistic input. Specifically, we introduce Conditional Batch Normalization (CBN) as an efficient mechanism to modulate convolutional feature maps by a linguistic embedding. We apply CBN to a pre-trained Residual Network (ResNet), leading to the MODulatEd ResNet (\MRN) architecture, and show that this significantly improves strong baselines on two visual question answering tasks. Our ablation study confirms that modulating from the early stages of the visual processing is beneficial.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether language should influence visual processing from its earliest stages. Many language-and-vision systems process the two inputs separately before combining their representations. The proposed approach instead lets linguistic input modulate the visual computation throughout the network, including stages that precede high-level visual concepts.

The mechanism is Conditional Batch Normalization, which uses a linguistic embedding to modulate convolutional feature maps. Applied to a pretrained ResNet, it produces the MODulatEd ResNet architecture. Language thus becomes an input to the processing of visual features themselves, allowing the visual representation to depend on the linguistic context.

The authors evaluate the architecture on two visual question answering tasks and report significant improvements over strong baselines. An ablation study specifically finds a benefit from introducing modulation at early visual stages. This gives evidence for where language should enter the model, alongside the overall performance result: early conditioning contributes to the gains observed in the evaluated question answering settings.
summary.tldr: Language-conditioned batch normalization improves visual question answering, with ablations supporting modulation from early visual layers.

title: Modulating early visual processing by language

abstract: We propose a metalearning approach for learning gradient-based reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms. The idea is to evolve a differentiable loss function, such that an agent, which optimizes its policy to minimize this loss, will achieve high rewards. The loss is parametrized via temporal convolutions over the agent's experience. Because this loss is highly flexible in its ability to take into account the agent's history, it enables fast task learning. Empirical results show that our evolved policy gradient algorithm (EPG) achieves faster learning on several randomized environments compared to an off-the-shelf policy gradient method. We also demonstrate that EPG's learned loss can generalize to out-of-distribution test time tasks, and exhibits qualitatively different behavior from other popular metalearning algorithms.
originalAbstract: We propose a metalearning approach for learning gradient-based reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms. The idea is to evolve a differentiable loss function, such that an agent, which optimizes its policy to minimize this loss, will achieve high rewards. The loss is parametrized via temporal convolutions over the agent's experience. Because this loss is highly flexible in its ability to take into account the agent's history, it enables fast task learning. Empirical results show that our evolved policy gradient algorithm (EPG) achieves faster learning on several randomized environments compared to an off-the-shelf policy gradient method. We also demonstrate that EPG's learned loss can generalize to out-of-distribution test time tasks, and exhibits qualitatively different behavior from other popular metalearning algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper treats the reinforcement learning update rule itself as something that can be learned. Rather than specifying a fixed training loss, it evolves a differentiable loss function. An agent then improves its policy by minimizing that learned loss, with the outer learning process seeking losses that lead to high rewards.

The loss is parameterized using temporal convolutions over the agent's experience. This gives the learning rule flexibility to use information from the agent's history when determining policy updates. The method therefore learns how experience should shape gradient-based policy improvement, alongside the ordinary process in which an agent learns how to act.

Experiments show that Evolved Policy Gradients learns faster than an off-the-shelf policy-gradient method in several randomized environments. The authors also demonstrate that the learned loss can transfer to test tasks outside the training distribution and produces behavior qualitatively different from other popular metalearning algorithms. These findings establish examples of useful learned update rules and transfer, with the reported advantage grounded in the environments examined.
summary.tldr: Evolved Policy Gradients learns a history-dependent training loss that accelerates learning in several environments and can transfer to new task distributions.

title: Evolved Policy Gradients

abstract: As opposed to standard empirical risk minimization (ERM), distributionally robust optimization aims to minimize the worst-case risk over a larger ambiguity set containing the original empirical distribution of the training data. In this work, we describe a minimax framework for statistical learning with ambiguity sets given by balls in Wasserstein space. In particular, we prove generalization bounds that involve the covering number properties of the original ERM problem. As an illustrative example, we provide generalization guarantees for transport-based domain adaptation problems where the Wasserstein distance between the source and target domain distributions can be reliably estimated from unlabeled samples.
originalAbstract: As opposed to standard empirical risk minimization (ERM), distributionally robust optimization aims to minimize the worst-case risk over a larger ambiguity set containing the original empirical distribution of the training data. In this work, we describe a minimax framework for statistical learning with ambiguity sets given by balls in Wasserstein space. In particular, we prove generalization bounds that involve the covering number properties of the original ERM problem. As an illustrative example, we provide generalization guarantees for transport-based domain adaptation problems where the Wasserstein distance between the source and target domain distributions can be reliably estimated from unlabeled samples.

paragraphs: Empirical risk minimization selects a model by its performance on the observed training distribution. Distributionally robust optimization instead considers a set of plausible distributions containing that empirical distribution and minimizes the worst risk within the set. This paper develops a statistical learning framework for that more cautious objective.

The ambiguity sets are balls defined by Wasserstein distance, so the distance determines which alternative distributions are considered. The authors prove generalization bounds using covering-number properties of the original empirical risk minimization problem. These properties describe the complexity of the original learning problem, connecting the robust formulation to a familiar way of assessing the range of models under consideration.

The paper illustrates the framework through transport-based domain adaptation, where learning must transfer from a source distribution to a target distribution. Its guarantees apply when the Wasserstein distance between those distributions can be reliably estimated using unlabeled samples. This condition matters because the estimated distributional separation provides the basis for the adaptation guarantee, even without target labels.
summary.tldr: The paper proves generalization bounds for Wasserstein-based robust learning, including conditional guarantees for transport-based domain adaptation.

title: Minimax Statistical Learning with Wasserstein distances

abstract: We consider learning problems where the training set consists of two types of examples: private and public. The goal is to design a learning algorithm that satisfies differential privacy only with respect to the private examples. This setting interpolates between private learning (where all examples are private) and classical learning (where all examples are public). We study the limits of learning in this setting in terms of private and public sample complexities. We show that any hypothesis class of VC-dimension $d$ can be agnostically learned up to an excess error of $\alpha$ using only (roughly) $d/\alpha$ public examples and $d/\alpha^2$ private labeled examples. This result holds even when the public examples are unlabeled. This gives a quadratic improvement over the standard $d/\alpha^2$ upper bound on the public sample complexity (where private examples can be ignored altogether if the public examples are labeled). Furthermore, we give a nearly matching lower bound, which we prove via a generic reduction from this setting to the one of private learning without public data.
originalAbstract: We consider learning problems where the training set consists of two types of examples: private and public. The goal is to design a learning algorithm that satisfies differential privacy only with respect to the private examples. This setting interpolates between private learning (where all examples are private) and classical learning (where all examples are public). We study the limits of learning in this setting in terms of private and public sample complexities. We show that any hypothesis class of VC-dimension $d$ can be agnostically learned up to an excess error of $\alpha$ using only (roughly) $d/\alpha$ public examples and $d/\alpha^2$ private labeled examples. This result holds even when the public examples are unlabeled. This gives a quadratic improvement over the standard $d/\alpha^2$ upper bound on the public sample complexity (where private examples can be ignored altogether if the public examples are labeled). Furthermore, we give a nearly matching lower bound, which we prove via a generic reduction from this setting to the one of private learning without public data.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning from a mixture of public and private examples, where differential privacy is required only for the private portion. Its question is how many examples of each kind are needed. Public data can assist learning without receiving the same protection, but the private examples must still be handled under the privacy requirement.

For a hypothesis class with VC dimension d, the authors show that agnostic learning to excess error alpha is possible using roughly d/alpha public examples and d/alpha² private labeled examples. Agnostic learning does not require the hypothesis class to contain a perfectly correct predictor. Crucially, the public examples can be unlabeled, so their usefulness does not depend on supplying additional public labels.

The public sample requirement improves from inverse-quadratic to inverse-linear dependence on the target error compared with the stated standard bound. The authors also establish a nearly matching lower bound through a reduction to private learning without public data. Together, the bounds describe both an achievable trade-off and a closely corresponding limit on the amount of public data needed.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes nearly matching bounds on how public examples, even unlabeled ones, can assist differentially private learning.

title: Limits of Private Learning with Access to Public Data

abstract: Machine learning on encrypted data has received a lot of attention thanks to recent breakthroughs in homomorphic encryption and secure multi-party computation. It allows outsourcing computation to untrusted servers without sacrificing privacy of sensitive data. We propose a practical framework to perform partially encrypted and privacy-preserving predictions which combines adversarial training and functional encryption. We first present a new functional encryption scheme to efficiently compute quadratic functions so that the data owner controls what can be computed but is not involved in the calculation: it provides a decryption key which allows one to learn a specific function evaluation of some encrypted data. We then show how to use it in machine learning to partially encrypt neural networks with quadratic activation functions at evaluation time and we provide a thorough analysis of the information leaks based on indistinguishability of data items of the same label. Last, since several encryption schemes cannot deal with the last thresholding operation used for classification, we propose a training method to prevent selected sensitive features from leaking which adversarially optimizes the network against an adversary trying to identify these features. This is of great interest for several existing works using partially encrypted machine learning as it comes with almost no cost on the model's accuracy and significantly improves data privacy.

paragraphs: The paper develops a framework for making neural-network predictions with partially encrypted computation while protecting sensitive data. It combines functional encryption with adversarial training. Functional encryption lets a data owner authorize evaluation of a particular function on encrypted data, without requiring the owner to participate in the calculation itself.

The authors introduce an efficient functional-encryption scheme for quadratic functions and use it with neural networks that have quadratic activations at evaluation time. They analyze information leakage through the indistinguishability of data items sharing a label. This makes the privacy analysis sensitive to what a prediction reveals about individual inputs within the same class.

The authors report substantially improved privacy with almost no accuracy cost. The contribution combines restricted encrypted computation with learned protection against feature leakage, addressing privacy at both the computation and model-training levels.
summary.tldr: Functional encryption and adversarial training enable partially encrypted neural predictions while reducing leakage of selected sensitive features.

title: Partially Encrypted Deep Learning using Functional Encryption

abstract: Graph embedding has been intensively studied recently, due to the advance of various neural network models. Theoretical analyses and empirical studies have pushed forward the translation of discrete graph structures into distributed representation vectors, but seldom considered the reverse direction, i.e., generation of graphs from given related context spaces. Particularly, since graphs often become more meaningful when associated with semantic contexts (e.g., social networks of certain communities, gene networks of certain diseases), the ability to infer graph structures according to given semantic conditions could be of great value. While existing graph generative models only consider graph structures without semantic contexts, we formulate the novel problem of conditional structure generation, and propose a novel unified model of graph variational generative adversarial nets (CondGen) to handle the intrinsic challenges of flexible context-structure conditioning and permutation-invariant generation. Extensive experiments on two deliberately created benchmark datasets of real-world context-enriched networks demonstrate the supreme effectiveness and generalizability of CondGen.

paragraphs: Graph embedding converts a network's discrete structure into a vector representation. This paper studies the reverse direction: generating graph structures from related semantic context. The motivating idea is that a graph becomes more meaningful when connected to a condition, such as a particular community for a social network or a disease for a gene network.

The authors formulate this as conditional structure generation and introduce CondGen, a unified graph variational generative adversarial model. It addresses two central challenges: flexibly relating semantic context to graph structure, and producing graphs in a permutation-invariant way. The latter means that the generation problem must respect graph structure without attaching significance to an arbitrary ordering of nodes.

The evaluation uses two deliberately constructed benchmark datasets containing real-world networks enriched with context. The authors report strong effectiveness and generalizability on these benchmarks. The contribution therefore extends graph generation toward structures guided by supplied meaning, with experiments supporting the model's ability to handle the relationship between context and network form.
summary.tldr: CondGen generates graph structures conditioned on semantic context while addressing flexible context relationships and permutation-invariant generation.

title: Conditional Structure Generation through Graph Variational Generative Adversarial Nets

abstract: Tensor-based multimodal fusion techniques have exhibited great predictive performance. However, one limitation is that existing approaches only consider bilinear or trilinear pooling, which fails to unleash the complete expressive power of multilinear fusion with restricted orders of interactions. More importantly, simply fusing features all at once ignores the complex local intercorrelations, leading to the deterioration of prediction. In this work, we first propose a polynomial tensor pooling (PTP) block for integrating multimodal features by considering high-order moments, followed by a tensorized fully connected layer. Treating PTP as a building block, we further establish a hierarchical polynomial fusion network (HPFN) to recursively transmit local correlations into global ones. By stacking multiple PTPs, the expressivity capacity of HPFN enjoys an exponential growth w.r.t. the number of layers, which is shown by the equivalence to a very deep convolutional arithmetic circuits. Various experiments demonstrate that it can achieve the state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Combining multiple kinds of input requires modeling relationships among their features. The paper argues that existing tensor-based fusion approaches restrict those relationships by considering only bilinear or trilinear interactions. It also identifies a second problem: combining all features at once can overlook local correlations that matter for prediction.

The proposed polynomial tensor pooling block captures higher-order moments when integrating multimodal features, followed by a tensorized fully connected layer. The authors then stack these blocks into a hierarchical polynomial fusion network. This hierarchy progressively carries local correlations into global relationships, making the organization of feature interactions part of the model's design.

This is a claim about representational power, rather than an exponential improvement in accuracy. Experiments report state-of-the-art predictive performance, supporting the use of both higher-order interactions and hierarchical fusion in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical polynomial pooling combines higher-order multimodal interactions with local-to-global fusion and reports state-of-the-art performance.

title: Deep Multimodal Multilinear Fusion with High-order Polynomial Pooling

abstract: We present a novel algorithm for non-linear instrumental variable (IV) regression, DualIV, which simplifies traditional two-stage methods via a dual formulation. Inspired by problems in stochastic programming, we show that two-stage procedures for non-linear IV regression can be reformulated as a convex-concave saddle-point problem. Our formulation enables us to circumvent the first-stage regression which is a potential bottleneck in real-world applications. We develop a simple kernel-based algorithm with an analytic solution based on this formulation. Empirical results show that we are competitive to existing, more complicated algorithms for non-linear instrumental variable regression.

paragraphs: The paper introduces DualIV, an algorithm for nonlinear instrumental variable regression. The authors seek a formulation that avoids this separate step while retaining a way to solve the nonlinear regression problem.

Drawing inspiration from stochastic programming, they reformulate the two-stage procedure as a convex-concave saddle-point problem. This changes how the estimation problem is expressed: instead of carrying out the original stages in sequence, the method works with a dual formulation. The significance is that the first-stage regression can be circumvented through the mathematical structure of the alternative problem.

The authors turn this formulation into a kernel-based algorithm with an analytic solution. Their empirical results are competitive with existing nonlinear instrumental variable methods that are more complicated. The contribution therefore combines a reformulation with a comparatively simple estimator: it shows that avoiding the conventional first stage can still produce competitive results in the reported comparisons.
summary.tldr: DualIV reformulates nonlinear instrumental variable regression as a saddle-point problem, avoiding a separate first-stage regression while achieving competitive empirical results.

title: Dual Instrumental Variable Regression

abstract: A hallmark of graph neural networks is their ability to distinguish the isomorphism class of their inputs. This study derives hardness results for the classification variant of graph isomorphism in the message-passing model (MPNN). MPNN encompasses the majority of graph neural networks used today and is universal when nodes are given unique features. The analysis relies on the introduced measure of communication capacity. Capacity measures how much information the nodes of a network can exchange during the forward pass and depends on the depth, message-size, global state, and width of the architecture. It is shown that the capacity of MPNN needs to grow linearly with the number of nodes so that a network can distinguish trees and quadratically for general connected graphs. The derived bounds concern both worst- and average-case behavior and apply to networks with/without unique features and adaptive architecture---they are also up to two orders of magnitude tighter than those given by simpler arguments. An empirical study involving 12 graph classification tasks and 420 networks reveals strong alignment between actual performance and theoretical predictions.

paragraphs: This paper studies how much information a message-passing graph neural network needs to distinguish graph structures. It introduces communication capacity, a measure of the information nodes can exchange during a forward pass. Capacity depends jointly on depth, message size, global state, and network width, bringing several architectural choices into one analysis.

The authors derive necessary capacity growth for the classification form of graph isomorphism: linear growth with node count for trees and quadratic growth for general connected graphs. These are lower bounds on the resources needed for distinguishing graphs. They address both worst-case and average-case behavior and apply with or without unique node features, including adaptive architectures.

The resulting bounds are up to two orders of magnitude tighter than those obtained through simpler arguments. An empirical study spanning 12 graph classification tasks and 420 networks finds strong agreement between observed performance and theoretical predictions. The work therefore connects limits on information exchange to practical architectural performance, even in a model family that is universal with unique node features.
summary.tldr: Communication-capacity bounds quantify how message-passing graph networks must scale to distinguish trees and general connected graphs.

title: How hard is to distinguish graphs with graph neural networks?

abstract: We develop Neuron Shapley as a new framework to quantify the contribution of individual neurons to the prediction and performance of a deep network. By accounting for interactions across neurons, Neuron Shapley is more effective in identifying important filters compared to common approaches based on activation patterns. Interestingly, removing just 30 filters with the highest Shapley scores effectively destroys the prediction accuracy of Inception-v3 on ImageNet. Visualization of these few critical filters provides insights into how the network functions. Neuron Shapley is a flexible framework and can be applied to identify responsible neurons in many tasks. We illustrate additional applications of identifying filters that are responsible for biased prediction in facial recognition and filters that are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Removing these filters is a quick way to repair models. Computing exact Shapley values is computationally infeasible and therefore sampling-based approximations are used in practice. We introduce a new multi-armed bandit algorithm that is able to efficiently detect neurons with the largest Shapley value orders of magnitude faster than existing Shapley value approximation methods.

paragraphs: A neuron's activity alone may not reveal how much it contributes to a network's predictions. Neuron Shapley measures individual contributions while accounting for interactions among neurons. The paper reports that this framework identifies important filters more effectively than common methods based on activation patterns.

One demonstration removes the 30 filters with the largest Shapley scores from Inception-v3, effectively destroying its ImageNet prediction accuracy. Visualizing these critical filters provides insight into the network's operation. The authors also apply the framework to filters associated with biased facial-recognition predictions and vulnerability to adversarial attacks, illustrating how targeted removal can serve as a quick model repair in these applications.

The paper introduces a multi-armed bandit algorithm designed to efficiently locate neurons with the largest scores. It reports detection orders of magnitude faster than existing Shapley approximation methods. The contribution therefore combines an interaction-aware measure of neuron importance with a computational strategy that makes identifying the most influential neurons more practical.
summary.tldr: Neuron Shapley identifies influential neurons by accounting for their interactions and uses a bandit algorithm to find high-scoring neurons efficiently.

title: Neuron Shapley: Discovering the Responsible Neurons

abstract: Raven’s Progressive Matrices are multiple-choice intelligence tests, where one tries to complete the missing location in a 3x3 grid of abstract images. Previous attempts to address this test have focused solely on selecting the right answer out of the multiple choices. In this work, we focus, instead, on generating a correct answer given the grid, which is a harder task, by definition. The proposed neural model combines multiple advances in generative models, including employing multiple pathways through the same network, using the reparameterization trick along two pathways to make their encoding compatible, a selective application of variational losses, and a complex perceptual loss that is coupled with a selective backpropagation procedure. Our algorithm is able not only to generate a set of plausible answers but also to be competitive to the state of the art methods in multiple-choice tests.

paragraphs: Raven's Progressive Matrices present a grid of abstract images with one location missing. Conventional computational approaches select a completion from supplied choices. This paper instead asks a neural model to generate a completion from the grid, making the task harder because the answer must be constructed rather than selected from a ready-made set.

The proposed model combines several generative-learning techniques. It uses multiple pathways through a shared network and applies the reparameterization trick along two pathways to make their encodings compatible. Variational losses are applied selectively, while a perceptual loss is paired with selective backpropagation. Together, these components define how the different pathways and training signals interact.

The reported result is that the algorithm can produce a set of plausible answers while remaining competitive with state-of-the-art approaches on multiple-choice tests. Generation is therefore explored without giving up the ability to perform the conventional selection task. The contribution broadens the evaluation of these visual reasoning problems from identifying an offered answer to constructing candidate answers directly.
summary.tldr: A generative neural model constructs plausible completions for progressive matrices while remaining competitive on multiple-choice versions of the task.

title: Generating Correct Answers for Progressive Matrices Intelligence Tests

abstract: Convex optimization problems with staged structure appear in several contexts, including optimal control, verification of deep neural networks, and isotonic regression. Off-the-shelf solvers can solve these problems but may scale poorly. We develop a nonconvex reformulation designed to exploit this staged structure. Our reformulation has only simple bound constraints, enabling solution via projected gradient methods and their accelerated variants. The method automatically generates a sequence of primal and dual feasible solutions to the original convex problem, making optimality certification easy. We establish theoretical properties of the nonconvex formulation, showing that it is (almost) free of spurious local minima and has the same global optimum as the convex problem. We modify projected gradient descent to avoid spurious local minimizers so it always converges to the global minimizer. For neural network verification, our approach obtains small duality gaps in only a few gradient steps. Consequently, it can provide tight duality gaps for many large-scale verification problems where both off-the-shelf and specialized solvers struggle.

paragraphs: Some convex optimization problems have a sequence of linked stages, as in optimal control, neural network verification, and isotonic regression. General solvers can handle these problems, but may struggle as they grow. This paper exploits their staged structure by rewriting them as nonconvex problems with only simple bounds on the variables.

Despite introducing nonconvexity, the reformulation preserves the original global optimum and is almost free of misleading local minima. The method generates feasible solutions for both the original problem and its dual. Comparing their values gives an optimality certificate: a small gap shows that little improvement remains possible. In neural network verification, the approach obtains small gaps after only a few gradient steps. The reported results show that this reformulation can deliver tight certificates on many large verification problems where general and specialized solvers struggle.
summary.tldr: A structured nonconvex reformulation makes staged convex problems easier to optimize while preserving their global optimum and enabling optimality certificates.

title: An efficient nonconvex reformulation of stagewise convex optimization problems

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms combined with modern function approximators such as kernel functions and deep neural networks have achieved significant empirical successes in large-scale application problems with a massive number of states. From a theoretical perspective, however, RL with functional approximation poses a fundamental challenge to developing algorithms with provable computational and statistical efficiency, due to the need to take into consideration both the exploration-exploitation tradeoff that is inherent in RL and the bias-variance tradeoff that is innate in statistical estimation. To address such a challenge, focusing on the episodic setting where the action-value functions are represented by a kernel function or over-parametrized neural network, we propose the first provable RL algorithm with both polynomial runtime and sample complexity, without additional assumptions on the data-generating model. In particular, for both the kernel and neural settings, we prove that an optimistic modification of the least-squares value iteration algorithm incurs an $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\delta_{\cF} H^2 \sqrt{T})$ regret, where $\delta_{\cF}$ characterizes the intrinsic complexity of the function class $\cF$, $H$ is the length of each episode, and $T$ is the total number of episodes. Our regret bounds are independent of the number of states and therefore even allows it to diverge, which exhibits the benefit of function approximation.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with function approximation must manage two difficulties together: deciding when to explore and estimating values from limited data. The paper seeks guarantees for both computation and sample use in episodic learning. It focuses on action-value functions represented by kernels or over-parameterized neural networks.

The proposed algorithm adds optimism to least-squares value iteration. For both representation settings, the authors establish polynomial runtime and sample complexity without additional assumptions on the data-generating model. They prove a regret bound proportional to the intrinsic complexity of the function class, the square of episode length, and the square root of the number of episodes, up to logarithmic factors.

A key feature of the bound is that it does not depend on the number of states, which may even diverge. The guarantee instead reflects the complexity of the chosen function representation. This explains the theoretical benefit of approximation in large state spaces: learning can be controlled through representational complexity rather than by counting states individually. The claim remains tied to the stated episodic kernel and over-parameterized neural settings.
summary.tldr: Optimistic least-squares value iteration achieves polynomial efficiency and state-count-independent regret guarantees with kernel or over-parameterized neural value representations.

title: Provably Efficient Reinforcement Learning with Kernel and Neural Function Approximations

abstract: We present a novel multi-source uncertainty prediction approach that enables deep learning (DL) models to be actively trained with much less labeled data. By leveraging the second-order uncertainty representation provided by subjective logic (SL), we conduct evidence-based theoretical analysis and formally decompose the predicted entropy over multiple classes into two distinct sources of uncertainty: vacuity and dissonance, caused by lack of evidence and conflict of strong evidence, respectively. The evidence based entropy decomposition provides deeper insights on the nature of uncertainty, which can help effectively explore a large and high-dimensional unlabeled data space. We develop a novel loss function that augments DL based evidence prediction with uncertainty anchor sample identification. The accurately estimated multiple sources of uncertainty are systematically integrated and dynamically balanced using a data sampling function for label-efficient active deep learning (ADL). Experiments conducted over both synthetic and real data and comparison with competitive AL methods demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed ADL model.

The evidence based entropy decomposition provides deeper insights on the nature of uncertainty, which can help effectively explore a large and high-dimensional unlabeled data space. We develop a novel loss function that augments DL based evidence prediction with uncertainty anchor sample identification. paragraphs: Active learning chooses which unlabeled examples should receive labels so that a model can learn with less annotation. This paper argues that uncertainty has distinct sources that should influence this choice. A model may lack supporting evidence, or it may have strong evidence pointing toward conflicting classes.

Using subjective logic, the authors formally decompose predicted class entropy into vacuity and dissonance. Vacuity represents missing evidence, while dissonance represents conflict among strong evidence. This distinction gives the sampling procedure more information than a single undifferentiated uncertainty value when exploring a large, high-dimensional pool of unlabeled examples.

The method introduces a loss that combines evidence prediction with identifying uncertainty anchor samples. A sampling function then integrates and dynamically balances the estimated uncertainty sources to select data for labeling. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets, including comparisons with competitive active-learning methods, demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The stated finding is that distinguishing why a model is uncertain can support more label-efficient training in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Separating missing evidence from conflicting evidence helps an active-learning system choose informative examples and train with fewer labels.

title: Multifaceted Uncertainty Estimation for Label-Efficient Deep Learning

abstract: Global information is essential for dense prediction problems, whose goal is to compute a discrete or continuous label for each pixel in the images. Traditional convolutional layers in neural networks, initially designed for image classification, are restrictive in these problems since the filter size limits their receptive fields. In this work, we propose to replace any traditional convolutional layer with an autoregressive moving-average (ARMA) layer, a novel module with an adjustable receptive field controlled by the learnable autoregressive coefficients. Compared with traditional convolutional layers, our ARMA layer enables explicit interconnections of the output neurons and learns its receptive field by adapting the autoregressive coefficients of the interconnections. ARMA layer is adjustable to different types of tasks: for tasks where global information is crucial, it is capable of learning relatively large autoregressive coefficients to allow for an output neuron's receptive field covering the entire input; for tasks where only local information is required, it can learn small or near zero autoregressive coefficients and automatically reduces to a traditional convolutional layer. We show both theoretically and empirically that the effective receptive field of networks with ARMA layers (named ARMA networks) expands with larger autoregressive coefficients. We also provably solve the instability problem of learning and prediction in the ARMA layer through a re-parameterization mechanism. Additionally, we demonstrate that ARMA networks substantially improve their baselines on challenging dense prediction tasks, including video prediction and semantic segmentation.

Compared with traditional convolutional layers, our ARMA layer enables explicit interconnections of the output neurons and learns its receptive field by adapting the autoregressive coefficients of the interconnections. ARMA layer is adjustable to different types of tasks: for tasks where global information is crucial, it is capable of learning relatively large autoregressive coefficients to allow for an output neuron's receptive field covering the entire input; for tasks where only local information is required, it can learn small or near zero autoregressive coefficients and automatically reduces to a traditional convolutional layer. We show both theoretically and empirically that the effective receptive field of networks with ARMA layers (named ARMA networks) expands with larger autoregressive coefficients. We also provably solve the instability problem of learning and prediction in the ARMA layer through a re-parameterization mechanism. Additionally, we demonstrate that ARMA networks substantially improve their baselines on challenging dense prediction tasks, including video prediction and semantic segmentation.

paragraphs: Dense prediction assigns a value or category to every image pixel. Doing this well can require information from far beyond a small neighborhood, but a conventional convolutional layer has a receptive field limited by its filter size. The paper introduces an autoregressive moving-average layer whose information range can be learned.

The ARMA layer explicitly connects output neurons through learnable autoregressive coefficients. Larger coefficients can support an output's dependence on the entire input when global information is useful. Small or nearly zero coefficients allow the layer to behave like a traditional convolution when local information is sufficient. This makes the receptive field adjustable through training.

The authors show theoretically and experimentally that larger autoregressive coefficients expand the effective receptive field. They also provide a reparameterization that provably addresses instability in learning and prediction. Experiments report substantial improvements over the evaluated baselines on video prediction and semantic segmentation. These results support learning the extent of spatial context as part of the layer itself, alongside the features used for prediction.
summary.tldr: ARMA layers learn how far information travels across an image, expanding receptive fields and improving evaluated dense-prediction tasks.

title: ARMA Nets: Expanding Receptive Field for Dense Prediction

abstract: Memory-based meta-learning is a powerful technique to build agents that adapt fast to any task within a target distribution. A previous theoretical study has argued that this remarkable performance is because the meta-training protocol incentivises agents to behave Bayes-optimally. We empirically investigate this claim on a number of prediction and bandit tasks. Inspired by ideas from theoretical computer science, we show that meta-learned and Bayes-optimal agents not only behave alike, but they even share a similar computational structure, in the sense that one agent system can approximately simulate the other. Furthermore, we show that Bayes-optimal agents are fixed points of the meta-learning dynamics. Our results suggest that memory-based meta-learning is a general technique for numerically approximating Bayes-optimal agents; that is, even for task distributions for which we currently don't possess tractable models.

The work provides evidence for a computational explanation of rapid adaptation through meta-training.
summary.tldr: Experiments find behavioral and computational similarities between meta-trained and Bayes-optimal agents, supporting meta-learning as a possible numerical approximation method.

title: Meta-trained agents implement Bayes-optimal agents

abstract: By filtering the content that users see, social media platforms have the ability to influence users' perceptions and decisions, from their dining choices to their voting preferences. This influence has drawn scrutiny, with many calling for regulations on filtering algorithms, but designing and enforcing regulations remains challenging. In this work, we examine three questions. First, given a regulation, how would one design an audit to enforce it? Second, does the audit impose a performance cost on the platform? Third, how does the audit affect the content that the platform is incentivized to filter? In response to these questions, we propose a method such that, given a regulation, an auditor can test whether that regulation is met with only black-box access to the filtering algorithm. We then turn to the platform's perspective. The platform's goal is to maximize an objective function while meeting regulation. We find that there are conditions under which the regulation does not place a high performance cost on the platform and, notably, that content diversity can play a key role in aligning the interests of the platform and regulators.

paragraphs: Social-media filtering shapes which information people encounter and can influence their decisions. This paper examines how regulation of that filtering could be enforced, what compliance could cost a platform, and how an audit changes the content a platform is encouraged to select. It treats auditing and platform incentives as connected questions.

The authors propose a method that lets an auditor test compliance with a given regulation using only black-box access to the filtering algorithm. The auditor therefore does not need to inspect its internal implementation. The analysis then adopts the platform's perspective: maximizing its own objective while satisfying the regulatory constraint.

The paper identifies conditions under which compliance does not impose a high performance cost. This is a conditional result, rather than a claim that regulation is always inexpensive. It also finds that content diversity can help align platform and regulator interests. The contribution connects an externally applicable audit with an analysis of the behavior it incentivizes, showing why the composition of filtered content matters alongside the platform's objective.
summary.tldr: A black-box auditing framework examines regulatory compliance and identifies conditions where content diversity helps align platform and regulator interests.

title: Regulating algorithmic filtering on social media

abstract: How related are the representations learned by neural language models, translation models, and language tagging tasks? We answer this question by adapting an encoder-decoder transfer learning method from computer vision to investigate the structure among 100 different feature spaces extracted from hidden representations of various networks trained on language tasks.This method reveals a low-dimensional structure where language models and translation models smoothly interpolate between word embeddings, syntactic and semantic tasks, and future word embeddings. We call this low-dimensional structure a language representation embedding because it encodes the relationships between representations needed to process language for a variety of NLP tasks. We find that this representation embedding can predict how well each individual feature space maps to human brain responses to natural language stimuli recorded using fMRI. Additionally, we find that the principal dimension of this structure can be used to create a metric which highlights the brain's natural language processing hierarchy. This suggests that the embedding captures some part of the brain's natural language representation structure.

paragraphs: Language models, translation systems, and tagging models learn different internal representations, but their relationships are not immediately apparent. This paper compares 100 feature spaces drawn from networks trained on language tasks. It adapts an encoder-decoder transfer-learning method from computer vision to investigate how these representations are organized relative to one another.

The analysis reveals a low-dimensional structure linking word embeddings, syntactic and semantic tasks, and future-word embeddings. Representations from language and translation models vary smoothly within this structure. The authors call it a language representation embedding: it describes relationships among feature spaces, rather than simply providing another representation of individual words or sentences.

A metric built from its principal dimension also highlights a hierarchy in the brain's language processing. These findings suggest that the embedding captures some aspects of neural language representation. They establish a correspondence, while the authors' interpretation remains appropriately qualified as capturing only part of that structure.
summary.tldr: Relationships among 100 language feature spaces form a low-dimensional structure that predicts their correspondence with human brain responses.

title: Low-dimensional Structure in the Space of Language Representations is Reflected in Brain Responses

abstract: Federated learning aims to learn a global model that performs well on client devices with limited cross-client communication. Personalized federated learning (PFL) further extends this setup to handle data heterogeneity between clients by learning personalized models. A key challenge in this setting is to learn effectively across clients even though each client has unique data that is often limited in size. Here we present pFedGP, a solution to PFL that is based on Gaussian processes (GPs) with deep kernel learning. GPs are highly expressive models that work well in the low data regime due to their Bayesian nature.However, applying GPs to PFL raises multiple challenges. Mainly, GPs performance depends heavily on access to a good kernel function, and learning a kernel requires a large training set. Therefore, we propose learning a shared kernel function across all clients, parameterized by a neural network, with a personal GP classifier for each client. We further extend pFedGP to include inducing points using two novel methods, the first helps to improve generalization in the low data regime and the second reduces the computational cost. We derive a PAC-Bayes generalization bound on novel clients and empirically show that it gives non-vacuous guarantees. Extensive experiments on standard PFL benchmarks with CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and CINIC-10, and on a new setup of learning under input noise show that pFedGP achieves well-calibrated predictions while significantly outperforming baseline methods, reaching up to 21% in accuracy gain.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning must share useful information across clients while accommodating their different, often small datasets. This paper proposes pFedGP, which combines a shared neural-network kernel with a separate Gaussian process classifier for each client. The design addresses a tension: Gaussian processes can work well with little data, but learning a good kernel requires broader evidence.

The authors report well-calibrated predictions and substantial improvements over baseline methods, with accuracy gains reaching up to 21%. That figure is a reported maximum rather than a uniform gain. The results support combining a common learned kernel with local Bayesian classifiers to handle client heterogeneity.
summary.tldr: pFedGP shares a learned kernel across clients while personalizing Gaussian process classifiers, improving accuracy and calibration in reported experiments.

title: Personalized Federated Learning With Gaussian Processes

abstract: All sequential decision-making agents explore so as to acquire knowledge about a particular target. It is often the responsibility of the agent designer to construct this target which, in rich and complex environments, constitutes a onerous burden; without full knowledge of the environment itself, a designer may forge a sub-optimal learning target that poorly balances the amount of information an agent must acquire to identify the target against the target's associated performance shortfall. While recent work has developed a connection between learning targets and rate-distortion theory to address this challenge and empower agents that decide what to learn in an automated fashion, the proposed algorithm does not optimally tackle the equally important challenge of efficient information acquisition. In this work, building upon the seminal design principle of information-directed sampling (Russo & Van Roy, 2014), we address this shortcoming directly to couple optimal information acquisition with the optimal design of learning targets. Along the way, we offer new insights into learning targets from the literature on rate-distortion theory before turning to empirical results that confirm the value of information when deciding what to learn.

paragraphs: An exploring agent needs a learning target: something it seeks to discover so that it can make better decisions. Choosing that target manually can be difficult in a complex environment. A target can demand substantial information while still leaving an undesirable performance shortfall, so deciding what to learn is itself an optimization problem.

Earlier work connects target selection to rate-distortion theory, which expresses a tradeoff between information requirements and tolerated loss. This paper addresses a remaining issue: an automatically chosen target still needs an efficient information-acquisition strategy. The authors build on information-directed sampling to couple optimal acquisition with optimal learning-target design.

The work also develops further interpretations of learning targets through rate-distortion theory and presents empirical results supporting the value of information in target selection. Its contribution is to treat the destination of learning and the process of gathering evidence as linked decisions. A target's usefulness therefore depends on both its associated performance shortfall and the information an agent must acquire to identify it.
summary.tldr: The paper couples learning-target design with information-directed acquisition so agents can jointly decide what to learn and how to learn it efficiently.

title: The Value of Information When Deciding What to Learn

abstract: Neural module networks (NMN) are a popular approach for solving multi-modal tasks such as visual question answering (VQA) and visual referring expression recognition (REF). A key limitation in prior implementations of NMN is that the neural modules do not effectively capture the association between the visual input and the relevant neighbourhood context of the textual input. This limits their generalizability. For instance, NMN fail to understand new concepts such as “yellow sphere to the left" even when it is a combination of known concepts from train data: “blue sphere", “yellow cube", and “metallic cube to the left". In this paper, we address this limitation by introducing a language-guided adaptive convolution layer (LG-Conv) into NMN, in which the filter weights of convolutions are explicitly multiplied with a spatially varying language-guided kernel. Our model allows the neural module to adaptively co-attend over potential objects of interest from the visual and textual inputs. Extensive experiments on VQA and REF tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Additionally, we propose a new challenging out-of-distribution test split for REF task, which we call C3-Ref+, for explicitly evaluating the NMN’s ability to generalize well to adversarial perturbations and unseen combinations of known concepts. Experiments on C3-Ref+ further demonstrate the generalization capabilities of our approach.

paragraphs: Visual question answering and referring expression recognition require connecting language with objects and relationships in an image. This paper identifies a weakness in earlier neural module networks: their modules do not adequately link visual information with the relevant surrounding text. That can make unfamiliar combinations of familiar concepts difficult to understand.

The proposed language-guided adaptive convolution layer modifies convolution filters using a spatially varying kernel guided by language. This lets each neural module adapt its attention jointly across visual and textual inputs when identifying potential objects of interest. The mechanism aims to make the visual computation sensitive to the contextual meaning of the expression being processed.

Experiments on visual question answering and referring expression recognition demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The authors also introduce C3-Ref+, an out-of-distribution test split for referring expressions that evaluates adversarial perturbations and unseen combinations of known concepts. Results on this split provide further evidence of generalization. The contribution couples a concrete language-conditioned computation with an evaluation aimed directly at the compositional failures motivating the design.
summary.tldr: Language-guided adaptive convolutions improve neural module networks' visual reasoning and generalization to tested perturbations and new concept combinations.

title: Robust Visual Reasoning via Language Guided Neural Module Networks

abstract: While safe reinforcement learning (RL) holds great promise for many practical applications like robotics or autonomous cars, current approaches require specifying constraints in mathematical form. Such specifications demand domain expertise, limiting the adoption of safe RL. In this paper, we propose learning to interpret natural language constraints for safe RL. To this end, we first introduce HAZARDWORLD, a new multi-task benchmark that requires an agent to optimize reward while not violating constraints specified in free-form text. We then develop an agent with a modular architecture that can interpret and adhere to such textual constraints while learning new tasks. Our model consists of (1) a constraint interpreter that encodes textual constraints into spatial and temporal representations of forbidden states, and (2) a policy network that uses these representations to produce a policy achieving minimal constraint violations during training. Across different domains in HAZARDWORLD, we show that our method achieves higher rewards (up to11x) and fewer constraint violations (by 1.8x) compared to existing approaches. However, in terms of absolute performance, HAZARDWORLD still poses significant challenges for agents to learn efficiently, motivating the need for future work.

This paper studies whether an agent can instead learn to interpret constraints expressed in ordinary language. The goal is to pursue rewards while respecting instructions about forbidden situations.

The authors introduce HAZARDWORLD, a multitask benchmark with free-form textual constraints. Their agent separates interpretation from policy learning. The work establishes a concrete setting and architecture for studying language-specified constraints.
summary.tldr: A modular agent interprets textual constraints and improves rewards and constraint adherence on HAZARDWORLD, though efficient learning remains challenging.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning with Natural Language Constraints

abstract: We study the theory of random bipartite graph whose adjacency matrix is generated according to a connectivity matrix $M$. We consider the bipartite graph to be sparse, i.e., the entries of $M$ are upper bounded by certain sparsity parameter. We show that the performance of estimating the connectivity matrix $M$ depends on the sparsity of the graph. We focus on two measurement of performance of estimation: the error of estimating $M$ and the error of estimating the column space of $M$. In the first case, we consider the operator norm and Frobenius norm of the difference between the estimation and the true connectivity matrix. In the second case, the performance will be measured by the difference between the estimated projection matrix and the true projection matrix in operator norm and Frobenius norm. We will show that the estimators we propose achieve the minimax optimal rate.

paragraphs: This paper studies what can be recovered from a random bipartite graph whose connections are generated according to a matrix M. The graph is sparse in the sense that entries of M are bounded above by a sparsity parameter. The authors investigate how this sparsity affects estimation of both the matrix and its underlying column space.

These are related but distinct targets. Estimating M seeks to recover the connectivity structure itself. Estimating its column space seeks the subspace represented by its columns, evaluated through the corresponding projection matrix. For both targets, the paper measures error using operator and Frobenius norms, giving two mathematical views of estimation accuracy.

The authors propose estimators and show that they attain minimax-optimal rates. This means their error rates match the best possible worst-case rates for the analyzed problem setting. The result makes sparsity part of the statistical account of recoverability and establishes optimal-rate performance for both direct connectivity estimation and the more structural task of recovering its column space.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes minimax-optimal rates for estimating connectivity matrices and their column spaces in sparse random bipartite graphs.

title: Rate-Optimal Subspace Estimation on Random Graphs

abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image denoising are typically trained on large datasets. These models achieve the current state of the art, but they do not generalize well to data that deviate from the training distribution. Recent work has shown that it is possible to train denoisers on a single noisy image. These models adapt to the features of the test image, but their performance is limited by the small amount of information used to train them. Here we propose "GainTuning'', a methodology by which CNN models pre-trained on large datasets can be adaptively and selectively adjusted for individual test images. To avoid overfitting, GainTuning optimizes a single multiplicative scaling parameter (the “Gain”) of each channel in the convolutional layers of the CNN. We show that GainTuning improves state-of-the-art CNNs on standard image-denoising benchmarks, boosting their denoising performance on nearly every image in a held-out test set. These adaptive improvements are even more substantial for test images differing systematically from the training data, either in noise level or image type. We illustrate the potential of adaptive GainTuning in a scientific application to transmission-electron-microscope images, using a CNN that is pre-trained on synthetic data. In contrast to the existing methodology, GainTuning is able to faithfully reconstruct the structure of catalytic nanoparticles from these data at extremely low signal-to-noise ratios.

Training a model on one noisy image offers adaptation, but provides little information to learn from. GainTuning combines these approaches by adjusting an already trained convolutional network to each individual test image.

The adjustment is deliberately restricted: the method learns one multiplicative gain for each channel in the network’s convolutional layers. These gains change how strongly existing channels contribute. Restricting adaptation to this small set of parameters is intended to avoid overfitting while retaining the knowledge acquired during large-scale training.

In that application, GainTuning faithfully reconstructs catalytic nanoparticle structure at extremely low signal-to-noise ratios, illustrating how selective adaptation can make pretrained denoisers useful under substantially different imaging conditions.
summary.tldr: GainTuning adapts pretrained image denoisers through per-channel scaling, improving results especially when test images differ from training data.

title: Adaptive Denoising via GainTuning

abstract: We consider the imitation learning problem of learning a policy in a Markov Decision Process (MDP) setting where the reward function is not given, but demonstrations from experts are available. Although the goal of imitation learning is to learn a policy that produces behaviors nearly as good as the experts’ for a desired task, assumptions of consistent optimality for demonstrated behaviors are often violated in practice. Finding a policy that is distributionally robust against noisy demonstrations based on an adversarial construction potentially solves this problem by avoiding optimistic generalizations of the demonstrated data. This paper studies Distributionally Robust Imitation Learning (DRoIL) and establishes a close connection between DRoIL and Maximum Entropy Inverse Reinforcement Learning. We show that DRoIL can be seen as a framework that maximizes a generalized concept of entropy. We develop a novel approach to transform the objective function into a convex optimization problem over a polynomial number of variables for a class of loss functions that are additive over state and action spaces. Our approach lets us optimize both stationary and non-stationary policies and, unlike prevalent previous methods, it does not require repeatedly solving an inner reinforcement learning problem. We experimentally show the significant benefits of DRoIL’s new optimization method on synthetic data and a highway driving environment.

paragraphs: Imitation learning seeks a policy from expert demonstrations when the reward function is unavailable. A difficulty is that demonstrated behavior may be noisy or inconsistently optimal. This paper studies a distributionally robust formulation that uses an adversarial construction to guard against overly optimistic conclusions from the demonstrations.

The analysis connects distributionally robust imitation learning with maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning. In this view, the robust objective maximizes a generalized form of entropy. For a class of losses that add contributions over states and actions, the authors transform the objective into a convex optimization problem with a polynomial number of variables.

The resulting method can optimize both stationary policies and policies that change over time. It also avoids repeatedly solving an inner reinforcement learning problem, a requirement of prevalent earlier approaches. Experiments on synthetic data and a highway driving environment show significant benefits from the new optimization method. The contribution combines a robustness-based account of imperfect demonstrations with a tractable optimization formulation for the stated class of losses.
summary.tldr: Distributionally robust imitation learning connects generalized entropy with a convex formulation for learning from imperfect demonstrations.

title: Distributionally Robust Imitation Learning

abstract: Learning to reconstruct 3D garments is important for dressing 3D human bodies of different shapes in different poses. Previous works typically rely on 2D images as input, which however suffer from the scale and pose ambiguities. To circumvent the problems caused by 2D images, we propose a principled framework, Garment4D, that uses 3D point cloud sequences of dressed humans for garment reconstruction. Garment4D has three dedicated steps: sequential garments registration, canonical garment estimation, and posed garment reconstruction. The main challenges are two-fold: 1) effective 3D feature learning for fine details, and 2) capture of garment dynamics caused by the interaction between garments and the human body, especially for loose garments like skirts. To unravel these problems, we introduce a novel Proposal-Guided Hierarchical Feature Network and Iterative Graph Convolution Network, which integrate both high-level semantic features and low-level geometric features for fine details reconstruction. Furthermore, we propose a Temporal Transformer for smooth garment motions capture. Unlike non-parametric methods, the reconstructed garment meshes by our method are separable from the human body and have strong interpretability, which is desirable for downstream tasks. As the first attempt at this task, high-quality reconstruction results are qualitatively and quantitatively illustrated through extensive experiments. Codes are available at https://github.com/hongfz16/Garment4D.
