title: Garment4D: Garment Reconstruction from Point Cloud Sequences

abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm to solve a range of complex yet specific control tasks. Training generalist agents that can quickly adapt to new tasks remains an outstanding challenge. Recent advances in unsupervised RL have shown that pre-training RL agents with self-supervised intrinsic rewards can result in efficient adaptation. However, these algorithms have been hard to compare and develop due to the lack of a unified benchmark. To this end, we introduce the Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning Benchmark (URLB). URLB consists of two phases: reward-free pre-training and downstream task adaptation with extrinsic rewards. Building on the DeepMind Control Suite, we provide twelve continuous control tasks from three domains for evaluation and open-source code for eight leading unsupervised RL methods. We find that the implemented baselines make progress but are not able to solve URLB and propose directions for future research.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents can solve complex individual control tasks, but adapting quickly to new tasks remains difficult. URLB provides a common benchmark for comparing methods built around that idea.

The benchmark separates evaluation into two phases. During pretraining, the agent does not receive the downstream task's external rewards. During adaptation, it receives extrinsic rewards for the task it must learn. This structure makes the transition from general preparation to task-specific learning central to the evaluation.

Built on the DeepMind Control Suite, URLB contains twelve continuous-control tasks across three domains. The authors provide open-source implementations of eight leading unsupervised reinforcement-learning methods. These baselines make progress but do not solve the benchmark. The findings establish a shared challenge for evaluating adaptation, while the common tasks and implementations support comparison and further development of methods intended to produce more broadly useful agents.
summary.tldr: URLB standardizes reward-free pretraining and rewarded task adaptation, revealing remaining challenges across twelve control tasks and eight implemented methods.

title: URLB: Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning Benchmark

abstract: Domain generalization aims at performing well on unseen test environments with data from a limited number of training environments. Despite a proliferation of proposed algorithms for this task, assessing their performance both theoretically and empirically is still very challenging. Distributional matching algorithms such as (Conditional) Domain Adversarial Networks [Ganin et al., 2016, Long et al., 2018] are popular and enjoy empirical success, but they lack formal guarantees. Other approaches such as Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) require a prohibitively large number of training environments---linear in the dimension of the spurious feature space $d_s$---even on simple data models like the one proposed by [Rosenfeld et al., 2021]. Under a variant of this model, we show that ERM and IRM can fail to find the optimal invariant predictor with $o(d_s)$ environments. We then present an iterative feature matching algorithm that is guaranteed with high probability to find the optimal invariant predictor after seeing only $O(\log d_s)$ environments. Our results provide the first theoretical justification for distribution-matching algorithms widely used in practice under a concrete nontrivial data model.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks whether a model trained in a limited set of environments can perform well in unseen ones. A central difficulty is separating stable predictive information from spurious features whose usefulness changes across environments. Although distribution-matching methods have empirical success, the paper notes that formal guarantees have been lacking.

Under a variant of an existing data model, the authors show that empirical risk minimization and invariant risk minimization can fail to recover the optimal invariant predictor when the number of environments is sublinear in the spurious-feature dimension. This gives a concrete setting in which having too few training environments obstructs those methods.

The proposed iterative feature matching algorithm has a stronger guarantee in that model: with high probability, it finds the optimal invariant predictor using only a logarithmic number of environments in the spurious dimension. The result is conditional on the modeled setting, rather than a guarantee for arbitrary distribution shifts. Its significance is to provide a theoretical explanation for how distribution matching can reduce the environment requirements of invariant prediction.
summary.tldr: Under a specified data model, iterative feature matching recovers an optimal invariant predictor with only logarithmically many training environments.

title: Iterative Feature Matching: Toward Provable Domain Generalization with Logarithmic Environments

abstract: A good state representation is crucial to solving complicated reinforcement learning (RL) challenges. Many recent works focus on designing auxiliary losses for learning informative representations. Unfortunately, these handcrafted objectives rely heavily on expert knowledge and may be sub-optimal. In this paper, we propose a principled and universal method for learning better representations with auxiliary loss functions, named Automated Auxiliary Loss Search (A2LS), which automatically searches for top-performing auxiliary loss functions for RL. Specifically, based on the collected trajectory data, we define a general auxiliary loss space of size $7.5 \times 10^{20}$ and explore the space with an efficient evolutionary search strategy. Empirical results show that the discovered auxiliary loss (namely, A2-winner) significantly improves the performance on both high-dimensional (image) and low-dimensional (vector) unseen tasks with much higher efficiency, showing promising generalization ability to different settings and even different benchmark domains. We conduct a statistical analysis to reveal the relations between patterns of auxiliary losses and RL performance.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning depends heavily on how well an agent represents its state. Auxiliary losses provide additional training objectives that can help build informative representations, but designing them usually requires expert judgment. This paper asks whether a search procedure can discover useful objectives instead of relying entirely on handcrafted choices.

Automated Auxiliary Loss Search defines a space of 7.5 × 10^20 possible auxiliary losses using collected trajectory data. It explores that space with an efficient evolutionary search strategy. The contribution is a systematic way to choose representation-learning objectives from a very large set of candidates, linking that choice to reinforcement learning performance.

The discovered objective, called A2-winner, significantly improves reported performance and efficiency on unseen tasks with both image observations and vector observations. Its results also suggest promising transfer across settings and benchmark domains. A statistical analysis examines how patterns in auxiliary losses relate to learning performance. These findings support automated objective design as a route to reusable representation learning, while the generalization claim remains grounded in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: A2LS searches a large space of auxiliary objectives and discovers a loss that improves reinforcement learning across unseen image and vector tasks.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Automated Auxiliary Loss Search

abstract: Value iteration (VI) is a foundational dynamic programming method, important for learning and planning in optimal control and reinforcement learning. VI proceeds in batches, where the update to the value of each state must be completed before the next batch of updates can begin. Completing a single batch is prohibitively expensive if the state space is large, rendering VI impractical for many applications. Asynchronous VI helps to address the large state space problem by updating one state at a time, in-place and in an arbitrary order. However, Asynchronous VI still requires a maximization over the entire action space, making it impractical for domains with large action space. To address this issue, we propose doubly-asynchronous value iteration (DAVI), a new algorithm that generalizes the idea of asynchrony from states to states and actions. More concretely, DAVI maximizes over a sampled subset of actions that can be of any user-defined size. This simple approach of using sampling to reduce computation maintains similarly appealing theoretical properties to VI without the need to wait for a full sweep through the entire action space in each update. In this paper, we show DAVI converges to the optimal value function with probability one, converges at a near-geometric rate with probability $1-\delta$, and returns a near-optimal policy in computation time that nearly matches a previously established bound for VI. We also empirically demonstrate DAVI's effectiveness in several experiments.

paragraphs: Value iteration computes values for states by repeatedly considering their possible actions. Updating one state at a time already avoids the need to finish a full batch of state updates. However, ordinary asynchronous value iteration still searches the complete action set for each update, which becomes expensive when many actions are available.

Doubly-Asynchronous Value Iteration extends the same computational flexibility to actions. Each update maximizes over a sampled subset of actions, with a subset size chosen by the user. This reduces the work required for an individual update without waiting for a complete sweep through the action space.

The authors prove convergence to the optimal value function with probability one and a near-geometric convergence rate with probability at least one minus delta. They also establish a computation-time guarantee for obtaining a near-optimal policy that nearly matches a previous value-iteration bound. Experiments support the method’s effectiveness, showing that sampled action updates can retain strong theoretical properties while making updates less costly.
summary.tldr: DAVI samples actions during value updates while retaining probability-one convergence and strong convergence-rate guarantees.

title: Doubly-Asynchronous Value Iteration: Making Value Iteration Asynchronous in Actions

abstract: The Mean-Teacher (MT) scheme is widely adopted in semi-supervised object detection (SSOD). In MT, sparse pseudo labels, offered by the final predictions of the teacher (e.g., after Non Maximum Suppression (NMS) post-processing), are adopted for the dense supervision for the student via hand-crafted label assignment. However, the "sparse-to-dense'' paradigm complicates the pipeline of SSOD, and simultaneously neglects the powerful direct, dense teacher supervision. In this paper, we attempt to directly leverage the dense guidance of teacher to supervise student training, i.e., the "dense-to-dense'' paradigm. Specifically, we propose the Inverse NMS Clustering (INC) and Rank Matching (RM) to instantiate the dense supervision, without the widely used, conventional sparse pseudo labels. INC leads the student to group candidate boxes into clusters in NMS as the teacher does, which is implemented by learning grouping information revealed in NMS procedure of the teacher. After obtaining the same grouping scheme as the teacher via INC, the student further imitates the rank distribution of the teacher over clustered candidates through Rank Matching. With the proposed INC and RM, we integrate Dense Teacher Guidance into Semi-Supervised Object Detection (termed "DTG-SSOD''), successfully abandoning sparse pseudo labels and enabling more informative learning on unlabeled data. On COCO benchmark, our DTG-SSOD achieves state-of-the-art performance under various labelling ratios. For example, under 10% labelling ratio, DTG-SSOD improves the supervised baseline from 26.9 to 35.9 mAP, outperforming the previous best method Soft Teacher by 1.9 points.

These results support dense teacher guidance as an effective source of supervision in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: DTG-SSOD improves semi-supervised detection by teaching students the teacher's candidate-box groupings and rankings directly.

title: DTG-SSOD: Dense Teacher Guidance for Semi-Supervised Object Detection

abstract: The best neural architecture for a given machine learning problem depends on many factors: not only the complexity and structure of the dataset, but also on resource constraints including latency, compute, energy consumption, etc. Neural architecture search (NAS) for tabular datasets is an important but under-explored problem. Previous NAS algorithms designed for image search spaces incorporate resource constraints directly into the reinforcement learning (RL) rewards. However, for NAS on tabular datasets, this protocol often discovers suboptimal architectures. This paper develops TabNAS, a new and more effective approach to handle resource constraints in tabular NAS using an RL controller motivated by the idea of rejection sampling. TabNAS immediately discards any architecture that violates the resource constraints without training or learning from that architecture. TabNAS uses a Monte-Carlo-based correction to the RL policy gradient update to account for this extra filtering step. Results on several tabular datasets demonstrate the superiority of TabNAS over previous reward-shaping methods: it finds better models that obey the constraints.

paragraphs: Choosing a neural-network architecture involves balancing predictive performance with constraints such as latency, computation, and energy use. This paper studies that search problem for tabular datasets. It observes that incorporating resource constraints into a reinforcement-learning controller’s reward, as done in earlier image-oriented search methods, often produces suboptimal tabular architectures.

TabNAS handles the constraints through a rejection-sampling-inspired procedure. When the controller proposes an architecture that violates a resource constraint, the method immediately discards it without training it or learning from that architecture. The search therefore filters out infeasible candidates before spending effort evaluating their predictive performance.

Filtering changes the sampling process, so TabNAS includes a Monte Carlo correction in the controller’s policy-gradient update to account for it. This correction is an integral part of the proposed approach. Experiments on several tabular datasets show that TabNAS finds better models satisfying the constraints than previous reward-shaping methods. The results support explicitly filtering candidate architectures, together with the corresponding update correction, for the evaluated constrained search problems.
summary.tldr: TabNAS rejects resource-violating architectures and corrects its search updates to find better feasible models for tabular data.

title: TabNAS: Rejection Sampling for Neural Architecture Search on Tabular Datasets

abstract: Releasing all pairwise shortest path (APSP) distances between vertices on general graphs under weight Differential Privacy (DP) is known as a challenging task. In previous work, to achieve DP with some fixed budget, with high probability the maximal absolute error among all published pairwise distances is roughly O(n) where n is the number of nodes. It was shown that this error could be reduced for some special graphs, which, however, is hard for general graphs. Therefore, whether the approximation error can be reduced to sublinear is posted as an interesting open problem.In this paper, we break the linear barrier on the distance approximation error of previous result, by proposing an algorithm that releases a constructed synthetic graph privately. Computing all pairwise distances on the constructed graph only introduces O(n^{1/2}) error in answering all pairwise shortest path distances for fixed privacy parameter. Our method is based on a novel graph diameter (link length) augmentation via constructing ``shortcuts'' for the paths. By adding a set of shortcut edges to the original graph, we show that any node pair has a shortest path with link length O(n^{1/2}). Then by adding noises with some positive mean to the edge weights, the new graph is differentially private and can be published to answer all pairwise shortest path distances with O(n^{1/2}) approximation error using standard APSP computation. Numerical examples are also provided.Additionally, we also consider the graph with small feedback vertex set number. A feedback vertex set (FVS) of a graph is a set of vertices whose removal leaves a graph without cycles, and the feedback vertex set number of a graph, k, is the size of a smallest feedback vertex set. We propose a DP algorithm with error rate O(k), which improves the error of general graphs provided k=o(n^{1/2}).

paragraphs: Publishing shortest-path distances for every pair of graph vertices while protecting edge weights is difficult. For general graphs, earlier work had roughly linear maximum absolute error in the number of vertices at a fixed privacy budget. This paper breaks that linear barrier with a method that privately releases a constructed synthetic graph.

The construction adds shortcut edges so that every vertex pair has a shortest path using only O(sqrt(n)) links. Noise with a positive mean is then added to edge weights to make the graph differentially private. Standard all-pairs shortest-path computation on the released graph gives O(sqrt(n)) approximation error for fixed privacy parameters. Shortening the number of links in paths is central to the construction.

The authors also study graphs with a small feedback vertex set: a set of vertices whose removal eliminates cycles. If the smallest such set has size k, their specialized algorithm achieves O(k) error. This improves on the general-graph result when k grows more slowly than sqrt(n), making the graph's cycle structure relevant to attainable accuracy.
summary.tldr: A private synthetic graph with shortcut edges reduces all-pairs shortest-path approximation error from roughly linear to O(sqrt(n)).

title: Private Graph All-Pairwise-Shortest-Path Distance Release with Improved Error Rate

abstract: Text generation is of great importance to many natural language processing applications. However, maximization-based decoding methods (e.g., beam search) of neural language models often lead to degenerate solutions---the generated text is unnatural and contains undesirable repetitions. Existing approaches introduce stochasticity via sampling or modify training objectives to decrease the probabilities of certain tokens (e.g., unlikelihood training). However, they often lead to solutions that lack coherence. In this work, we show that an underlying reason for model degeneration is the anisotropic distribution of token representations. We present a contrastive solution: (i) SimCTG, a contrastive training objective to calibrate the model's representation space, and (ii) a decoding method---contrastive search---to encourage diversity while maintaining coherence in the generated text. Extensive experiments and analyses on three benchmarks from two languages demonstrate that our proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art text generation methods as evaluated by both human and automatic metrics.

paragraphs: Neural language models can produce repetitive, unnatural text when decoding favors the most likely continuation. Adding randomness or discouraging particular tokens can reduce repetition, but the resulting text may lose coherence. This paper investigates the model’s internal token representations as an underlying contributor to that problem.

The authors identify an anisotropic representation space: token representations are distributed unevenly across directions. Their proposed framework addresses both training and generation. SimCTG is a contrastive training objective intended to calibrate that space. Contrastive search is a decoding method designed to encourage varied text while preserving a coherent continuation. Together, these components connect the organization of internal representations to the choices made when producing text.

Experiments and analyses cover three benchmarks in two languages. The authors report improvements over state-of-the-art generation methods according to both human assessments and automatic metrics. These findings support addressing representation geometry alongside decoding, rather than treating unwanted repetition only as a problem of which token to select next.
summary.tldr: SimCTG and contrastive search jointly address token representations and decoding to improve text diversity while maintaining coherence.

title: A Contrastive Framework for Neural Text Generation

abstract: The promise of Mobile Health (mHealth) is the ability to use wearable sensors to monitor participant physiology at high frequencies during daily life to enable temporally-precise health interventions. However, a major challenge is frequent missing data. Despite a rich imputation literature, existing techniques are ineffective for the pulsative signals which comprise many mHealth applications, and a lack of available datasets has stymied progress. We address this gap with PulseImpute, the first large-scale pulsative signal imputation challenge which includes realistic mHealth missingness models, an extensive set of baselines, and clinically-relevant downstream tasks. Our baseline models include a novel transformer-based architecture designed to exploit the structure of pulsative signals. We hope that PulseImpute will enable the ML community to tackle this important and challenging task.

paragraphs: Wearable sensors can monitor physiology frequently during daily life, potentially supporting precisely timed health interventions. Missing measurements are a major obstacle. The paper focuses on filling gaps in pulsative signals, whose repeating pulse structure makes them a challenging target for existing imputation methods.

PulseImpute provides a large-scale benchmark for this problem. It combines realistic models of missing data in mobile health with a broad set of baseline methods and clinically relevant downstream tasks. These components bring together the conditions under which data disappear, methods for reconstructing them, and tasks that make the reconstruction useful.

The baseline collection includes a new transformer architecture designed to exploit the structure of pulsative signals. The paper's central contribution is the benchmark and its accompanying methods, addressing the shortage of available datasets that has hindered progress. Its stated aim is to enable further machine-learning research on physiological signal imputation; the abstract does not present the benchmark as an already demonstrated improvement in patient outcomes.
summary.tldr: PulseImpute supplies a large-scale benchmark, realistic missingness models, and baselines for reconstructing missing pulsative physiological signals.

title: PulseImpute: A Novel Benchmark Task for Pulsative Physiological Signal Imputation

abstract: Learning from label proportions (LLP) is a weakly supervised classification problem where data points are grouped into bags, and the label proportions within each bag are observed instead of the instance-level labels. The task is to learn a classifier to predict the labels of future individual instances. Prior work on LLP for multi-class data has yet to develop a theoretically grounded algorithm. In this work, we propose an approach to LLP based on a reduction to learning with label noise, using the forward correction (FC) loss of \textcite{Patrini2017MakingDN}. We establish an excess risk bound and generalization error analysis for our approach, while also extending the theory of the FC loss which may be of independent interest. Our approach demonstrates improved empirical performance in deep learning scenarios across multiple datasets and architectures, compared to the leading methods.

paragraphs: Learning from label proportions addresses a situation where examples arrive in groups and only each group's class proportions are known. Individual labels remain unavailable, yet the goal is to classify individual examples in the future. This makes the supervision indirect: the learner must extract useful classification information from aggregate descriptions.

The paper turns this problem into one of learning with noisy labels. It uses the forward correction loss to build that connection, providing a theoretically grounded approach for multiclass data. This reduction matters because it makes tools for handling unreliable labels applicable to a setting where the original supervision consists of group-level proportions.

The authors establish an excess-risk bound and analyze generalization error for their method. They also extend the theory of the forward correction loss itself. Experiments with deep-learning models across multiple datasets and architectures show improved performance over leading methods. The result combines a mathematical account of learning from aggregate supervision with evidence that the approach can improve practical individual-level classification.
summary.tldr: Reducing learning from label proportions to noisy-label learning yields a multiclass method with theoretical guarantees and improved empirical performance.

title: Learning from Label Proportions by Learning with Label Noise

abstract: Sketch design concepts are recurring patterns found in parametric CAD sketches. Though rarely explicitly formalized by the CAD designers, these concepts are implicitly used in design for modularity and regularity. In this paper, we propose a learning based approach that discovers the modular concepts by induction over raw sketches. We propose the dual implicit-explicit representation of concept structures that allows implicit detection and explicit generation, and the separation of structure generation and parameter instantiation for parameterized concept generation, to learn modular concepts by end-to-end training. We demonstrate the design concept learning on a large scale CAD sketch dataset and show its applications for design intent interpretation and auto-completion.

paragraphs: Parametric CAD sketches contain recurring design patterns that help designers build modular and regular structures. Designers often use these patterns without explicitly defining them as reusable concepts. This paper develops a learning approach that discovers such concepts directly from raw sketches, turning repeated structure in existing designs into something a model can recognize and generate.

The method represents concept structure in two complementary ways. An implicit representation supports detecting concepts in sketches, while an explicit representation supports generating them. It also separates the generation of a concept's structure from the assignment of its parameters. This distinction lets the learned concept describe a reusable pattern whose particular parameter values can vary.

These components are learned together through end-to-end training. The authors demonstrate concept learning on a large CAD sketch dataset and show applications to interpreting design intent and automatically completing sketches. The significance is that the learned units concern recurring modular structure, providing a way to connect sketch recognition with the generation of parameterized design elements.
summary.tldr: The method learns recurring modular concepts from CAD sketches and uses them to interpret design intent and complete sketches.

title: Discovering Design Concepts for CAD Sketches

abstract: Learning disentangled representations is important for unraveling the underlying complex interactions between latent generative factors. Disentanglement has been formalized using a symmetry-centric notion for unstructured spaces, however, graphs have eluded a similarly rigorous treatment. We fill this gap with a new notion of conditional symmetry for disentanglement, and leverage tools from Lie algebras to encode graph properties into subgroups using suitable adaptations of generative models such as Variational Autoencoders. Unlike existing works on disentanglement, the proposed models segregate the latent space into uncoupled and entangled parts. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets suggest that these models can learn effective disengaged representations, and improve performance on downstream tasks such as few-shot classification and molecular generation.

paragraphs: Disentangled representations aim to make underlying generative factors easier to distinguish and understand. Symmetry-based definitions already existed for unstructured spaces, but graphs lacked a comparable rigorous treatment. This paper develops a graph-focused notion of conditional symmetry to address that gap and reason about how latent factors interact.

The authors use tools from Lie algebras to encode graph properties into subgroups, adapting generative models such as variational autoencoders. Their models separate the latent space into uncoupled and entangled components. This distinction allows the representation to express both factors that can be separated and factors whose interactions remain coupled within the model.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets suggest that the proposed models learn effective disengaged representations. They also show improved performance on downstream tasks including few-shot classification and molecular generation. These findings support the usefulness of the proposed framework for learning graph representations. The contribution combines a more rigorous symmetry-based treatment with a model structure that explicitly accommodates both separation and interaction among latent factors.
summary.tldr: A conditional-symmetry framework separates graph latent representations into uncoupled and entangled parts, with promising results for classification and molecular generation.

title: Symmetry-induced Disentanglement on Graphs

abstract: This paper studies a conceptually simple extension of Masked Autoencoders (MAE) to spatiotemporal representation learning from videos. We randomly mask out spacetime patches in videos and learn an autoencoder to reconstruct them in pixels. Interestingly, we show that our MAE method can learn strong representations with almost no inductive bias on spacetime (only except for patch and positional embeddings), and spacetime-agnostic random masking performs the best. We observe that the optimal masking ratio is as high as 90% (vs. 75% on images), supporting the hypothesis that this ratio is related to information redundancy of the data. A high masking ratio leads to a large speedup, e.g., > 4x in wall-clock time or even more. We report competitive results on several challenging video datasets using vanilla Vision Transformers. We observe that MAE can outperform supervised pre-training by large margins. We further report encouraging results of training on real-world, uncurated Instagram data. Our study suggests that the general framework of masked autoencoding (BERT, MAE, etc.) can be a unified methodology for representation learning with minimal domain knowledge.

paragraphs: This paper extends masked autoencoding to video by hiding randomly selected patches across space and time and training an autoencoder to reconstruct their pixels. The resulting task teaches representations from the video itself. Beyond patch and positional embeddings, the approach incorporates almost no explicit assumptions about spatial or temporal structure.

The experiments find that random masking without special treatment of space and time performs best. The optimal masking ratio reaches 90%, compared with 75% for images. This supports the hypothesis that useful masking levels relate to information redundancy. The high masking ratio also produces substantial computational savings, including reported wall-clock speedups greater than fourfold.

Using standard Vision Transformers, the method achieves competitive results on several challenging video datasets and can outperform supervised pretraining by large margins. Training on uncurated Instagram video data also gives encouraging results. Together, these observations suggest that masked reconstruction can support strong video representations with little domain-specific design, extending the case for masked autoencoding as a broadly applicable representation-learning framework.
summary.tldr: Reconstructing heavily masked video patches learns strong representations with minimal spacetime assumptions and substantial training speedups.

title: Masked Autoencoders As Spatiotemporal Learners

abstract: Given a set of points of interest, a volumetric spanner is a subset of the points using which all the points can be expressed using "small" coefficients (measured in an appropriate norm). Formally, given a set of vectors $X = [v_1, v_2, \dots, v_n]$, the goal is to find $T \subseteq [n]$ such that every $v \in X$ can be expressed as $\sum_{i\in T} \alpha_i v_i$, with $\Vert \alpha \Vert$ being small. This notion, which has also been referred to as a well-conditioned basis, has found several applications, including bandit linear optimization, determinant maximization, and matrix low rank approximation. In this paper, we give almost optimal bounds on the size of volumetric spanners for all $\ell_p$ norms, and show that they can be constructed using a simple local search procedure. We then show the applications of our result to other tasks and in particular the problem of finding coresets for the Minimum Volume Enclosing Ellipsoid (MVEE) problem.

paragraphs: A volumetric spanner selects a subset of vectors that can represent every vector in a larger collection using small coefficients. The requirement concerns more than whether representation is possible: the coefficients must remain small under a chosen norm. This makes the selected subset useful as a well-conditioned representation of the original collection.

The paper establishes nearly optimal bounds on how large such a subset needs to be across all ℓp norms. It also shows that a simple local search procedure can construct these spanners. The result therefore addresses both the number of vectors required and an algorithmic route to finding them.

Volumetric spanners already have applications in bandit linear optimization, determinant maximization, and low-rank matrix approximation. The authors develop further applications of their bounds, particularly to constructing coresets for the minimum-volume enclosing ellipsoid problem. The broader value is a compact geometric representation with controlled coefficients, together with size guarantees that are close to optimal for the norms considered.
summary.tldr: Nearly optimal size bounds and a simple local search construction strengthen volumetric spanners across all ℓp norms.

title: Tight Bounds for Volumetric Spanners and Applications

abstract: What can be learned about causality and experimentation from passive data? This question is salient given recent successes of passively-trained language models in interactive domains such as tool use. Passive learning is inherently limited. However, we show that purely passive learning can in fact allow an agent to learn generalizable strategies for determining and using causal structures, as long as the agent can intervene at test time. We formally illustrate that learning a strategy of first experimenting, then seeking goals, can allow generalization from passive learning in principle. We then show empirically that agents trained via imitation on expert data can indeed generalize at test time to infer and use causal links which are never present in the training data; these agents can also generalize experimentation strategies to novel variable sets never observed in training.We then show that strategies for causal intervention and exploitation can be generalized from passive data even in a more complex environment with high-dimensional observations, with the support of natural language explanations. Explanations can even allow passive learners to generalize out-of-distribution from perfectly-confounded training data. Finally, we show that language models, trained only on passive next-word prediction, can generalize causal intervention strategies from a few-shot prompt containing explanations and reasoning. These results highlight the surprising power of passive learning of active causal strategies, and have implications for understanding the behaviors and capabilities of language models.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether an agent trained only on passive data can learn how to perform useful causal experiments. The crucial condition is that it can intervene at test time. The authors formally show that learning a strategy of experimenting first and pursuing goals afterward can, in principle, support generalization. Passive training can therefore teach a procedure for gathering causal knowledge later.

Empirically, agents trained by imitating experts infer and use causal links absent from their training data. They also transfer experimentation strategies to variable sets never encountered during training. In a more complex environment with high-dimensional observations, natural-language explanations help agents generalize intervention and exploitation strategies. Explanations even support out-of-distribution generalization from perfectly confounded training data.

The authors further show that language models trained through passive next-word prediction can generalize causal-intervention strategies from a few-shot prompt containing explanations and reasoning. These results concern learning how to act and investigate once interaction becomes possible. They demonstrate a route from passive examples to active causal behavior, while retaining the essential role of test-time interventions.
summary.tldr: Passive training can teach generalizable causal-experimentation strategies when agents are able to intervene at test time.

title: Passive learning of active causal strategies in agents and language models

abstract: Latent image representations arising from vision-language models have proved immensely useful for a variety of downstream tasks. However, their utility is limited by their entanglement with respect to different visual attributes. For instance, recent work has shown that CLIP image representations are often biased toward specific visual properties (such as objects or actions) in an unpredictable manner. In this paper, we propose to separate representations of the different visual modalities in CLIP’s joint vision-language space by leveraging the association between parts of speech and specific visual modes of variation (e.g. nouns relate to objects, adjectives describe appearance). This is achieved by formulating an appropriate component analysis model that learns subspaces capturing variability corresponding to a specific part of speech, while jointly minimising variability to the rest. Such a subspace yields disentangled representations of the different visual properties of an image or text in closed form while respecting the underlying geometry of the manifold on which the representations lie. What’s more, we show the proposed model additionally facilitates learning subspaces corresponding to specific visual appearances (e.g. artists’ painting styles), which enables the selective removal of entire visual themes from CLIP-based text-to-image synthesis. We validate the model both qualitatively, by visualising the subspace projections with a text-to-image model and by preventing the imitation of artists’ styles, and quantitatively, through class invariance metrics and improvements to baseline zero-shot classification.

paragraphs: CLIP representations combine different image properties in ways that can make particular attributes difficult to isolate. An image's objects, actions, and appearance may receive uneven or unpredictable emphasis. This paper uses associations between grammatical categories and visual properties, such as nouns with objects and adjectives with appearance, to separate these sources of variation.

The authors formulate a component-analysis model that learns subspaces emphasizing variation linked to a chosen part of speech while reducing variation linked to the others. The resulting representations can be obtained in closed form and respect the geometry of the underlying representation manifold. The same framework can also learn subspaces associated with particular visual appearances, including artists' painting styles.

Experiments assess the subspaces through visualizations, class-invariance measures, and improvements to baseline zero-shot classification. The paper also demonstrates selective removal of visual themes from CLIP-based image synthesis, including preventing imitation of artists' styles in the evaluations. These findings connect more separated representations with practical control over both recognition and generated visual appearance.
summary.tldr: Parts-of-speech-guided subspaces separate CLIP attributes and enable selective control over visual themes in image synthesis.

title: Parts of Speech–Grounded Subspaces in Vision-Language Models

abstract: We show that a simple single-pass semi-streaming variant of the Pivot algorithm for Correlation Clustering gives a (3+eps)-approximation using O(n/eps) words of memory. This is a slight improvement over the recent results of Cambus, Kuhn, Lindy, Pai, and Uitto, who gave a (3+eps)-approximation using O(n log n) words of memory, and Behnezhad, Charikar, Ma, and Tan, who gave a 5-approximation using O(n) words of memory. One of the main contributions of our paper is that the algorithm and its analysis are simple and easy to understand.

This is a slight improvement over the recent results of Cambus, Kuhn, Lindy, Pai, and Uitto, who gave a (3+eps)-approximation using O(n log n) words of memory, and Behnezhad, Charikar, Ma, and Tan, who gave a 5-approximation using O(n) words of memory. paragraphs: This paper presents a simple streaming variant of the Pivot algorithm for correlation clustering. The algorithm processes the input in a single pass and uses a controlled amount of memory. Its main result combines a near-three approximation guarantee with a memory requirement that depends explicitly on an accuracy parameter, epsilon.

Specifically, it gives a (3+epsilon)-approximation using O(n/epsilon) words of memory. The bound expresses a tradeoff: bringing the approximation factor closer to three increases the memory allowance. For a fixed epsilon, the stated memory requirement scales linearly with n. The single-pass property means the algorithm does not need repeated scans of the input.

The authors compare this result with earlier guarantees of a (3+epsilon)-approximation using O(n log n) memory and a 5-approximation using O(n) memory. They describe their improvement as slight and emphasize that both the algorithm and its analysis are easy to understand. The contribution is therefore a combination of a competitive guarantee, explicit memory dependence, and conceptual simplicity.
summary.tldr: A simple single-pass Pivot variant achieves a (3+epsilon)-approximation for correlation clustering using O(n/epsilon) words of memory.

title: Single-Pass Pivot Algorithm for Correlation Clustering. Keep it simple!

abstract: By encoding time series as a string of numerical digits, we can frame time series forecasting as next-token prediction in text. Developing this approach, we find that large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-3 and LLaMA-2 can surprisingly zero-shot extrapolate time series at a level comparable to or exceeding the performance of purpose-built time series models trained on the downstream tasks. To facilitate this performance, we propose procedures for effectively tokenizing time series data and converting discrete distributions over tokens into highly flexible densities over continuous values. We argue the success of LLMs for time series stems from their ability to naturally represent multimodal distributions, in conjunction with biases for simplicity, and repetition, which align with the salient features in many time series, such as repeated seasonal trends. We also show how LLMs can naturally handle missing data without imputation through non-numerical text, accommodate textual side information, and answer questions to help explain predictions. While we find that increasing model size generally improves performance on time series, we show GPT-4 can perform worse than GPT-3 because of how it tokenizes numbers, and poor uncertainty calibration, which is likely the result of alignment interventions such as RLHF.

paragraphs: This paper turns time-series forecasting into text continuation by expressing numerical observations as strings of digits. Under this formulation, a language model predicts future numbers through next-token prediction. The authors find that GPT-3 and LLaMA-2 can forecast without task-specific training at levels comparable to, or better than, purpose-built models trained on the downstream tasks.

Making the approach effective requires careful numerical tokenization and a way to convert discrete token probabilities into densities over continuous values. The authors argue that language models' ability to represent multiple possible outcomes, together with preferences for simplicity and repetition, suits recurring time-series structure. They also demonstrate using text to represent missing observations, supply additional information, and ask questions about predictions.

Larger models generally perform better in the reported work, but the relationship has exceptions. GPT-4 can underperform GPT-3 because of numerical tokenization and poorly calibrated uncertainty. The authors suggest that alignment interventions such as RLHF likely contribute to the calibration issue. This qualification shows why language-model forecasting quality depends on more than model size.
summary.tldr: Language models can forecast numerical time series zero-shot, though tokenization and uncertainty calibration strongly affect performance.

title: Large Language Models Are Zero-Shot Time Series Forecasters

abstract: Vision models are often vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) samples without adapting. While visual prompts offer a lightweight method of input-space adaptation for large-scale vision models, they rely on a high-dimensional additive vector and labeled data. This leads to overfitting when adapting models in a self-supervised test-time setting without labels. We introduce convolutional visual prompts (CVP) for label-free test-time adaptation for robust visual perception. The structured nature of CVP demands fewer trainable parameters, less than 1\% compared to standard visual prompts, combating overfitting. Extensive experiments and analysis on a wide variety of OOD visual perception tasks show that our approach is effective, improving robustness by up to 5.87\% over several large-scale models.

The structured nature of CVP demands fewer trainable parameters, less than 1\% compared to standard visual prompts, combating overfitting. paragraphs: Vision models can become less reliable when their inputs differ from the data encountered during training. Visual prompting adapts the input presented to a model, offering a lightweight way to respond to that shift. However, standard prompts use large additive vectors and rely on labeled data, creating an overfitting problem when adaptation must happen without labels at test time.

This paper introduces convolutional visual prompts, or CVP, for that label-free setting. Their convolutional structure uses fewer than one percent of the trainable parameters required by standard visual prompts. The central idea is to restrict the adaptation through structure, reducing the number of adjustable quantities that could overfit during self-supervised adaptation.

Experiments across varied out-of-distribution visual perception tasks report robustness improvements of up to 5.87 percent over several large-scale models. That figure describes the largest reported improvement, rather than a uniform gain. The findings support structured input adaptation as a practical approach to improving robustness when labels are unavailable at deployment.
summary.tldr: Convolutional visual prompts use very few trainable parameters to improve vision-model robustness through label-free test-time adaptation.

title: Convolutional Visual Prompt for Robust Visual Perception

abstract: Graph Neural Network (GNN) architectures are defined by their implementations of update and aggregation modules. While many works focus on new ways to parametrise the update modules, the aggregation modules receive comparatively little attention. Because it is difficult to parametrise aggregation functions, currently most methods select a ``standard aggregator'' such as mean, sum, or max. While this selection is often made without any reasoning, it has been shown that the choice in aggregator has a significant impact on performance, and the best choice in aggregator is problem-dependent. Since aggregation is a lossy operation, it is crucial to select the most appropriate aggregator in order to minimise information loss. In this paper, we present GenAgg, a generalised aggregation operator, which parametrises a function space that includes all standard aggregators. In our experiments, we show that GenAgg is able to represent the standard aggregators with much higher accuracy than baseline methods. We also show that using GenAgg as a drop-in replacement for an existing aggregator in a GNN often leads to a significant boost in performance across various tasks.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks combine information through aggregation operations such as mean, sum, or maximum. Combining many inputs into one representation inevitably discards information, and different aggregation choices retain different aspects of those inputs. The best choice depends on the problem, yet aggregation often receives less design attention than the network's update modules.

The paper introduces GenAgg, an aggregation operator with a parameterized function space that includes all standard aggregators. This expands the available aggregation choices within a single operator. Its purpose is to make aggregation more adaptable to the task rather than depending only on an initially selected standard function.

Experiments show that GenAgg represents standard aggregators much more accurately than the compared baseline methods. Replacing an existing GNN aggregator with GenAgg also often produces substantial performance improvements across tasks. These findings suggest that aggregation itself is a useful source of model flexibility. The reported gains are frequent rather than universal, consistent with the paper's emphasis on problem-dependent information loss.
summary.tldr: GenAgg parameterizes a family containing standard graph aggregators and often improves GNN performance when substituted for an existing aggregation function.

title: Generalised f-Mean Aggregation for Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their recent impressive accomplishments, are notably cost-prohibitive to deploy, particularly for applications involving long-content generation, such as dialogue systems and story writing. Often, a large amount of transient state information, referred to as the $\mathsf{KV}$ $\mathsf{cache}$, is stored in GPU memory in addition to model parameters, scaling linearly with the sequence length and batch size. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach for implementing the $\mathsf{KV}$ $\mathsf{cache}$ which significantly reduces its memory footprint. Our approach is based on the noteworthy observation that a small portion of tokens contributes most of the value when computing attention scores. We call these tokens Heavy Hitters ($\mathsf{H_2}$). Through a comprehensive investigation, we find that ($i$) the emergence of $\mathsf{H_2}$ is natural and strongly correlates with the frequent co-occurrence of tokens in the text, and ($ii$) removing them results in significant performance degradation. Based on these insights, we propose Heavy Hitter Oracle ($\mathsf{H_2O}$), a $\mathsf{KV}$ $\mathsf{cache}$ eviction policy that dynamically retains a balance of recent and $\mathsf{H_2}$ tokens. title: H2O: Heavy-Hitter Oracle for Efficient Generative Inference of Large Language Models

abstract: A long line of works characterizes the sample complexity of regret minimization in sequential decision-making by min-max programs. In the corresponding saddle-point game, the min-player optimizes the sampling distribution against an adversarial max-player that chooses confusing models leading to large regret. The most recent instantiation of this idea is the decision-estimation coefficient (DEC), which was shown to provide nearly tight lower and upper bounds on the worst-case expected regret in structured bandits and reinforcement learning. By re-parametrizing the offset DEC with the confidence radius and solving the corresponding min-max program, we derive an anytime variant of the Estimation-To-Decisions algorithm (Anytime-E2D). Importantly, the algorithm optimizes the exploration-exploitation trade-off online instead of via the analysis. Our formulation leads to a practical algorithm for finite model classes and linear feedback models. We further point out connections to the information ratio, decoupling coefficient and PAC-DEC, and numerically evaluate the performance of E2D on simple examples.

title: Regret Minimization via Saddle Point Optimization

abstract: Knowledge distillation is commonly used to compress an ensemble of models into a single model. In this work we study the problem of progressive ensemble distillation: Given a large, pretrained teacher model , we seek to decompose the model into an ensemble of smaller, low-inference cost student models . The resulting ensemble allows for flexibly tuning accuracy vs. inference cost, which can be useful for a multitude of applications in efficient inference. Our method, B-DISTIL, uses a boosting procedure that allows function composition based aggregation rules to construct expressive ensembles with similar performance as using much smaller student models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of B-DISTIL by decomposing pretrained models across a variety of image, speech, and sensor datasets. Our method comes with strong theoretical guarantees in terms of convergence as well as generalization.

paragraphs: Progressive ensemble distillation starts with a large pretrained teacher and seeks to represent it through an ensemble of smaller student models with low inference costs. The resulting collection supports flexible choices between predictive accuracy and computation. This changes how distillation serves deployment: the output is a set of smaller models that can offer adjustable inference behavior.

The proposed method, B-DISTIL, builds that ensemble using a boosting procedure. Its aggregation rules allow function composition, giving the combined students an expressive way to represent the teacher. This composition is central to the approach because the ensemble must provide useful predictive performance while being assembled from small constituent models.

The authors demonstrate B-DISTIL by decomposing pretrained models across image, speech, and sensor datasets. They also provide theoretical guarantees for convergence and generalization. Together, these contributions support a route from a single large model to an ensemble designed around inference flexibility, with both empirical evaluations across data types and formal analysis of the learning procedure.
summary.tldr: B-DISTIL decomposes a large pretrained model into smaller students that offer a flexible accuracy-versus-inference-cost tradeoff.

title: Progressive Ensemble Distillation: Building Ensembles for Efficient Inference

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) works impressively in some environments and fails catastrophically in others. Ideally, RL theory should be able to provide an understanding of why this is, i.e. bounds predictive of practical performance. Unfortunately, current theory does not quite have this ability. We compare standard deep RL algorithms to prior sample complexity bounds by introducing a new dataset, BRIDGE. It consists of 155 MDPs from common deep RL benchmarks, along with their corresponding tabular representations, which enables us to exactly compute instance-dependent bounds. We find that prior bounds do not correlate well with when deep RL succeeds vs. fails, but discover a surprising property that does. When actions with the highest Q-values under the *random* policy also have the highest Q-values under the *optimal* policy—i.e., when it is optimal to act greedily with respect to the random's policy Q function—deep RL tends to succeed; when they don't, deep RL tends to fail. We generalize this property into a new complexity measure of an MDP that we call the *effective horizon*, which roughly corresponds to how many steps of lookahead search would be needed in that MDP in order to identify the next optimal action, when leaf nodes are evaluated with random rollouts. Using BRIDGE, we show that the effective horizon-based bounds are more closely reflective of the empirical performance of PPO and DQN than prior sample complexity bounds across four metrics. We also show that, unlike existing bounds, the effective horizon can predict the effects of using reward shaping or a pre-trained exploration policy. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/cassidylaidlaw/effective-horizon.

summary.tldr: Effective horizon connects the lookahead needed for good decisions with observed deep reinforcement-learning performance more closely than prior bounds.

title: Bridging RL Theory and Practice with the Effective Horizon

abstract: What role do augmentations play in contrastive learning? Recent work suggests that good augmentations are label-preserving with respect to a specific downstream task. We complicate this picture by showing that label-destroying augmentations can be useful in the foundation model setting, where the goal is to learn diverse, general-purpose representations for multiple downstream tasks. We perform contrastive learning experiments on a range of image and audio datasets with multiple downstream tasks (e.g. for digits superimposed on photographs, predicting the class of one vs. the other). We find that Viewmaker Networks, a recently proposed model for learning augmentations for contrastive learning, produce label-destroying augmentations that stochastically destroy features needed for different downstream tasks. These augmentations are interpretable (e.g. altering shapes, digits, or letters added to images) and surprisingly often result in better performance compared to expert-designed augmentations, despite not preserving label information. To support our empirical results, we theoretically analyze a simple contrastive learning setting with a linear model. In this setting, label-destroying augmentations are crucial for preventing one set of features from suppressing the learning of features useful for another downstream task. Our results highlight the need for analyzing the interaction between multiple downstream tasks when trying to explain the success of foundation models.

paragraphs: A common explanation for effective contrastive-learning augmentations is that they preserve the labels needed for a downstream task. This paper examines a different setting: learning representations for several tasks at once. In that setting, the authors find that augmentations which sometimes destroy task-relevant information can still help produce useful, general-purpose representations.

Experiments span image and audio datasets with multiple downstream tasks. Learned Viewmaker augmentations randomly remove or alter features needed by different tasks, including interpretable changes to shapes, digits, or letters in images. Despite losing some label information, these augmentations often outperform expert-designed alternatives. The findings suggest that preserving every task's information in every augmented view is not always required for strong performance.

In that setting, label-destroying augmentation is crucial for preventing one feature set from suppressing the learning of features useful to another task. The paper therefore motivates analyzing competition among downstream tasks when explaining how augmentations support broadly useful representations.
summary.tldr: Augmentations that randomly destroy task-relevant features can improve multitask representations by reducing competition between feature sets.

title: Feature Dropout: Revisiting the Role of Augmentations in Contrastive Learning

abstract: We investigate the problem of reducing mistake severity for fine-grained classification. Fine-grained classification can be challenging, mainly due to the requirement of knowledge or domain expertise for accurate annotation. However, humans are particularly adept at performing coarse classification as it requires relatively low levels of expertise. To this end, we present a novel approach for Post-Hoc Correction called Hierarchical Ensembles (HiE) that utilizes label hierarchy to improve the performance of fine-grained classification at test-time using the coarse-grained predictions. By only requiring the parents of leaf nodes, our method significantly reduces avg. mistake severity while improving top-1 accuracy on the iNaturalist-19 and tieredImageNet-H datasets, achieving a new state-of-the-art on both benchmarks. We also investigate the efficacy of our approach in the semi-supervised setting. Our approach brings notable gains in top-1 accuracy while significantly decreasing the severity of mistakes as training data decreases for the fine-grained classes. The simplicity and post-hoc nature of HiE renders it practical to be used with any off-the-shelf trained model to improve its predictions further.

paragraphs: Fine-grained classification can make errors that differ substantially in severity: a prediction can be wrong while remaining close to the correct category, or it can miss the broader category too. This paper aims to reduce that severity. Its motivation is that coarse classification requires less specialized knowledge than distinguishing closely related fine-grained classes.

Hierarchical Ensembles, or HiE, uses coarse predictions to correct a trained fine-grained classifier at test time. It relies on the label hierarchy and requires only the parents of the leaf classes. Because the correction is post hoc, it can be applied to an existing trained model, using broader category information to amend its detailed predictions.

On iNaturalist-19 and tieredImageNet-H, the authors report reduced average mistake severity alongside improved top-1 accuracy, reaching state-of-the-art results on both benchmarks. They also examine semi-supervised settings and find gains as fine-grained training data decreases. The findings suggest that readily available coarse distinctions can help both the correctness of predictions and the consequences of remaining errors, particularly when detailed labels are scarce.
summary.tldr: HiE uses coarse category predictions to amend fine-grained classifiers at test time, improving accuracy and reducing mistake severity.

title: Test-Time Amendment with a Coarse Classifier for Fine-Grained Classification

abstract: This paper studies two fundamental problems in regularized Graphon Mean-Field Games (GMFGs). First, we establish the existence of a Nash Equilibrium (NE) of any $\lambda$-regularized GMFG (for $\lambda\geq 0$). This result relies on weaker conditions than previous works analyzing both unregularized GMFGs ($\lambda=0$) and $\lambda$-regularized MFGs, which are special cases of GMFGs. Second, we propose provably efficient algorithms to learn the NE in weakly monotone GMFGs, motivated by Lasry and Lions (2007). Previous literature either only analyzed continuous-time algorithms or required extra conditions to analyze discrete-time algorithms. In contrast, we design a discrete-time algorithm and derive its convergence rate solely under weakly monotone conditions. Furthermore, we develop and analyze the action-value function estimation procedure during the online learning process, which is absent from algorithms for monotone GMFGs. This serves as a sub-module in our optimization algorithm. The efficiency of the designed algorithm is corroborated by empirical evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper addresses two questions in regularized graphon mean-field games: whether a Nash equilibrium exists and how an algorithm can learn one. An equilibrium represents mutually compatible decisions in which agents have no incentive to change their own strategy unilaterally. Establishing existence and providing a learning procedure are separate parts of making this framework useful.

The authors prove existence for nonnegative regularization strengths under conditions weaker than those used in earlier analyses. Their result includes the unregularized case when the regularization strength is zero. They then design a discrete-time learning algorithm and establish its convergence rate under weak monotonicity, without the additional conditions previously required for discrete-time analyses.

The learning procedure also includes an analyzed method for estimating action values during online learning. This estimation component supplies information needed by the optimization algorithm, connecting equilibrium learning with quantities that must themselves be learned. Empirical evaluations support the algorithm's efficiency. The theoretical learning guarantee remains tied to weakly monotone games, while the existence result addresses a broader foundational question.
summary.tldr: The paper proves equilibrium existence under weaker conditions and develops efficient discrete-time learning for weakly monotone graphon mean-field games.

title: Learning Regularized Monotone Graphon Mean-Field Games

abstract: Recently an influx of studies claims emergent cognitive abilities in large language models (LLMs). Yet, most rely on anecdotes, overlook contamination of training sets, or lack systematic Evaluation involving multiple tasks, control conditions, multiple iterations, and statistical robustness tests. Here we make two major contributions. First, we propose CogEval, a cognitive science-inspired protocol for the systematic evaluation of cognitive capacities in LLMs. The CogEval protocol can be followed for the evaluation of various abilities. Second, here we follow CogEval to systematically evaluate cognitive maps and planning ability across eight LLMs (OpenAI GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo-175B, davinci-003-175B, Google Bard, Cohere-xlarge-52.4B, Anthropic Claude-1-52B, LLaMA-13B, and Alpaca-7B). We base our task prompts on human experiments, which offer both established construct validity for evaluating planning, and are absent from LLM training sets. We find that, while LLMs show apparent competence in a few planning tasks with simpler structures, systematic evaluation reveals striking failure modes in planning tasks, including hallucinations of invalid trajectories and falling in loops. These findings do not support the idea of emergent out-of-the-box planning ability in LLMs. This could be because LLMs do not understand the latent relational structures underlying planning problems, known as cognitive maps, and fail at unrolling goal-directed trajectories based on the underlying structure. Implications for application and future directions are discussed.

paragraphs: A convincing answer to one planning problem does not by itself establish a general planning capability. This paper introduces CogEval, a protocol inspired by cognitive science for evaluating such claims systematically. It emphasizes multiple tasks, control conditions, repeated evaluations, and statistical robustness, addressing weaknesses the authors identify in anecdotal evaluations.

The authors apply the protocol to cognitive maps and planning across eight language models. Cognitive maps refer here to the relational structure underlying a planning problem: the connections that determine which trajectories are possible. The task prompts draw on human experiments, which the abstract describes as offering established validity for assessing planning and being absent from the models' training sets.

Although the models appear competent on some simpler tasks, broader evaluation reveals invalid trajectories and loops. The findings do not support out-of-the-box emergent planning ability in the evaluated models. The authors suggest that difficulty representing underlying relationships and unfolding goal-directed trajectories could explain the failures; this is a possible explanation, not an established diagnosis.
summary.tldr: CogEval systematically tests language-model planning and finds failures that undermine claims of out-of-the-box planning ability in the evaluated models.

title: Evaluating Cognitive Maps and Planning in Large Language Models with CogEval

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of estimating the 3-DoF camera pose for a ground-level image with respect to a satellite image that encompasses the local surroundings. We propose a novel end-to-end approach that leverages the learning of dense pixel-wise flow fields in pairs of ground and satellite images to calculate the camera pose. Our approach differs from existing methods by constructing the feature metric at the pixel level, enabling full-image supervision for learning distinctive geometric configurations and visual appearances across views. Specifically, our method employs two distinct convolution networks for ground and satellite feature extraction. Then, we project the ground feature map to the bird's eye view (BEV) using a fixed camera height assumption to achieve preliminary geometric alignment. To further establish the content association between the BEV and satellite features, we introduce a residual convolution block to refine the projected BEV feature. Optical flow estimation is performed on the refined BEV feature map and the satellite feature map using flow decoder networks based on RAFT. After obtaining dense flow correspondences, we apply the least square method to filter matching inliers and regress the ground camera pose. Extensive experiments demonstrate significant improvements compared to state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our approach reduces the median localization error by 89\%, 19\%, 80\%, and 35\% on the KITTI, Ford multi-AV, VIGOR, and Oxford RobotCar datasets, respectively.

title: Learning Dense Flow Field for Highly-accurate Cross-view Camera Localization

abstract: Projection robust Wasserstein (PRW) distance is recently proposed to efficiently mitigate the curse of dimensionality in the classical Wasserstein distance. In this paper, by equivalently reformulating the computation of the PRW distance as an optimization problem over the Cartesian product of the Stiefel manifold and the Euclidean space with additional nonlinear inequality constraints, we propose a Riemannian exponential augmented Lagrangian method (REALM) for solving this problem. Compared with the existing Riemannian exponential penalty-based approaches, REALM can potentially avoid too small penalty parameters and exhibit more stable numerical performance. To solve the subproblems in REALM efficiently, we design an inexact Riemannian Barzilai-Borwein method with Sinkhorn iteration (iRBBS), which selects the stepsizes adaptively rather than tuning the stepsizes in efforts as done in the existing methods. We show that iRBBS can return an $\epsilon$-stationary point of the original PRW distance problem within $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3})$ iterations, which matches the best known iteration complexity result. Extensive numerical results demonstrate that our proposed methods outperform the state-of-the-art solvers for computing the PRW distance.

We show that iRBBS can return an $\epsilon$-stationary point of the original PRW distance problem within $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3})$ iterations, which matches the best known iteration complexity result. Extensive numerical results demonstrate that our proposed methods outperform the state-of-the-art solvers for computing the PRW distance.

paragraphs: Projection robust Wasserstein distance was introduced to reduce the difficulties that high dimensionality creates for classical Wasserstein distance. This paper develops a method for computing that quantity. It first rewrites the calculation as an equivalent constrained optimization problem, combining a space of orthonormal matrices, called the Stiefel manifold, with ordinary Euclidean variables and nonlinear inequality constraints.

The proposed solver, REALM, uses a Riemannian exponential augmented Lagrangian method. Compared with existing exponential penalty approaches, it may avoid excessively small penalty parameters and provide more stable numerical behavior. For its internal subproblems, the authors introduce iRBBS, which combines a Riemannian Barzilai-Borwein method with Sinkhorn iteration. Its adaptive step sizes reduce the need to tune those choices manually.

The analysis shows that iRBBS can reach an epsilon-stationary point within O(epsilon^-3) iterations, matching the best known iteration complexity. Stationarity is the stated target, rather than a guarantee of global optimality. Numerical experiments report better performance than leading PRW solvers, supporting the practical value of the reformulation and adaptive optimization procedure.
summary.tldr: REALM reformulates projection robust Wasserstein computation to improve numerical optimization while matching the best known iteration complexity for approximate stationarity.

title: A Riemannian Exponential Augmented Lagrangian Method for Computing the Projection Robust Wasserstein Distance

abstract: Existing approaches for learning representations of time-series keep the temporal arrangement of the time-steps intact with the presumption that the original order is the most optimal for learning. However, non-adjacent sections of real-world time-series may have strong dependencies. Accordingly, we raise the question: Is there an alternative arrangement for time-series which could enable more effective representation learning? To address this, we propose a simple plug-and-play neural network layer called Segment, Shuffle, and Stitch (S3) designed to improve representation learning in time-series models. S3 works by creating non-overlapping segments from the original sequence and shuffling them in a learned manner that is optimal for the task at hand. It then re-attaches the shuffled segments back together and performs a learned weighted sum with the original input to capture both the newly shuffled sequence along with the original sequence. S3 is modular and can be stacked to achieve different levels of granularity, and can be added to many forms of neural architectures including CNNs or Transformers with negligible computation overhead. Through extensive experiments on several datasets and state-of-the-art baselines, we show that incorporating S3 results in significant improvements for the tasks of time-series classification, forecasting, and anomaly detection, improving performance on certain datasets by up to 68\%. We also show that S3 makes the learning more stable with a smoother training loss curve and loss landscape compared to the original baseline. The code is available at https://github.com/shivam-grover/S3-TimeSeries.

S3 divides the sequence into non-overlapping segments, learns how to reorder them, and joins them into a new sequence. It then combines this rearranged sequence with the original using a learned weighted sum. The model therefore retains access to the original ordering while also using the learned arrangement. Multiple layers can be stacked to operate at different levels of granularity.

The layer can be added to architectures including convolutional networks and transformers with negligible reported computational overhead. The authors also report smoother training loss curves and loss landscapes, indicating more stable learning in the evaluated comparisons.

title: Segment, Shuffle, and Stitch: A Simple Layer for Improving Time-Series Representations

abstract: The attention mechanism within the transformer architecture enables the model to weigh and combine tokens based on their relevance to the query. While self-attention has enjoyed major success, it notably treats all queries $q$ in the same way by applying the mapping $V^\top\text{softmax}(Kq)$, where $V,K$ are the value and key embeddings respectively. In this work, we argue that this uniform treatment hinders the ability to control contextual sparsity and relevance. As a solution, we introduce the Selective Self-Attention (SSA) layer that augments the softmax nonlinearity with a principled temperature scaling strategy. By controlling temperature, SSA adapts the contextual sparsity of the attention map to the query embedding and its position in the context window. Through theory and experiments, we demonstrate that this alleviates attention dilution, aids the optimization process, and enhances the model's ability to control softmax spikiness of individual queries. We also incorporate temperature scaling for value embeddings and show that it boosts the model's ability to suppress irrelevant/noisy tokens. Notably, SSA is a lightweight method which introduces less than 0.5\% new parameters through a weight-sharing strategy and can be fine-tuned on existing LLMs. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that SSA-equipped models achieve a noticeable and consistent accuracy improvement on language modeling benchmarks.
