paragraphs: Selecting pretraining examples individually can miss how their value depends on relationships with other training data. Group-MATES models those relationships to improve the tradeoff between language-model training cost and downstream quality. It approximates expensive group-level selection using a learned relational data influence model.

To train that model, the authors sample language-model training trajectories and collect oracle influence measurements. The model combines individual influence with relationship-based weights to estimate group influence. For efficient selection, those same relationships partition the dataset into small clusters, within which examples are selected independently. This makes relational selection manageable without treating the entire dataset as one selection problem.

Across the evaluated DCLM configurations and 22 downstream tasks, Group-MATES improves performance by 3.5%–9.4% relative to random selection. Its improvements are nearly twice those achieved by leading individual-selection baselines. It also reduces the tokens needed to reach a given downstream performance by up to a factor of 1.75. Further analyses support both the relationship weights and cluster-based selection.
summary.tldr: Group-MATES selects pretraining data using relationships between examples, improving downstream quality and reducing the tokens needed for a target performance.

title: Group-Level Data Selection for Efficient Pretraining

abstract: Watermarking LLM-generated text is critical for content attribution and misinformation prevention, yet existing methods compromise text quality and require white-box model access with logit manipulation or training, which exclude API-based models and multilingual scenarios. We propose SAEMark, an **inference-time framework** for *multi-bit* watermarking that embeds personalized information through *feature-based rejection sampling*, fundamentally different from logit-based or rewriting-based approaches: we **do not modify model outputs directly** and require only **black-box access**, while naturally supporting multi-bit message embedding and generalizing across diverse languages and domains. We instantiate the framework using *Sparse Autoencoders* as deterministic feature extractors and provide theoretical worst-case analysis relating watermark accuracy to computational budget. Experiments across 4 datasets demonstrate strong watermarking performance on English, Chinese, and code while preserving text quality. SAEMark establishes a new paradigm for **scalable, quality-preserving watermarks** that work seamlessly with closed-source LLMs across languages and domains.

paragraphs: Text watermarking aims to embed information that can help attribute generated content. Many methods require access to a model’s internal token scores or involve training, which limits their use with closed-source APIs. SAEMark proposes an inference-time approach that needs only black-box access and can embed personalized messages containing multiple bits.

The framework uses feature-based rejection sampling. Sparse autoencoders serve as deterministic feature extractors, and the resulting features guide which generated samples are accepted. This places the watermarking mechanism in sample selection: the method does not directly rewrite the outputs or manipulate the model’s logits. The authors also provide worst-case theory relating watermark accuracy to the available computational budget.

Experiments across four datasets report strong watermarking performance on English, Chinese, and code while preserving text quality. These results support applying the same framework across languages and domains. Its practical contribution is a way to carry personalized watermark information through black-box generation, with an explicit analysis of the relationship between computational effort and watermark accuracy.
summary.tldr: SAEMark embeds personalized multi-bit text watermarks through feature-based sample selection using only black-box model access.

title: SAEMark: Steering Personalized Multilingual LLM Watermarks with Sparse Autoencoders

abstract: We propose Grid-like Code Quantization (GCQ), a brain-inspired method for compressing observation-action sequences into discrete representations using grid-like patterns in attractor dynamics. Unlike conventional vector quantization approaches that operate on static inputs, GCQ performs spatiotemporal compression through an action-conditioned codebook, where codewords are derived from continuous attractor neural networks and dynamically selected based on actions. This enables GCQ to jointly compress space and time, serving as a unified world model. The resulting representation supports long-horizon prediction, goal-directed planning, and inverse modeling. Experiments across diverse tasks demonstrate GCQ's effectiveness in compact encoding and downstream performance. Our work offers both a computational tool for efficient sequence modeling and a theoretical perspective on the formation of grid-like codes in neural systems.

Unlike conventional vector quantization approaches that operate on static inputs, GCQ performs spatiotemporal compression through an action-conditioned codebook, where codewords are derived from continuous attractor neural networks and dynamically selected based on actions. This enables GCQ to jointly compress space and time, serving as a unified world model. The resulting representation supports long-horizon prediction, goal-directed planning, and inverse modeling. Experiments across diverse tasks demonstrate GCQ's effectiveness in compact encoding and downstream performance. paragraphs: Grid-like Code Quantization compresses sequences of observations and actions into discrete representations. Conventional vector quantization usually assigns codes to static inputs. This paper instead makes the codebook depend on actions, aiming to represent how observations unfold through both space and time within a unified world model.

The codewords come from continuous attractor neural networks and use grid-like patterns in their dynamics. Actions influence which codewords are selected, making the representation responsive to the sequence's evolution. The key idea is that a compact code can capture spatiotemporal structure jointly, rather than treating each observation as an isolated input to be compressed.

The resulting representation supports long-horizon prediction, goal-directed planning, and inverse modeling. Experiments across diverse tasks report effective compression and downstream performance. The work contributes a computational method for sequence modeling and a theoretical perspective on how grid-like neural codes might form. That brain-inspired perspective accompanies the engineering results; the abstract does not present the method as direct evidence that biological systems implement this exact mechanism.
summary.tldr: Grid-like Code Quantization uses action-conditioned attractor codes to compress sequences and support prediction, planning, and inverse modeling.

title: Vector Quantization in the Brain: Grid-like Codes in World Models

abstract: Compilers, while essential, are notoriously complex systems that demand prohibitively expensive human expertise to develop and maintain. The recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a compelling new paradigm: Neural Compilation, which could potentially simplify compiler development for new architectures and facilitate the discovery of innovative optimization techniques. However, several critical obstacles impede its practical adoption. Firstly, a significant lack of dedicated benchmarks and robust evaluation methodologies hinders objective assessment and tracking of progress in the field. Secondly, systematically enhancing the reliability and performance of LLM-generated assembly remains a critical challenge. Addressing these challenges, this paper introduces NeuComBack, a novel benchmark dataset specifically designed for IR-to-assembly compilation. Leveraging this dataset, we first define a foundational Neural Compilation workflow and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the capabilities of recent frontier LLMs on Neural Compilation, establishing new performance baselines. We further propose a self-evolving prompt optimization method that enables LLMs to iteratively evolve their internal prompt strategies by extracting insights from prior self-debugging traces, thereby enhancing their neural compilation capabilities. Experiments demonstrate that our method significantly improves both the functional correctness and the performance of LLM-generated assembly code. Compared to baseline prompts, the functional correctness rates improved from 44% to 64% on x86_64 and from 36% to 58% on aarch64, respectively. More significantly, among the 16 correctly generated x86_64 programs using our method, 14 (87.5%) surpassed clang-O3 performance. These consistent improvements across diverse architectures (x86_64 and aarch64) and program distributions (NeuComBack L1 and L2) validate our method's superiority over conventional approaches and its potential for broader adoption in low-level neural compilation.

paragraphs: This paper studies language models as translators from compiler intermediate representations to assembly code. summary.tldr: NeuComBack benchmarks neural compilation, while a debugging-informed prompt optimization method improves assembly correctness and performance in the reported tests.

title: QiMeng-NeuComBack: Self-Evolving Translation from IR to Assembly Code

abstract: The Orthant-Wise Limited memory Quasi-Newton (OWL-QN) method has been demonstrated to be very effective in solving the \ell_1-regularized sparse learning problem. OWL-QN extends the L-BFGS from solving unconstrained smooth optimization problems to \ell_1-regularized (non-smooth) sparse learning problems. At each iteration, OWL-QN does not involve any \ell_1-regularized quadratic optimization subproblem and only requires matrix-vector multiplications without an explicit use of the (inverse) Hessian matrix, which enables OWL-QN to tackle large-scale problems efficiently. Although many empirical studies have demonstrated that OWL-QN works quite well in practice, several recent papers point out that the existing convergence proof of OWL-QN is flawed and a rigorous convergence analysis for OWL-QN still remains to be established. In this paper, we propose a modified Orthant-Wise Limited memory Quasi-Newton (mOWL-QN) algorithm by slightly modifying the OWL-QN algorithm. As the main technical contribution of this paper, we establish a rigorous convergence proof for the mOWL-QN algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, our work fills the theoretical gap by providing the first rigorous convergence proof for the OWL-QN-type algorithm on solving \ell_1-regularized sparse learning problems. We also provide empirical studies to show that mOWL-QN works well and is as efficient as OWL-QN.

paragraphs: Sparse learning often uses an ℓ1 penalty, which encourages solutions with many zero coefficients but makes the optimization objective nonsmooth. OWL-QN adapts the limited-memory quasi-Newton method L-BFGS to this setting. It is attractive for large problems because its iterations use matrix-vector operations without explicitly storing the Hessian or its inverse, and avoid solving an ℓ1-regularized quadratic subproblem.

Despite substantial evidence that OWL-QN works well in practice, its existing convergence proof had been identified as flawed. This paper addresses that theoretical gap by making a small modification to the algorithm. The resulting method, mOWL-QN, comes with a rigorous convergence proof for ℓ1-regularized sparse learning.

The distinction between the original and modified algorithms matters: the established guarantee is for mOWL-QN. The contribution connects an efficient practical optimization approach to a sound mathematical analysis. Empirical studies also find that the modified method works well and is as efficient as OWL-QN, suggesting that obtaining the guarantee need not sacrifice the practical efficiency motivating this family of methods.
summary.tldr: A small modification to OWL-QN supplies a rigorous convergence guarantee while retaining comparable empirical efficiency for sparse learning.

title: A Modified Orthant-Wise Limited Memory Quasi-Newton Method with Convergence Analysis

abstract: We present an adaptive online gradient descent algorithm to solve online convex optimization problems with long-term constraints, which are constraints that need to be satisfied when accumulated over a finite number of rounds T, but can be violated in intermediate rounds. For some user-defined trade-off parameter βin (0, 1), the proposed algorithm achieves cumulative regret bounds of O(T^maxβ,1_β) and O(T^1_β/2), respectively for the loss and the constraint violations. Our results hold for convex losses, can handle arbitrary convex constraints and rely on a single computationally efficient algorithm. Our contributions improve over the best known cumulative regret bounds of Mahdavi et al. (2012), which are respectively O(T^1/2) and O(T^3/4) for general convex domains, and respectively O(T^2/3) and O(T^2/3) when the domain is further restricted to be a polyhedral set. We supplement the analysis with experiments validating the performance of our algorithm in practice.

paragraphs: The paper considers online decisions subject to constraints that matter over a sequence of rounds. A decision may violate a constraint temporarily, provided accumulated behavior meets the long-term requirement. This creates two connected goals: keep cumulative loss competitive and control the amount of accumulated constraint violation.

The authors propose an adaptive online gradient descent algorithm with a user-chosen parameter between zero and one. That parameter adjusts the trade-off between the loss-regret guarantee and the constraint-violation guarantee. A single computationally efficient algorithm handles convex losses and arbitrary convex constraints, allowing the same approach to cover different convex constraint geometries.

The analysis establishes cumulative bounds and reports improvements over earlier guarantees for general convex domains and for the more restricted polyhedral case. The trade-off parameter matters because the two performance criteria must be considered together when interpreting these improvements. Experiments also validate the algorithm’s practical behavior. The contribution gives a way to manage temporary infeasibility while maintaining theoretical control over both learning performance and long-term constraints.
summary.tldr: Adaptive online gradient descent provides tunable guarantees for cumulative loss and constraint violations under long-term convex constraints.

title: Adaptive Algorithms for Online Convex Optimization with Long-term Constraints

abstract: There has been a surge of research interest in developing tools and analysis for Bayesian optimization, the task of finding the global maximizer of an unknown, expensive function through sequential evaluation using Bayesian decision theory. However, many interesting problems involve optimizing multiple, expensive to evaluate objectives simultaneously, and relatively little research has addressed this setting from a Bayesian theoretic standpoint. A prevailing choice when tackling this problem, is to model the multiple objectives as being independent, typically for ease of computation. In practice, objectives are correlated to some extent. In this work, we incorporate the modelling of inter-task correlations, developing an approximation to overcome intractable integrals. We illustrate the power of modelling dependencies between objectives on a range of synthetic and real world multi-objective optimization problems.
originalAbstract: There has been a surge of research interest in developing tools and analysis for Bayesian optimization, the task of finding the global maximizer of an unknown, expensive function through sequential evaluation using Bayesian decision theory. However, many interesting problems involve optimizing multiple, expensive to evaluate objectives simultaneously, and relatively little research has addressed this setting from a Bayesian theoretic standpoint. A prevailing choice when tackling this problem, is to model the multiple objectives as being independent, typically for ease of computation. In practice, objectives are correlated to some extent. In this work, we incorporate the modelling of inter-task correlations, developing an approximation to overcome intractable integrals. We illustrate the power of modelling dependencies between objectives on a range of synthetic and real world multi-objective optimization problems.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization when several objectives must be considered together and evaluating them is expensive. Bayesian optimization selects evaluations sequentially using a probabilistic model and decision theory. In the multi-objective setting, the relevant goal involves understanding tradeoffs among objectives, making relationships between their outcomes potentially useful to the search.

A common simplification is to model each objective independently, which makes computation easier. The authors instead incorporate correlations between objectives. This lets the model represent dependencies that independence would exclude. Accounting for those dependencies introduces intractable integrals, so the paper develops an approximation to make the resulting approach computationally manageable.

The authors illustrate the value of modeling objective dependencies on a range of synthetic and real-world multi-objective problems. These examples support treating correlation as useful information when learning about expensive objectives. The contribution brings dependence modeling into the Bayesian treatment of the problem and supplies an approximation for the computational difficulty it creates, with empirical evidence for its usefulness in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian multi-objective optimization approach models correlations between expensive objectives and approximates the resulting intractable integrals.

title: Pareto Frontier Learning with Expensive Correlated Objectives

abstract: We develop and analyze a variant of Nesterov’s accelerated gradient descent (AGD) for minimization of smooth non-convex functions. We prove that one of two cases occurs: either our AGD variant converges quickly, as if the function was convex, or we produce a certificate that the function is “guilty” of being non-convex. This non-convexity certificate allows us to exploit negative curvature and obtain deterministic, dimension-free acceleration of convergence for non-convex functions. For a function $f$ with Lipschitz continuous gradient and Hessian, we compute a point $x$ with $\|\nabla f(x)\| \le \epsilon$ in $O(\epsilon^{-7/4} \log(1/ \epsilon) )$ gradient and function evaluations. Assuming additionally that the third derivative is Lipschitz, we require only $O(\epsilon^{-5/3} \log(1/ \epsilon) )$ evaluations.
originalAbstract: We develop and analyze a variant of Nesterov’s accelerated gradient descent (AGD) for minimization of smooth non-convex functions. We prove that one of two cases occurs: either our AGD variant converges quickly, as if the function was convex, or we produce a certificate that the function is “guilty” of being non-convex. This non-convexity certificate allows us to exploit negative curvature and obtain deterministic, dimension-free acceleration of convergence for non-convex functions. For a function $f$ with Lipschitz continuous gradient and Hessian, we compute a point $x$ with $\|\nabla f(x)\| \le \epsilon$ in $O(\epsilon^{-7/4} \log(1/ \epsilon) )$ gradient and function evaluations. Assuming additionally that the third derivative is Lipschitz, we require only $O(\epsilon^{-5/3} \log(1/ \epsilon) )$ evaluations.

paragraphs: Accelerated gradient methods work especially well on convex objectives, but non-convex objectives can violate the geometry those methods rely on. This paper develops a variant of Nesterov's accelerated gradient descent that uses this tension constructively. It either makes rapid progress resembling the convex case or produces evidence that the objective is non-convex.

That evidence is a certificate the algorithm can use to exploit negative curvature. Instead of treating the failure of convex-like progress as an unexplained obstacle, the method turns it into information for further optimization. The resulting acceleration is deterministic, and its stated evaluation bounds do not explicitly grow with the dimension.

For functions with Lipschitz-continuous gradients and Hessians, the method finds a point with gradient norm at most epsilon using O(epsilon^(-7/4) log(1/epsilon)) evaluations. A further Lipschitz assumption on the third derivative improves this to O(epsilon^(-5/3) log(1/epsilon)). The guaranteed target is a small gradient, rather than a globally optimal solution.
summary.tldr: An accelerated method either makes convex-like progress or exploits certified non-convexity to reach small-gradient points faster.

title: “Convex Until Proven Guilty”: Dimension-Free Acceleration of Gradient Descent on Non-Convex Functions

abstract: State-of-the-art methods for clustering data drawn from a union of subspaces are based on sparse and low-rank representation theory and convex optimization algorithms. Existing results guaranteeing the correctness of such methods require the dimension of the subspaces to be small relative to the dimension of the ambient space. When this assumption is violated, as is, e.g., in the case of hyperplanes, existing methods are either computationally too intensive (e.g., algebraic methods) or lack sufficient theoretical support (e.g., K-Hyperplanes or RANSAC). In this paper we provide theoretical and algorithmic contributions to the problem of clustering data from a union of hyperplanes, by extending a recent subspace learning method called Dual Principal Component Pursuit (DPCP) to the multi-hyperplane case. We give theoretical guarantees under which, the non-convex $\ell_1$ problem associated with DPCP admits a unique global minimizer equal to the normal vector of the most dominant hyperplane. Inspired by this insight, we propose sequential (RANSAC-style) and iterative (K-Hyperplanes-style) hyperplane learning DPCP algorithms, which, via experiments on synthetic and real data, are shown to outperform or be competitive to the state-of-the-art.

Existing results guaranteeing the correctness of such methods require the dimension of the subspaces to be small relative to the dimension of the ambient space. When this assumption is violated, as is, e.g., in the case of hyperplanes, existing methods are either computationally too intensive (e.g., algebraic methods) or lack sufficient theoretical support (e.g., K-Hyperplanes or RANSAC). In this paper we provide theoretical and algorithmic contributions to the problem of clustering data from a union of hyperplanes, by extending a recent subspace learning method called Dual Principal Component Pursuit (DPCP) to the multi-hyperplane case. We give theoretical guarantees under which, the non-convex $\ell_1$ problem associated with DPCP admits a unique global minimizer equal to the normal vector of the most dominant hyperplane. Inspired by this insight, we propose sequential (RANSAC-style) and iterative (K-Hyperplanes-style) hyperplane learning DPCP algorithms, which, via experiments on synthetic and real data, are shown to outperform or be competitive to the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Clustering data from multiple subspaces becomes challenging when those subspaces occupy many of the available dimensions. Hyperplanes are a prominent example. Existing correctness guarantees for sparse and low-rank clustering methods assume relatively low-dimensional subspaces, while alternatives for hyperplanes can be computationally demanding or have insufficient theoretical support.

This paper extends Dual Principal Component Pursuit to data drawn from multiple hyperplanes. Its theoretical contribution gives conditions under which the associated nonconvex ℓ1 problem has a unique global minimizer equal to the normal vector of the most dominant hyperplane. A normal vector describes a hyperplane's orientation, so recovering it provides a route to identifying that component.

Motivated by this result, the authors propose both sequential, RANSAC-style algorithms and iterative, K-Hyperplanes-style algorithms. Experiments on synthetic and real data show performance that exceeds or is competitive with existing methods. The work connects a conditional recovery guarantee for one dominant hyperplane with practical procedures for learning several hyperplanes and clustering their data.
summary.tldr: Extending Dual Principal Component Pursuit yields conditional hyperplane recovery guarantees and competitive algorithms for clustering multiple hyperplanes.

title: Hyperplane Clustering via Dual Principal Component Pursuit

abstract: Despite the recent successes of probabilistic programming languages (PPLs) in AI applications, PPLs offer only limited support for random variables whose distributions combine discrete and continuous elements. We develop the notion of measure-theoretic Bayesian networks (MTBNs) and use it to provide more general semantics for PPLs with arbitrarily many random variables defined over arbitrary measure spaces. We develop two new general sampling algorithms that are provably correct under the MTBN framework: the lexicographic likelihood weighting (LLW) for general MTBNs and the lexicographic particle filter (LPF), a specialized algorithm for state-space models. We further integrate MTBNs into a widely used PPL system, BLOG, and verify the effectiveness of the new inference algorithms through representative examples.

paragraphs: Probabilistic programming languages let users describe uncertain models and then perform inference about them. The paper addresses a gap in their support for variables whose distributions contain both discrete and continuous elements. Handling these mixtures requires a mathematical foundation broad enough to describe both parts within the same probabilistic model.

The authors introduce measure-theoretic Bayesian networks, or MTBNs, to supply that foundation. Their framework supports arbitrarily many random variables defined over arbitrary measure spaces. They use it to give probabilistic programs more general semantics: a precise account of what the programs mean as probabilistic objects.

The paper also develops two sampling algorithms with correctness guarantees under this framework. Lexicographic likelihood weighting applies to general MTBNs, while the lexicographic particle filter specializes to state-space models. The authors integrate the framework into BLOG and demonstrate the inference algorithms on representative examples. The contribution thus joins broader modeling semantics with concrete inference procedures and an implementation in an existing probabilistic programming system.
summary.tldr: Measure-theoretic Bayesian networks extend probabilistic programming to mixed discrete-continuous distributions and support two provably correct sampling algorithms.

title: Discrete-Continuous Mixtures in Probabilistic Programming: Generalized Semantics and Inference Algorithms

abstract: The aim of this work is to enable inference of deep networks that retain high accuracy for the least possible model complexity, with the latter deduced from the data during inference. To this end, we revisit deep networks that comprise competing linear units, as opposed to nonlinear units that do not entail any form of (local) competition. In this context, our main technical innovation consists in an inferential setup that leverages solid arguments from Bayesian nonparametrics. We infer both the needed set of connections or locally competing sets of units, as well as the required floating-point precision for storing the network parameters. Specifically, we introduce auxiliary discrete latent variables representing which initial network components are actually needed for modeling the data at hand, and perform Bayesian inference over them by imposing appropriate stick-breaking priors. As we experimentally show using benchmark datasets, our approach yields networks with less computational footprint than the state-of-the-art, and with no compromises in predictive accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper aims to learn deep networks that retain high predictive accuracy with low model complexity. The amount of complexity is inferred from the data. The architecture uses locally competing linear units, making competition among units part of the network's design and part of the inference problem.

The authors develop a Bayesian nonparametric formulation that determines which connections or sets of competing units are needed. Auxiliary discrete latent variables indicate whether components of the initial network are necessary for modeling the data. Bayesian inference over these variables uses stick-breaking priors. The method also infers the floating-point precision required to store network parameters.

This links architectural selection and numerical storage requirements within the same overall approach to reducing complexity. On benchmark datasets, the authors report a smaller computational footprint than the state of the art without sacrificing predictive accuracy. The finding supports inferring which components and parameter precision the data require, with the demonstrated efficiency gains coming from the reported benchmark experiments.
summary.tldr: Bayesian inference selects network components and parameter precision in locally competitive deep networks, reducing computational footprint without reported accuracy loss.

title: Nonparametric Bayesian Deep Networks with Local Competition

abstract: We study reward maximisation in a wide class of structured stochastic multi-armed bandit problems, where the mean rewards of arms satisfy some given structural constraints, e.g. linear, unimodal, sparse, etc. Our aim is to develop methods that are \emph{flexible} (in that they easily adapt to different structures), \emph{powerful} (in that they perform well empirically and/or provably match instance-dependent lower bounds) and \emph{efficient} in that the per-round computational burden is small. We develop asymptotically optimal algorithms from instance-dependent lower-bounds using iterative saddle-point solvers. Our approach generalises recent iterative methods for pure exploration to reward maximisation, where a major challenge arises from the estimation of the sub-optimality gaps and their reciprocals. Still we manage to achieve all the above desiderata. Notably, our technique avoids the computational cost of the full-blown saddle point oracle employed by previous work, while at the same time enabling finite-time regret bounds. Our experiments reveal that our method successfully leverages the structural assumptions, while its regret is at worst comparable to that of vanilla UCB.

paragraphs: Structured stochastic bandits impose relationships among the mean rewards of different actions, such as linearity, unimodality, or sparsity. The paper seeks reward-maximizing algorithms that can exploit different structures while keeping computation per round small. Its design begins with instance-dependent lower bounds, which describe performance limits for particular problem instances.

The authors use iterative saddle-point solvers to construct asymptotically optimal algorithms from those bounds. This extends iterative methods for pure exploration to reward maximization. A central difficulty is estimating how far each inferior action falls below the best action, together with the reciprocals of these gaps.

The resulting approach avoids the expense of a full saddle-point oracle used in earlier work and also permits finite-time regret bounds. Experiments show that it exploits the assumed structure, with regret at worst comparable to ordinary UCB in those experiments. The paper thus combines asymptotic guarantees, finite-time analysis, and evidence of practical adaptability; the empirical UCB comparison should be read within the tested settings.
summary.tldr: Iterative saddle-point methods yield efficient, asymptotically optimal bandit algorithms that exploit reward structure and admit finite-time regret bounds.

title: Structure Adaptive Algorithms for Stochastic Bandits

abstract: We consider the problem of online adaptive control of the linear quadratic regulator, where the true system parameters are unknown. We prove new upper and lower bounds demonstrating that the optimal regret scales as $\tilde{\Theta} (\sqrt{d_{\mathbf{u}}^2 d_{\mathbf{x}} T})$, where $T$ is the number of time steps, $d_{\mathbf{u}}$ is the dimension of the input space, and $d_{\mathbf{x}}$ is the dimension of the system state. Notably, our lower bounds rule out the possibility of a $\mathrm{poly}(\log{T})$-regret algorithm, which had been conjectured due to the apparent strong convexity of the problem. Our upper bound is attained by a simple variant of certainty equivalent control, where the learner selects control inputs according to the optimal controller for their estimate of the system while injecting exploratory random noise. While this approach was shown to achieve $\sqrt{T}$ regret by Mania et al. (2019), we show that if the learner continually refines their estimates of the system matrices, the method attains optimal dimension dependence as well. Central to our upper and lower bounds is a new approach for controlling perturbations of Riccati equations called the self-bounding ODE method, which we use to derive suboptimality bounds for the certainty equivalent controller synthesized from estimated system dynamics. This in turn enables regret upper bounds which hold for any stabilizable instance and scale with natural control-theoretic quantities.

paragraphs: This paper studies adaptive control of a linear quadratic regulator when the system parameters are unknown. Matching upper and lower bounds show that optimal regret scales as the square root of d_u squared times d_x times T, up to logarithmic factors, where the dimensions describe controls and states.

A new self-bounding ODE method controls perturbations of Riccati equations, linking errors in estimated dynamics to controller suboptimality. This analysis supports upper bounds for any stabilizable instance, with dependence on natural control-theoretic quantities. The result gives a precise theoretical justification for a simple exploration strategy.
summary.tldr: Certainty-equivalent control with random exploration and continually refined estimates achieves optimal time and dimension dependence for online LQR regret.

title: Naive Exploration is Optimal for Online LQR

abstract: Obtaining a useful estimate of an object from highly incomplete imaging measurements remains a holy grail of imaging science. Deep learning methods have shown promise in learning object priors or constraints to improve the conditioning of an ill-posed imaging inverse problem. In this study, a framework for estimating an object of interest that is semantically related to a known prior image, is proposed. An optimization problem is formulated in the disentangled latent space of a style-based generative model, and semantically meaningful constraints are imposed using the disentangled latent representation of the prior image. Stable recovery from incomplete measurements with the help of a prior image is theoretically analyzed. Numerical experiments demonstrating the superior performance of our approach as compared to related methods are presented.

paragraphs: Reconstructing an object from highly incomplete imaging measurements is difficult because the observations do not sufficiently constrain the answer. This paper considers a setting with an additional source of information: a known prior image that is semantically related to the object being reconstructed. The aim is to turn that relationship into useful reconstruction constraints.

The authors formulate an optimization problem in the disentangled latent space of a style-based generative model. They use the prior image's representation in that space to impose semantically meaningful constraints. This lets the relationship between the prior image and the desired object guide the reconstruction through the model's latent representation.

The paper theoretically analyzes stable recovery from incomplete measurements with assistance from a prior image. Numerical experiments also show superior performance compared with related methods. The contribution brings together incomplete measurement data, a generative representation, and information from a related image. The prior-image relationship is central to the setting, providing the additional structure that the proposed optimization is designed to exploit.
summary.tldr: A style-based generative model uses a semantically related prior image to constrain reconstruction from incomplete measurements.

title: Prior Image-Constrained Reconstruction using Style-Based Generative Models

abstract: Deep graph neural networks (GNNs) have achieved excellent results on various tasks on increasingly large graph datasets with millions of nodes and edges. However, memory complexity has become a major obstacle when training deep GNNs for practical applications due to the immense number of nodes, edges, and intermediate activations. To improve the scalability of GNNs, prior works propose smart graph sampling or partitioning strategies to train GNNs with a smaller set of nodes or sub-graphs. In this work, we study reversible connections, group convolutions, weight tying, and equilibrium models to advance the memory and parameter efficiency of GNNs. We find that reversible connections in combination with deep network architectures enable the training of overparameterized GNNs that significantly outperform existing methods on multiple datasets. Our models RevGNN-Deep (1001 layers with 80 channels each) and RevGNN-Wide (448 layers with 224 channels each) were both trained on a single commodity GPU and achieve an ROC-AUC of 87.74 $\pm$ 0.13 and 88.14 $\pm$ 0.15 on the ogbn-proteins dataset. To the best of our knowledge, RevGNN-Deep is the deepest GNN in the literature by one order of magnitude.

paragraphs: Deep graph neural networks must handle large graphs as well as the intermediate activations produced during training. This creates a substantial memory obstacle. While earlier approaches reduce the graph processed at a time through sampling or partitioning, this paper investigates architectural techniques that improve memory and parameter efficiency.

The authors study reversible connections, group convolutions, weight tying, and equilibrium models. Their key empirical finding is that combining reversible connections with deep architectures makes it possible to train overparameterized graph networks that significantly outperform existing methods on multiple datasets. The contribution links architectural efficiency to the ability to explore much deeper and wider models.

On ogbn-proteins, their reported ROC-AUC values are 87.74 ± 0.13 and 88.14 ± 0.15, respectively. These results demonstrate the feasibility and evaluated performance of the architectures; the authors also describe the deeper model as an order of magnitude deeper than prior GNNs.
summary.tldr: Reversible architectures enable a 1001-layer graph neural network to train on one commodity GPU and achieve strong evaluated performance.

title: Training Graph Neural Networks with 1000 Layers

abstract: Many video classification applications require access to personal data, thereby posing an invasive security risk to the users’ privacy. We propose a privacy-preserving implementation of single-frame method based video classification with convolutional neural networks that allows a party to infer a label from a video without necessitating the video owner to disclose their video to other entities in an unencrypted manner. Similarly, our approach removes the requirement of the classifier owner from revealing their model parameters to outside entities in plaintext. To this end, we combine existing Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) protocols for private image classification with our novel MPC protocols for oblivious single-frame selection and secure label aggregation across frames. The result is an end-to-end privacy-preserving video classification pipeline. We evaluate our proposed solution in an application for private human emotion recognition. Our results across a variety of security settings, spanning honest and dishonest majority configurations of the computing parties, and for both passive and active adversaries, demonstrate that videos can be classified with state-of-the-art accuracy, and without leaking sensitive user information.

paragraphs: Video classification can require sharing sensitive personal footage, while a classifier’s owner may also want to keep model parameters private. This paper develops a pipeline that lets a party infer a video label without requiring the video or model parameters to be disclosed to other entities in plaintext.

The approach builds on secure multi-party computation protocols for private image classification. The authors add protocols for oblivious single-frame selection and secure aggregation of labels across frames. Together, these components support the full video classification process using a method that classifies individual frames, extending protection beyond the image classifier to frame selection and combination of results.

The system is evaluated for private human emotion recognition across several security settings. These include honest- and dishonest-majority configurations among the computing parties, as well as passive and active adversaries. The reported results achieve state-of-the-art classification accuracy without leaking sensitive user information in those settings. The contribution is an end-to-end secure implementation that protects both the video owner’s input and the classifier owner’s parameters under the considered configurations.
summary.tldr: Secure multi-party computation enables video classification while protecting both footage and model parameters in the evaluated security settings.

title: Privacy-Preserving Video Classification with Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: Feedforward computation, such as evaluating a neural network or sampling from an autoregressive model, is ubiquitous in machine learning. The sequential nature of feedforward computation, however, requires a strict order of execution and cannot be easily accelerated with parallel computing. To enable parallelization, we frame the task of feedforward computation as solving a system of nonlinear equations. We then propose to find the solution using a Jacobi or Gauss-Seidel fixed-point iteration method, as well as hybrid methods of both. Crucially, Jacobi updates operate independently on each equation and can be executed in parallel. Our method is guaranteed to give exactly the same values as the original feedforward computation with a reduced (or equal) number of parallelizable iterations, and hence reduced time given sufficient parallel computing power. Experimentally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in accelerating (i) backpropagation of RNNs, (ii) evaluation of DenseNets, and (iii) autoregressive sampling of MADE and PixelCNN++, with speedup factors between 2.1 and 26 under various settings.

paragraphs: Evaluating a neural network or generating samples with an autoregressive model often requires computations to happen in a strict sequence. That dependency limits how much extra computing hardware can help. This paper reformulates feedforward computation as a system of nonlinear equations, creating another route to the same outputs.

The authors solve those equations using Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel fixed-point iterations, together with methods that combine them. Jacobi updates are especially useful because each equation can be updated independently, allowing simultaneous execution. The approach guarantees the same values as the original computation using no more parallelizable iterations, with fewer iterations possible. A reduction in elapsed time depends on having sufficient parallel computing power.

Experiments apply the approach to recurrent-network backpropagation, DenseNet evaluation, and autoregressive sampling with MADE and PixelCNN++. Reported speedups range from 2.1 to 26 across the tested settings. The contribution is a way to reorganize computation while preserving its result, showing that apparently sequential machine-learning workloads can sometimes benefit substantially from parallel equation solving.
summary.tldr: Recasting feedforward computation as nonlinear equation solving enables parallel execution with identical outputs and substantial reported speedups.

title: Accelerating Feedforward Computation via Parallel Nonlinear Equation Solving

abstract: Universal methods achieve optimal convergence rate guarantees in convex optimization without any prior knowledge of the problem’s regularity parameters or the attributes of the gradient oracle employed by the method. In this regard, existing state-of-the-art algorithms achieve an $O(1/T^2)$ convergence rate in Lipschitz smooth problems with a perfect gradient oracle, and an $O(1/sqrt{T})$ convergence speed when the underlying problem is non-smooth and/or the gradient oracle is stochastic. On the downside, these methods do not take into account the dependence of these guarantees on the problem’s dimensionality, and this can have a catastrophic impact on a method’s convergence, in both theory and practice. Our paper aims to bridge this gap by providing a scalable universal method - dubbed UnDERGrad - which enjoys an almost dimension-free oracle complexity in problems with a favorable geometry (like the simplex, $\ell_1$-ball or trace-constraints), while retaining the order-optimal dependence on T described above. These "best of both worlds" guarantees are achieved via a primal-dual update scheme inspired by the dual exploration method for variational inequalities.

paragraphs: Universal convex optimization methods adapt without advance knowledge of smoothness parameters or gradient-oracle properties. Existing methods can achieve optimal iteration rates in both smooth and noisy or nonsmooth settings. However, their guarantees can hide unfavorable dependence on the number of dimensions, which may undermine scalability despite an attractive dependence on iteration count.

UnderGrad addresses this dimensional dependence while preserving universal adaptation. For problems with favorable geometry, including the simplex, the l1 ball, and trace-constrained domains, it has almost dimension-free oracle complexity. The method uses a primal-dual update scheme inspired by dual exploration for variational inequalities.

Its guarantees retain an O(1/T²) rate for smooth problems with exact gradients and an O(1/√T) rate for nonsmooth problems or stochastic gradient information. Here T represents the iteration horizon. The contribution combines these order-optimal rates with improved dimensional behavior under the specified geometric conditions. This distinction matters: the almost dimension-free claim is associated with favorable domains, rather than being asserted for every convex optimization problem.
summary.tldr: UnderGrad combines universal optimal iteration rates with almost dimension-free oracle complexity on convex problems with favorable geometry.

title: UnderGrad: A Universal Black-Box Optimization Method with Almost Dimension-Free Convergence Rate Guarantees

abstract: The Q-learning algorithm is a simple, fundamental and practically very effective reinforcement learning algorithm. However, the basic protocol can exhibit an unstable behavior when implemented even with simple linear function approximation. While tools like target networks and experience replay are often implemented to stabilize the learning process, the individual contribution of each of these mechanisms is not well understood theoretically. This work proposes an exploration variant of the basic Q-learning protocol with linear function approximation. Our modular analysis illustrates the role played by each algorithmic tool that we adopt: a second order update rule, a set of target networks, and a mechanism akin to experience replay. Together, they enable state of the art regret bounds on linear MDPs while preserving the most prominent feature of the algorithm, namely a space complexity independent of the number of steps elapsed. Furthermore, we show that the performance of the algorithm degrades very gracefully under a new, more permissive notion of approximation error. Finally, the algorithm partially inherits problem dependent regret bounds, function of the number of ‘effective’ feature dimension.

paragraphs: Q-learning can become unstable even when its value estimates use simple linear function approximation. Practical systems often add target networks and experience replay, but the separate theoretical contributions of these tools are not fully understood. This paper develops an exploration variant of linear Q-learning and analyzes how its stabilizing components work together.

The algorithm combines a second-order update rule, a collection of target networks, and a mechanism resembling experience replay. A modular analysis identifies the roles of these components. Together, they yield state-of-the-art regret bounds for linear Markov decision processes while retaining memory requirements that do not grow with the number of elapsed learning steps.

The analysis also considers a more permissive notion of approximation error and shows that performance degrades gracefully under it. In addition, the algorithm partially inherits problem-dependent regret bounds involving an effective feature dimension. The contribution connects stability, learning efficiency, and bounded memory within the analyzed setting, while also examining how departures from exact approximation affect performance.
summary.tldr: A stabilized linear Q-learning variant achieves strong regret guarantees with memory independent of elapsed steps and graceful degradation under approximation error.

title: Stabilizing Q-learning with Linear Architectures for Provable Efficient Learning

abstract: In this paper, we introduce BNN-DP, an efficient algorithmic framework for analysis of adversarial robustness of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). Given a compact set of input points $T\subset \mathbb{R}^n$, BNN-DP computes lower and upper bounds on the BNN’s predictions for all the points in $T$. The framework is based on an interpretation of BNNs as stochastic dynamical systems, which enables the use of Dynamic Programming (DP) algorithms to bound the prediction range along the layers of the network. Specifically, the method uses bound propagation techniques and convex relaxations to derive a backward recursion procedure to over-approximate the prediction range of the BNN with piecewise affine functions. The algorithm is general and can handle both regression and classification tasks. On a set of experiments on various regression and classification tasks and BNN architectures, we show that BNN-DP outperforms state-of-the-art methods by up to four orders of magnitude in both tightness of the bounds and computational efficiency.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we introduce BNN-DP, an efficient algorithmic framework for analysis of adversarial robustness of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). Given a compact set of input points $T\subset \mathbb{R}^n$, BNN-DP computes lower and upper bounds on the BNN’s predictions for all the points in $T$. The framework is based on an interpretation of BNNs as stochastic dynamical systems, which enables the use of Dynamic Programming (DP) algorithms to bound the prediction range along the layers of the network. Specifically, the method uses bound propagation techniques and convex relaxations to derive a backward recursion procedure to over-approximate the prediction range of the BNN with piecewise affine functions. The algorithm is general and can handle both regression and classification tasks. On a set of experiments on various regression and classification tasks and BNN architectures, we show that BNN-DP outperforms state-of-the-art methods by up to four orders of magnitude in both tightness of the bounds and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Assessing adversarial robustness requires understanding predictions throughout a set of possible inputs. BNN-DP tackles this problem for Bayesian neural networks by computing lower and upper prediction bounds that hold for every point in a specified compact input set. This makes the prediction range, rather than a few sampled outputs, the central object of analysis.

The framework treats a Bayesian neural network as a stochastic dynamical system evolving across layers. That interpretation allows dynamic programming to organize the bounding calculation. Bound propagation and convex relaxations produce a backward recursion, using piecewise affine functions to enclose the possible prediction range. The enclosure is an over-approximation, so it is designed to contain the range rather than reproduce it exactly.

BNN-DP supports both regression and classification. Across the tested tasks and network architectures, the authors report improvements of up to four orders of magnitude over state-of-the-art methods in bound tightness and computational efficiency. Tighter bounds provide a more informative robustness assessment, while faster computation makes that assessment more practical. The reported maximum improvements describe the experiments, not a uniform gain for every network.
summary.tldr: BNN-DP uses dynamic programming to efficiently bound Bayesian neural network predictions over entire input sets.

title: BNN-DP: Robustness Certification of Bayesian Neural Networks via Dynamic Programming

abstract: This paper proposes an online, provably robust, and scalable Bayesian approach for changepoint detection. The resulting algorithm has key advantages over previous work: it provides provable robustness by leveraging the generalised Bayesian perspective, and also addresses the scalability issues of previous attempts. Specifically, the proposed generalised Bayesian formalism leads to conjugate posteriors whose parameters are available in closed form by leveraging diffusion score matching. The resulting algorithm is exact, can be updated through simple algebra, and is more than 10 times faster than its closest competitor.

paragraphs: Online changepoint detection looks for changes as observations arrive, making the cost of repeated updates central to its usefulness. This paper proposes a Bayesian approach that combines provable robustness with scalability. It addresses the difficulty of obtaining both properties in one procedure, rather than treating robustness and efficient updating as separate objectives.

The method uses a generalized Bayesian formulation together with diffusion score matching. This combination produces conjugate posteriors whose parameters have closed-form expressions. In practical terms, the posterior update can be carried out through simple algebra. The mathematical construction therefore supplies both the robustness guarantee and a tractable form for the ongoing inference calculations.

The resulting algorithm is exact within the proposed formulation, and the authors report that it runs more than ten times faster than its closest competitor. Exactness here describes computation under that formulation, while robustness is a separately established property. The contribution is a route to robust Bayesian changepoint analysis whose updates remain computationally simple, directly addressing the scalability problems associated with earlier attempts.
summary.tldr: A generalized Bayesian changepoint detector combines provable robustness, exact algebraic updates, and a reported speedup exceeding tenfold.

title: Robust and Scalable Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection

abstract: In digital online advertising, advertisers procure ad impressions simultaneously on multiple platforms, or so-called channels, such as Google Ads, Meta Ads Manager, etc., each of which consists of numerous ad auctions. We study how an advertiser maximizes total conversion (e.g. ad clicks) while satisfying aggregate return-on-investment (ROI) and budget constraints across all channels. In practice, an advertiser does not have control over, and thus cannot globally optimize, which individual ad auctions she participates in for each channel, and instead authorizes a channel to procure impressions on her behalf: the advertiser can only utilize two levers on each channel, namely setting a per-channel budget and per-channel target ROI. In this work, we first analyze the effectiveness of each of these levers for solving the advertiser’s global multi-channel problem. We show that when an advertiser only optimizes over per-channel ROIs, her total conversion can be arbitrarily worse than what she could have obtained in the global problem. Further, we show that the advertiser can achieve the global optimal conversion when she only optimizes over per-channel budgets. In light of this finding, under a bandit feedback setting that mimics real-world scenarios where advertisers have limited information on ad auctions in each channels and how channels procure ads, we present an efficient learning algorithm that produces per-channel budgets whose resulting conversion approximates that of the global optimal problem.

paragraphs: An advertiser buying impressions across multiple channels wants to maximize total conversions while meeting an overall budget and return-on-investment constraint. Individual auctions are handled by the channels, so the advertiser cannot directly optimize every purchase. Instead, the available controls are each channel’s budget and target return on investment.

The paper analyzes how much these two controls can accomplish. Under the studied formulation, optimizing only channel-level ROI targets can produce conversions arbitrarily worse than the global optimum. By contrast, optimizing only channel budgets can achieve the globally optimal conversion total. This identifies budget allocation as a sufficient control for reaching that optimum in the analyzed problem.

The authors then consider learning with bandit feedback, reflecting limited knowledge of auctions and how channels procure impressions. They provide an efficient algorithm that learns per-channel budgets whose resulting conversions approximate the global optimum. The distinction between the results matters: budget control can attain optimality in the optimization analysis, while the learning algorithm provides an approximation under limited feedback.
summary.tldr: Per-channel budgets can achieve the studied global advertising optimum, and a bandit algorithm learns budgets that approximate it.

title: Multi-channel Autobidding with Budget and ROI Constraints

abstract: The geometric structure of data is an important inductive bias in machine learning. In this work, we characterize the data manifolds entailed by structural causal models. The strengths of the proposed framework are twofold: firstly, the geometric structure of the data manifolds is causally informed, and secondly, it enables causal reasoning about the data manifolds in an interventional and a counterfactual sense. We showcase the versatility of the proposed framework by applying it to the generation of causally-grounded counterfactual explanations for machine learning classifiers, measuring distances along the data manifold in a differential geometric-principled manner.

We showcase the versatility of the proposed framework by applying it to the generation of causally-grounded counterfactual explanations for machine learning classifiers, measuring distances along the data manifold in a differential geometric-principled manner.

paragraphs: The geometric organization of data can guide machine learning, but this paper asks how that organization relates to a causal model of the data. It characterizes the data manifolds implied by structural causal models. The aim is to give the geometry a causal basis, connecting the shape of the data to the relationships specified by the model.

The resulting framework supports reasoning about the manifold under interventions and counterfactuals. These capabilities connect geometric questions about data to causal questions about changes in the modeled system. Its two stated strengths are therefore linked: the causal model informs the manifold’s structure, and that structure becomes a setting in which causal reasoning can be performed.

The authors illustrate the framework through counterfactual explanations for machine learning classifiers. They generate causally grounded explanations while measuring distances along the data manifold using differential-geometric principles. This application brings together the causal grounding of a proposed counterfactual and a geometric way to quantify its distance, showing how the framework can inform classifier explanations.
summary.tldr: The paper derives causally informed data geometry from structural causal models and applies it to manifold-based counterfactual explanations.

title: On Data Manifolds Entailed by Structural Causal Models

abstract: We consider random walks on discrete state spaces, such as general undirected graphs, where the random walkers are designed to approximate a target quantity over the network topology via sampling and neighborhood exploration in the form of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) procedures. Given any Markov chain corresponding to a target probability distribution, we design a self-repellent random walk (SRRW) which is less likely to transition to nodes that were highly visited in the past, and more likely to transition to seldom visited nodes. For a class of SRRWs parameterized by a positive real $\alpha$, we prove that the empirical distribution of the process converges almost surely to the the target (stationary) distribution of the underlying Markov chain kernel. We then provide a central limit theorem and derive the exact form of the arising asymptotic co-variance matrix, which allows us to show that the SRRW with a stronger repellence (larger $\alpha$) always achieves a smaller asymptotic covariance, in the sense of Loewner ordering of co-variance matrices. Especially for SRRW-driven MCMC algorithms, we show that the decrease in the asymptotic sampling variance is of the order $O(1/\alpha)$, eventually going down to zero. Finally, we provide numerical simulations complimentary to our theoretical results, also empirically testing a version of SRRW with $\alpha$ increasing in time to combine the benefits of smaller asymptotic variance due to large $\alpha$, with empirically observed faster mixing properties of SRRW with smaller $\alpha$.

paragraphs: Random walks can estimate quantities over a network by sampling its nodes. This paper modifies a given Markov chain so that its walker favors seldom-visited nodes and avoids repeatedly visited ones. The aim is more efficient sampling while retaining the target distribution associated with the original chain.

For a class of self-repellent walks controlled by a positive parameter alpha, the authors prove almost-sure convergence of the empirical distribution to the target. They also establish a central limit theorem and derive the exact asymptotic covariance. Increasing alpha reduces that covariance in the matrix ordering considered, giving a precise sense in which stronger repulsion improves long-run sampling precision.

For MCMC estimation, the asymptotic sampling variance decreases on the order of 1/alpha and approaches zero as alpha grows. This concerns asymptotic variance rather than zero error after finitely many samples. Simulations support the theory and explore increasing alpha over time, aiming to combine the empirically faster mixing seen at smaller alpha with the smaller asymptotic variance available at larger alpha.
summary.tldr: Self-repellent random walks preserve the target distribution while stronger repulsion provably reduces asymptotic sampling variance.

title: Self-Repellent Random Walks on General Graphs - Achieving Minimal Sampling Variance via Nonlinear Markov Chains

abstract: Existing neural active learning algorithms have aimed to optimize the predictive performance of neural networks (NNs) by selecting data for labelling. However, other than a good predictive performance, being robust against random parameter initializations is also a crucial requirement in safety-critical applications. To this end, we introduce our expected variance with Gaussian processes (EV-GP) criterion for neural active learning, which is theoretically guaranteed to select data points which lead to trained NNs with both (a) good predictive performances and (b) initialization robustness. Importantly, our EV-GP criterion is training-free, i.e., it does not require any training of the NN during data selection, which makes it computationally efficient. We empirically demonstrate that our EV-GP criterion is highly correlated with both initialization robustness and generalization performance, and show that it consistently outperforms baseline methods in terms of both desiderata, especially in situations with limited initial data or large batch sizes.

paragraphs: Active learning selects which examples should receive labels so that a model can learn effectively from a limited labeled set. This paper adds a second objective to predictive quality: reducing sensitivity to the neural network’s random initial parameters. That concern matters when different training initializations could otherwise yield inconsistent predictive behavior.

The authors introduce EV-GP, an expected-variance criterion based on Gaussian processes. They provide a theoretical guarantee connecting its selections to both good predictive performance and robustness to initialization in trained neural networks. The selection process does not require training the neural network, making it computationally efficient. Training-free here describes choosing data; the selected examples are still used to train the resulting network.

Empirically, EV-GP is strongly correlated with both generalization performance and initialization robustness. The method consistently outperforms the evaluated baselines on both objectives, particularly when the initial labeled set is small or selection batches are large. The contribution treats stable outcomes across initializations as an explicit data-selection objective alongside predictive accuracy.
summary.tldr: EV-GP selects labeling candidates without neural-network training, with theoretical and empirical support for predictive performance and initialization robustness.

title: Training-Free Neural Active Learning with Initialization-Robustness Guarantees

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is a critical requirement for the deployment of deep neural networks. This paper introduces the HEAT model, a new post-hoc OOD detection method estimating the density of in-distribution (ID) samples using hybrid energy-based models (EBM) in the feature space of a pre-trained backbone. HEAT complements prior density estimators of the ID density, e.g. parametric models like the Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), to provide an accurate yet robust density estimation. A second contribution is to leverage the EBM framework to provide a unified density estimation and to compose several energy terms. Extensive experiments demonstrate the significance of the two contributions. HEAT sets new state-of-the-art OOD detection results on the CIFAR-10 / CIFAR-100 benchmark as well as on the large-scale Imagenet benchmark. The code is available at: https://github.com/MarcLafon/heatood.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection aims to recognize inputs that differ from the data a model is expected to handle. HEAT approaches this by estimating the density of familiar, in-distribution examples in the feature space of a pretrained backbone. It is a post-hoc method, applied using an already trained representation.

The model combines existing density estimators with a hybrid energy-based formulation. For example, a Gaussian mixture model can provide a prior density estimate that HEAT complements. The aim is an estimate that is both accurate and robust. A second contribution uses the energy-based framework to bring density estimation into a unified form and combine several energy terms.

The experiments support the usefulness of both contributions: complementing prior estimators and composing energy terms. The authors report state-of-the-art out-of-distribution detection results on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 and the large-scale ImageNet benchmark. These findings show that modeling the distribution of learned features can provide an effective basis for detection, with the hybrid formulation improving the use of existing density estimates.
summary.tldr: HEAT combines density estimators and energy-based modeling in pretrained feature spaces to achieve strong out-of-distribution detection results.

title: Hybrid Energy Based Model in the Feature Space for Out-of-Distribution Detection

abstract: Policy Optimization (PO) is one of the most popular methods in Reinforcement Learning (RL). Thus, theoretical guarantees for PO algorithms have become especially important to the RL community. In this paper, we study PO in adversarial MDPs with a challenge that arises in almost every real-world application – delayed bandit feedback . We give the first near-optimal regret bounds for PO in tabular MDPs, and may even surpass state-of-the-art (which uses less efficient methods). Our novel Delay-Adapted PO (DAPO) is easy to implement and to generalize, allowing us to extend our algorithm to: (i) infinite state space under the assumption of linear $Q$-function, proving the first regret bounds for delayed feedback with function approximation. (ii) deep RL, demonstrating its effectiveness in experiments on MuJoCo domains.

paragraphs: Policy optimization learns a decision rule by updating it using feedback from interaction. Delayed bandit feedback complicates this process: information about a chosen action arrives later, while the learner continues making decisions. This paper studies that challenge in adversarial Markov decision processes, seeking guarantees for a widely used family of reinforcement learning methods.

The proposed algorithm, Delay-Adapted Policy Optimization, achieves the first near-optimal regret bounds for policy optimization in tabular MDPs. Regret measures the performance shortfall relative to a comparison policy. The authors also state that their bounds may surpass the existing state of the art, which relies on less efficient methods. That comparison is presented as a possibility rather than an unconditional improvement.

The design extends beyond finite tables. Assuming a linear Q-function, the authors handle infinite state spaces and prove the first delayed-feedback regret bounds with function approximation. They also adapt the approach to deep reinforcement learning and demonstrate effectiveness on MuJoCo domains. These contributions combine a tabular theoretical result, a function-approximation result under a stated assumption, and an empirical deep-learning extension.
summary.tldr: DAPO provides near-optimal tabular policy-optimization regret bounds with delayed feedback and extends to linear function approximation and deep reinforcement learning.

title: Delay-Adapted Policy Optimization and Improved Regret for Adversarial MDP with Delayed Bandit Feedback

abstract: The cost of vision-and-language pre-training has become increasingly prohibitive due to end-to-end training of large-scale models. This paper proposes BLIP-2, a generic and efficient pre-training strategy that bootstraps vision-language pre-training from off-the-shelf frozen pre-trained image encoders and frozen large language models. BLIP-2 bridges the modality gap with a lightweight Querying Transformer, which is pre-trained in two stages. The first stage bootstraps vision-language representation learning from a frozen image encoder. The second stage bootstraps vision-to-language generative learning from a frozen language model. BLIP-2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on various vision-language tasks, despite having significantly fewer trainable parameters than existing methods. For example, our model outperforms Flamingo80B by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2 with 54x fewer trainable parameters. We also demonstrate the model’s emerging capabilities of zero-shot image-to-text generation that can follow natural language instructions.

paragraphs: BLIP-2 addresses the expense of training large vision-and-language systems end to end. It starts with an already trained image encoder and an already trained large language model, keeping both frozen. The learning effort instead centers on a lightweight Querying Transformer that connects visual information with the language model’s capabilities.

This connecting component is pretrained in two stages. The first develops vision-language representations using the frozen image encoder. The second develops image-to-language generation using the frozen language model. Splitting the process this way provides a route to combining existing models while training substantially fewer parameters than methods that update larger portions of the system.

The paper reports state-of-the-art results across various vision-language tasks. On zero-shot VQAv2, BLIP-2 outperforms Flamingo80B by 8.7% while using 54 times fewer trainable parameters. It also demonstrates emerging image-to-text generation abilities that follow natural-language instructions without task-specific examples. These results show that learning the connection between frozen components can deliver strong performance with a much smaller trainable component.
summary.tldr: BLIP-2 connects frozen vision and language models through a lightweight transformer, achieving strong vision-language results with far fewer trainable parameters.

title: BLIP-2: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training with Frozen Image Encoders and Large Language Models

abstract: This paper presents a stochastic differential equation (SDE) approach for general-purpose image restoration. The key construction consists in a mean-reverting SDE that transforms a high-quality image into a degraded counterpart as a mean state with fixed Gaussian noise. Then, by simulating the corresponding reverse-time SDE, we are able to restore the origin of the low-quality image without relying on any task-specific prior knowledge. Crucially, the proposed mean-reverting SDE has a closed-form solution, allowing us to compute the ground truth time-dependent score and learn it with a neural network. Moreover, we propose a maximum likelihood objective to learn an optimal reverse trajectory that stabilizes the training and improves the restoration results. The experiments show that our proposed method achieves highly competitive performance in quantitative comparisons on image deraining, deblurring, and denoising, setting a new state-of-the-art on two deraining datasets. Finally, the general applicability of our approach is further demonstrated via qualitative results on image super-resolution, inpainting, and dehazing. Code is available at https://github.com/Algolzw/image-restoration-sde.

paragraphs: This paper frames image restoration as reversing a stochastic degradation process. Its mean-reverting stochastic differential equation transforms a high-quality image toward a degraded counterpart, which serves as the mean state with fixed Gaussian noise. Simulating the corresponding reverse-time equation then provides a way to recover the image without relying on task-specific prior knowledge.

A key advantage is that the forward equation has a closed-form solution. This lets the authors compute the ground-truth time-dependent score used to train a neural network. They also introduce a maximum likelihood objective for learning an optimal reverse trajectory, reporting that it stabilizes training and improves restoration quality.

Quantitative experiments show highly competitive performance on removing rain, blur, and noise, including new state-of-the-art results on two deraining datasets. Qualitative examples extend the demonstration to super-resolution, inpainting, and dehazing. These two forms of evidence have different scope: the former support numerical comparisons on the evaluated tasks, while the latter illustrate the approach's broader applicability through example outputs.
summary.tldr: A reversible mean-reverting stochastic process supports image restoration across tasks, with strong reported results for rain, blur, and noise removal.

title: Image Restoration with Mean-Reverting Stochastic Differential Equations

abstract: Federated bilevel optimization has attracted increasing attention due to emerging machine learning and communication applications. The biggest challenge lies in computing the gradient of the upper-level objective function (i.e., hypergradient) in the federated setting due to the nonlinear and distributed construction of a series of global Hessian matrices. In this paper, we propose a novel communication-efficient federated hypergradient estimator via aggregated iterative differentiation (AggITD). AggITD is simple to implement and significantly reduces the communication cost by conducting the federated hypergradient estimation and the lower-level optimization simultaneously. We show that the proposed AggITD-based algorithm achieves the same sample complexity as existing approximate implicit differentiation (AID)-based approaches with much fewer communication rounds in the presence of data heterogeneity. Our results also shed light on the great advantage of ITD over AID in the federated/distributed hypergradient estimation. This differs from the comparison in the non-distributed bilevel optimization, where ITD is less efficient than AID. Our extensive experiments demonstrate the great effectiveness and communication efficiency of the proposed method.
