paragraphs: Bilevel optimization links an upper-level objective to a lower-level optimization problem. In federated learning, computing the upper-level gradient, called a hypergradient, is particularly challenging because the required curvature information is distributed across participants. The paper identifies the nonlinear construction of sequences of global Hessian matrices as a major obstacle to efficient communication.

The proposed estimator, aggregated iterative differentiation or AggITD, computes hypergradient information while lower-level optimization is taking place. Performing these operations together substantially reduces communication. The authors show that an algorithm using AggITD attains the same sample complexity as existing approaches based on approximate implicit differentiation, while requiring far fewer communication rounds even when participants have heterogeneous data.

This result separates the cost of using data from the cost of exchanging information. It also changes the comparison between differentiation strategies: iterative differentiation has an advantage here despite being less efficient than approximate implicit differentiation in the non-distributed comparison discussed by the authors. Experiments support the method’s effectiveness and communication efficiency, reinforcing the importance of designing optimization procedures around the distributed setting.
summary.tldr: AggITD combines lower-level optimization with hypergradient estimation to reduce federated communication without worsening the stated sample complexity.

title: Communication-Efficient Federated Hypergradient Computation via Aggregated Iterative Differentiation

abstract: We propose a new method to measure the task-specific accuracy of Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models (RAG). Evaluation is performed by scoring the RAG on an automatically-generated synthetic exam composed of multiple choice questions based on the corpus of documents associated with the task. Our method is an automated, cost-efficient, interpretable, and robust strategy to select the optimal components for a RAG system. We leverage Item Response Theory (IRT) to estimate the quality of an exam and its informativeness on task-specific accuracy. IRT also provides a natural way to iteratively improve the exam by eliminating the exam questions that are not sufficiently informative about a model’s ability. We demonstrate our approach on four new open-ended Question-Answering tasks based on Arxiv abstracts, StackExchange questions, AWS DevOps troubleshooting guides, and SEC filings. In addition, our experiments reveal more general insights into factors impacting RAG performance like size, retrieval mechanism, prompting and fine-tuning. Most notably, our findings show that choosing the right retrieval algorithms often leads to bigger performance gains than simply using a larger language model.

paragraphs: A retrieval-augmented language model depends on both the language model and the machinery that retrieves relevant documents. This paper proposes evaluating those choices with an automatically generated multiple-choice exam built from the document collection associated with the task. The exam provides a task-specific basis for comparing system components.

The method uses Item Response Theory to assess exam quality and how much its questions reveal about a model's ability. Questions that provide insufficient information can be removed, allowing the exam to improve iteratively. This makes evaluation itself an object of measurement, rather than treating every generated question as equally useful.

The authors demonstrate the approach on question-answering tasks involving Arxiv abstracts, StackExchange questions, AWS troubleshooting guides, and SEC filings. Their experiments examine model size, retrieval, prompting, and fine-tuning. A notable finding is that selecting an appropriate retrieval algorithm often brings larger gains than increasing language-model size. The reported results support using targeted exams to guide practical RAG design decisions.
summary.tldr: Automatically generated, statistically refined exams help compare RAG components and show that retrieval choices often matter more than model size.

title: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Language Models with Task-Specific Exam Generation

abstract: We study the problem of training an unbiased and accurate model given a dataset with multiple biases. This problem is challenging since the multiple biases cause multiple undesirable shortcuts during training, and even worse, mitigating one may exacerbate the other. We propose a novel training method to tackle this challenge. Our method first groups training data so that different groups induce different shortcuts, and then optimizes a linear combination of group-wise losses while adjusting their weights dynamically to alleviate conflicts between the groups in performance; this approach, rooted in the multi-objective optimization theory, encourages to achieve the minimax Pareto solution. We also present a new benchmark with multiple biases, dubbed MultiCelebA, for evaluating debiased training methods under realistic and challenging scenarios. Our method achieved the best on three datasets with multiple biases, and also showed superior performance on conventional single-bias datasets.

paragraphs: A dataset can contain several misleading correlations that a model uses as shortcuts. Removing reliance on one shortcut can increase reliance on another, so addressing biases independently may create competing training pressures. This paper treats those conflicts as a multi-objective optimization problem.

The proposed method first divides training data into groups that induce different shortcuts. It then trains on a weighted combination of the groups’ losses, dynamically adjusting the weights to reduce conflicts in performance. The optimization is designed to encourage a minimax Pareto solution, balancing the competing group objectives with attention to the worst-performing objective. The abstract describes this as an encouraged outcome rather than an unconditional guarantee.

Their method achieves the best reported performance on three datasets containing multiple biases and also performs strongly on conventional single-bias datasets. These results support coordinating bias mitigation across groups instead of assuming that improvements against separate shortcuts will automatically reinforce one another.
summary.tldr: Dynamically balancing group losses helps models address multiple shortcut correlations whose mitigation can otherwise conflict.

title: Improving Robustness to Multiple Spurious Correlations by Multi-Objective Optimization

abstract: Planning is a fundamental property of human intelligence. Reasoning about asynchronous plans is challenging since it requires sequential and parallel planning to optimize time costs. Can large language models (LLMs) succeed at this task? Here, we present the first large-scale study investigating this question. We find that a representative set of closed and open-source LLMs, including GPT-4 and LLaMA-2, behave poorly when not supplied with illustrations about the task-solving process in our benchmark AsyncHow. We propose a novel technique called Plan Like a Graph (PLaG) that combines graphs with natural language prompts and achieves state-of-the-art results. We show that although PLaG can boost model performance, LLMs still suffer from drastic degradation when task complexity increases, highlighting the limits of utilizing LLMs for simulating digital devices. We see our study as an exciting step towards using LLMs as efficient autonomous agents. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/fangru-lin/graph-llm-asynchow-plan.

paragraphs: Asynchronous planning requires reasoning about actions that must happen in sequence and actions that can happen in parallel. A successful plan must account for both to optimize time costs. The paper investigates whether large language models can handle this kind of reasoning through a large-scale study using the AsyncHow benchmark.

The authors find poor performance among representative closed and open-source models, including GPT-4 and LLaMA-2, when examples of the task-solving process are absent. They introduce Plan Like a Graph, or PLaG, which combines graph representations with natural-language prompts. The technique achieves state-of-the-art results in the study, showing that graph-enhanced prompting can improve asynchronous planning performance.

The improvement does not remove the difficulty of more complex tasks. The authors report sharp performance degradation as complexity increases, even with PLaG. This finding matters for proposed autonomous agents: better task representation helps, but the evaluated models still face substantial limits when reasoning about demanding plans and simulating digital devices.
summary.tldr: Graph-enhanced prompting improves asynchronous planning, but evaluated language models still deteriorate sharply as task complexity grows.

title: Graph-enhanced Large Language Models in Asynchronous Plan Reasoning

abstract: Growing concerns over negligent or malicious uses of AI have increased the appetite for tools that help manage the risks of the technology. In 2018, licenses with behaviorial-use clauses (commonly referred to as Responsible AI Licenses) were proposed to give developers a framework for releasing AI assets while specifying their users to mitigate negative applications. As of the end of 2023, on the order of 40,000 software and model repositories have adopted responsible AI licenses licenses. Notable models licensed with behavioral use clauses include BLOOM (language) and LLaMA2 (language), Stable Diffusion (image), and GRID (robotics). This paper explores why and how these licenses have been adopted, and why and how they have been adapted to fit particular use cases. We use a mixed-methods methodology of qualitative interviews, clustering of license clauses, and quantitative analysis of license adoption. Based on this evidence we take the position that responsible AI licenses need standardization to avoid confusing users or diluting their impact. At the same time, customization of behavioral restrictions is also appropriate in some contexts (e.g., medical domains). We advocate for “standardized customization” that can meet users’ needs and can be supported via tooling.

paragraphs: Responsible AI licenses include clauses governing how released software or models may be used. They are intended to help developers address negligent or malicious applications while distributing AI assets. This position paper examines their adoption and adaptation, then argues that standardization is necessary to preserve their usefulness as adoption grows.

The authors combine qualitative interviews, clustering of license clauses, and quantitative analysis of adoption. These methods examine both why organizations choose such licenses and how they modify restrictions for particular situations. The abstract reports adoption across roughly 40,000 repositories by the end of 2023, making variation in license language a practical issue for many users.

They also recognize that some settings, such as medical applications, warrant tailored behavioral restrictions. This is an evidence-informed recommendation about license design, balancing consistency with the needs of distinct application contexts.
summary.tldr: The authors argue for standardized but customizable responsible AI licenses to reduce confusion while accommodating domain-specific behavioral restrictions.

title: Position: Standardization of Behavioral Use Clauses is Necessary for the Adoption of Responsible Licensing of AI

abstract: Online convex optimization (OCO) with arbitrary delays, in which gradients or other information of functions could be arbitrarily delayed, has received increasing attention recently. Different from previous studies that focus on stationary environments, this paper investigates the delayed OCO in non-stationary environments, and aims to minimize the dynamic regret with respect to any sequence of comparators. To this end, we first propose a simple algorithm, namely DOGD, which performs a gradient descent step for each delayed gradient according to their arrival order. Despite its simplicity, our novel analysis shows that the dynamic regret of DOGD can be automatically bounded by $O(\sqrt{\bar{d}T}(P_T+1))$ under mild assumptions, and $O(\sqrt{dT}(P_T+1))$ in the worst case, where $\bar{d}$ and $d$ denote the average and maximum delay respectively, $T$ is the time horizon, and $P_T$ is the path-length of comparators. Furthermore, we develop an improved algorithm, which reduces those dynamic regret bounds achieved by DOGD to $O(\sqrt{\bar{d}T(P_T+1)})$ and $O(\sqrt{dT(P_T+1)})$, respectively. The key idea is to run multiple DOGD with different learning rates, and utilize a meta-algorithm to track the best one based on their delayed performance. Finally, we demonstrate that our improved algorithm is optimal in the worst case by deriving a matching lower bound.

paragraphs: This paper studies online convex optimization when feedback arrives late and the environment changes over time. Performance is measured by dynamic regret against a sequence of comparison decisions. The sequence's path length measures how much those decisions move, making it possible to express the difficulty of tracking a changing target.

The first algorithm, DOGD, takes a gradient descent step whenever a delayed gradient arrives, following arrival order. Under mild assumptions, its regret scales with the square root of average delay times the horizon, multiplied by path length plus one. Its worst-case bound replaces average delay with maximum delay. Thus, even this simple update rule has guarantees that account for both delay and change.

An improved algorithm runs several DOGD instances with different learning rates and uses delayed performance to track the best one. It brings the path-length factor inside the square root in both bounds, improving the dependence on target movement. A matching lower bound establishes worst-case optimality for the improved algorithm, giving the result a theoretical benchmark beyond an upper-bound analysis alone.
summary.tldr: Combining delayed gradient-descent learners yields improved dynamic-regret bounds for changing environments and achieves worst-case optimality.

title: Non-stationary Online Convex Optimization with Arbitrary Delays

abstract: Aligning image pairs captured by different sensors or those undergoing significant appearance changes is crucial for various computer vision and robotics applications. Existing approaches cope with this problem via either Sparse feature Matching (SM) or Dense direct Alignment (DA) paradigms. Sparse methods are efficient but lack accuracy in textureless scenes, while dense ones are more accurate in all scenes but demand for good initialization. In this paper, we propose SDME, a Sparse-to-Dense Multimodal feature Extractor based on a novel multi-task network that simultaneously predicts SM and DA features for robust multimodal image registration. We propose the sparse-to-dense registration paradigm: we first perform initial registration via SM and then refine the result via DA. By using the well-designed SDME, the sparse-to-dense approach combines the merits from both SM and DA. Extensive experiments on MSCOCO, GoogleEarth, VIS-NIR and VIS-IR-drone datasets demonstrate that our method achieves remarkable performance on multimodal cases. Furthermore, our approach exhibits robust generalization capabilities, enabling the fine-tuning of models initially trained on single-modal datasets for use with smaller multimodal datasets. Our code is available at https://github.com/KN-Zhang/SDME.

paragraphs: Image registration aligns two views of the same content, including views captured by different sensors or with substantial appearance changes. Sparse feature matching is efficient but can struggle where there is little texture. Dense alignment offers greater accuracy but needs a good initial alignment. This paper combines the two approaches into a sequential procedure.

Its Sparse-to-Dense Multimodal feature Extractor, SDME, uses a multi-task network to predict features for both sparse matching and dense alignment. Registration begins with sparse matching to establish an initial solution. Dense alignment then refines that solution. The first stage therefore supplies the initialization needed by the second, while the shared feature extractor supports both operations.

Experiments on MSCOCO, GoogleEarth, VIS-NIR, and VIS-IR-drone demonstrate strong performance on multimodal cases. The authors also report that models trained initially on single-modal datasets can be fine-tuned using smaller multimodal datasets. This supports the approach’s generalization across imaging conditions. Its practical value comes from joining efficient initial matching with detailed refinement and supporting adaptation when multimodal training data are comparatively limited.
summary.tldr: SDME learns features for sparse matching and dense refinement together to align images across sensors and appearance changes.

title: Sparse-to-dense Multimodal Image Registration via Multi-Task Learning

abstract: Training a unified model to take multiple targets into account is a trend towards artificial general intelligence. However, how to efficiently mitigate the training conflicts among heterogeneous data collected from different domains or tasks remains under-explored. In this study, we explore to leverage Mixture of Low-rank Adapters (MoLA) to mitigate conflicts in heterogeneous data training, which requires to jointly train the multiple low-rank adapters and their shared backbone. Specifically, we introduce two variants of MoLA, namely, MoLA-Grad and MoLA-Router, to respectively handle the target-aware and target-agnostic scenarios during inference. The former uses task identifiers to assign personalized low-rank adapters to each task, disentangling task-specific knowledge towards their adapters, thereby mitigating heterogeneity conflicts. The latter uses a novel Task-wise Decorrelation (TwD) loss to intervene the router to learn oriented weight combinations of adapters to homogeneous tasks, achieving similar effects. We conduct comprehensive experiments to verify the superiority of MoLA over previous state-of-the-art methods and present in-depth analysis on its working mechanism. Source code is available at: https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MoLA

paragraphs: Training one model on several domains or tasks can create conflicts because different examples push learning toward different targets. This paper investigates Mixture of Low-rank Adapters, or MoLA, as a way to reduce those conflicts. Its approach jointly trains multiple adapters and their shared backbone, allowing task-specific adaptation within a unified model.

The authors propose two variants depending on what is known at inference time. MoLA-Grad uses task identifiers to assign dedicated adapters, directing task-specific knowledge into those components. MoLA-Router handles cases where the target is not supplied. It uses a Task-wise Decorrelation loss to guide the router toward suitable combinations of adapters for similar tasks.

Both variants aim to keep heterogeneous training signals from interfering as strongly while retaining a shared model. The reported experiments show superiority over previous state-of-the-art methods, and the paper analyzes how the approach works. Its practical distinction is the treatment of task information: explicit identifiers determine adaptation in one variant, while learned routing supplies the corresponding selection mechanism in the other.
summary.tldr: MoLA reduces conflicts in mixed-task training through multiple jointly trained adapters, selected by task identifiers or a learned router.

title: Exploring Training on Heterogeneous Data with Mixture of Low-rank Adapters

abstract: With recent dramatic increases in AI system capabilities, there has been growing interest in utilizing machine learning for reasoning-heavy, quantitative tasks, particularly mathematics. While there are many resources capturing mathematics at the high-school, undergraduate, and graduate level, there are far fewer resources available that align with the level of difficulty and open endedness encountered by professional mathematicians working on open problems. To address this, we introduce a new collection of datasets, the Algebraic Combinatorics Dataset Repository (ACD Repo), representing either foundational results or open problems in algebraic combinatorics, a subfield of mathematics that studies discrete structures arising from abstract algebra. Further differentiating our dataset collection is the fact that it aims at the conjecturing process. Each dataset includes an open-ended research level question and a large collection of examples (up to 10M in some cases) from which conjectures should be generated. We describe all nine datasets, the different ways machine learning models can be applied to them (e.g., training with narrow models followed by interpretability analysis or program synthesis with LLMs), and discuss some of the challenges involved in designing datasets like these.

Its contribution is a collection and accompanying research framework for studying conjecture generation, rather than a reported claim that models have resolved the included open problems.
summary.tldr: The ACD Repo provides nine research-level datasets for generating mathematical conjectures from large collections of algebraic-combinatorial examples.

title: Machine Learning meets Algebraic Combinatorics: A Suite of Datasets Capturing Research-level Conjecturing Ability in Pure Mathematics

abstract: We address the problem of uncertainty quantification in time series forecasting by exploiting observations at correlated sequences. Relational deep learning methods leveraging graph representations are among the most effective tools for obtaining point estimates from spatiotemporal data and correlated time series. However, the problem of exploiting relational structures to estimate the uncertainty of such predictions has been largely overlooked in the same context. To this end, we propose a novel distribution-free approach based on the conformal prediction framework and quantile regression. Despite the recent applications of conformal prediction to sequential data, existing methods operate independently on each target time series and do not account for relationships among them when constructing the prediction interval. We fill this void by introducing a novel conformal prediction method based on graph deep learning operators. Our approach, named Conformal Relational Prediction (CoRel), does not require the relational structure (graph) to be known a priori and can be applied on top of any pre-trained predictor. Additionally, CoRel includes an adaptive component to handle non-exchangeable data and changes in the input time series. Our approach provides accurate coverage and achieves state-of-the-art uncertainty quantification in relevant benchmarks.

paragraphs: Forecasts for related time series can benefit from information shared across sequences. Existing relational models exploit such connections to predict values, but uncertainty estimation has received less attention. This paper asks how relationships between sequences can also help construct prediction intervals, which express a range of possible future values.

Conformal Relational Prediction, or CoRel, combines conformal prediction, quantile regression, and graph deep-learning operators. Its interval construction uses relationships among time series rather than treating every target sequence independently. The method does not require a graph of those relationships to be supplied beforehand and can operate on top of any pretrained predictor.

CoRel also includes an adaptive component for non-exchangeable data and changes in the input sequences. This addresses the sequential setting in which observations need not behave as interchangeable samples. The authors report accurate coverage and state-of-the-art uncertainty quantification on relevant benchmarks. The contribution extends relational information from improving point forecasts to improving how uncertainty around those forecasts is represented.
summary.tldr: CoRel uses relationships among time series to construct adaptive prediction intervals on top of pretrained forecasting models.

title: Relational Conformal Prediction for Correlated Time Series

abstract: We propose smoothed primal-dual algorithms for solving stochastic nonconvex optimization problems with linear inequality constraints. Our algorithms are single-loop and only require a single (or two) samples of stochastic gradients at each iteration. A defining feature of our algorithm is that it is based on an inexact gradient descent framework for the Moreau envelope, where the gradient of the Moreau envelope is estimated using one step of a stochastic primal-dual (linearized) augmented Lagrangian algorithm. To handle inequality constraints and stochasticity, we combine the recently established global error bounds in constrained optimization with a Moreau envelope-based analysis of stochastic proximal algorithms. We establish the optimal (in their respective cases) $O(\varepsilon^{-4})$ and $O(\varepsilon^{-3})$ sample complexity guarantees for our algorithms and provide extensions to stochastic linear constraints. Unlike existing methods, iterations of our algorithms are free of subproblems, large batch sizes or increasing penalty parameters in their iterations and they use dual variable updates to ensure feasibility.

paragraphs: This paper studies stochastic nonconvex optimization with linear inequality constraints. The challenge combines noisy gradient information, a nonconvex objective, and the need to satisfy constraints. The proposed algorithms use a single loop and require only one or two stochastic gradient samples per iteration, keeping each update comparatively simple.

Its gradient is estimated using one step of a stochastic primal-dual augmented Lagrangian algorithm. The analysis combines global error bounds for constrained optimization with a Moreau-envelope treatment of stochastic proximal methods to handle inequalities and noise together.

The contribution pairs these theoretical efficiency guarantees with an algorithmic structure that avoids several sources of expensive work inside each iteration.
summary.tldr: Single-loop primal-dual algorithms achieve case-specific optimal sample complexity for stochastic nonconvex problems with linear inequality constraints.

title: Stochastic Smoothed Primal-Dual Algorithms for Nonconvex Optimization with Linear Inequality Constraints

abstract: The goal of offline reinforcement learning (RL) is to extract the best possible policy from the previously collected dataset considering the out-of-distribution (OOD) sample issue. Offline model-based RL (MBRL) is a captivating solution capable of alleviating such issues through a state-action transition augmentation with a learned dynamic model. Unfortunately, offline MBRL methods have been observed to fail in sparse rewarded and long-horizon environments for a long time. In this work, we propose a novel MBRL method, dubbed Temporal Distance-Aware Transition Augmentation (TempDATA), that generates additional transitions in a geometrically structured representation space, instead of state space. For comprehending long-horizon behaviors efficiently, our main idea is to learn state abstraction, which captures a temporal distance from both trajectory and transition levels of state space. Our experiments empirically confirm that TempDATA outperforms previous offline MBRL methods and achieves matching or surpassing the performance of diffusion-based trajectory augmentation and goal-conditioned RL on the D4RL AntMaze, FrankaKitchen, CALVIN, and pixel-based FrankaKitchen.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning seeks a strong policy using an existing dataset, with out-of-distribution samples posing a central challenge. Model-based methods can augment that data using learned transitions, but they have struggled with sparse rewards and long horizons. TempDATA changes the space in which additional transitions are generated.

The method learns a geometrically structured representation of states that captures temporal distance. It draws this information from both complete trajectories and individual transitions, aiming to represent long-horizon behavior efficiently. Additional transitions are then generated in this learned representation space, giving augmentation access to temporal structure beyond the original state description.

Experiments show that TempDATA outperforms earlier offline model-based methods. It also matches or exceeds the performance of diffusion-based trajectory augmentation and goal-conditioned reinforcement learning on D4RL AntMaze, FrankaKitchen, CALVIN, and pixel-based FrankaKitchen. These are empirical comparisons across the named benchmarks. The findings support using a representation organized around temporal distance to make transition augmentation more effective for the evaluated sparse-reward and long-horizon problems.
summary.tldr: TempDATA improves offline reinforcement learning by generating transitions in a representation that captures temporal distance.

title: Temporal Distance-aware Transition Augmentation for Offline Model-based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Continual learning of multiple tasks remains a major challenge for neural networks. Here, we investigate how task order influences continual learning and propose a strategy for optimizing it. Leveraging a linear teacher-student model with latent factors, we derive an analytical expression relating task similarity and ordering to learning performance. Our analysis reveals two principles that hold under a wide parameter range: (1) tasks should be arranged from the least representative to the most typical, and (2) adjacent tasks should be dissimilar. We validate these rules on both synthetic data and real-world image classification datasets (Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100), demonstrating consistent performance improvements in both multilayer perceptrons and convolutional neural networks. Our work thus presents a generalizable framework for task-order optimization in task-incremental continual learning.

Leveraging a linear teacher-student model with latent factors, we derive an analytical expression relating task similarity and ordering to learning performance. Our analysis reveals two principles that hold under a wide parameter range: (1) tasks should be arranged from the least representative to the most typical, and (2) adjacent tasks should be dissimilar. We validate these rules on both synthetic data and real-world image classification datasets (Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100), demonstrating consistent performance improvements in both multilayer perceptrons and convolutional neural networks. Our work thus presents a generalizable framework for task-order optimization in task-incremental continual learning.

paragraphs: Continual learning trains a model on multiple tasks over time, so the sequence of those tasks can affect its eventual performance. This paper studies how to choose that sequence. It begins with a linear teacher-student model containing latent factors, allowing task relationships and learning outcomes to be analyzed mathematically.

The authors derive an expression connecting task similarity, task order, and performance. Their analysis yields two principles over a wide range of parameters: begin with less representative tasks and progress toward more typical ones, and place dissimilar tasks next to one another. These are supported principles within the analyzed range, rather than unconditional rules for every learning setting.

Experiments test the principles on synthetic data and on Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. Both multilayer perceptrons and convolutional networks show consistent performance improvements. The findings make task order an explicit optimization choice in task-incremental continual learning and demonstrate that a simplified theoretical model can provide useful guidance for more complex image-classification experiments.
summary.tldr: Theory and experiments support ordering continual-learning tasks from less typical to more typical while keeping neighboring tasks dissimilar.

title: Optimal Task Order for Continual Learning of Multiple Tasks

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success, yet most are developed under the in-distribution assumption and fail to generalize to out-of-distribution (OOD) environments. To tackle this problem, some graph invariant learning methods aim to learn invariant subgraph against distribution shifts, which heavily rely on predefined or automatically generated environment labels. However, directly annotating or estimating such environment labels from biased graph data is typically impractical or inaccurate for real-world graphs. Consequently, GNNs may become biased toward variant patterns, resulting in poor OOD generalization. In this paper, we propose to learn disentangled invariant subgraph via self-supervised contrastive variant subgraph estimation for achieving satisfactory OOD generalization. Specifically, we first propose a GNN-based invariant subgraph generator to disentangle the invariant and variant subgraphs. Then, we estimate the degree of the spurious correlations by conducting self-supervised contrastive learning on variant subgraphs. Thanks to the accurate identification and estimation of the variant subgraphs, we can capture invariant subgraphs effectively and further eliminate spurious correlations by inverse propensity score reweighting. We provide theoretical analyses to show that our model can disentangle the ground-truth invariant and variant subgraphs for OOD generalization. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our model over state-of-the-art baselines.

Those estimates support inverse propensity score reweighting, which adjusts how examples influence learning so that misleading associations can be reduced and invariant structure captured more effectively.

The authors provide theoretical analyses showing that their model can recover the underlying invariant and varying subgraphs, alongside experiments reporting improvements over leading baselines. The distinctive idea is to study unstable graph structure directly as a source of information about bias. This makes estimating spurious variation an active part of learning representations intended to generalize across distributions.
summary.tldr: The method estimates spurious graph variation through contrastive learning and reweights training to recover more transferable subgraphs.

title: Disentangling Invariant Subgraph via Variance Contrastive Estimation under Distribution Shifts

abstract: This study investigates the self-rationalization framework constructed with a cooperative game, where a generator initially extracts the most informative segment from raw input, and a subsequent predictor utilizes the selected subset for its input. The generator and predictor are trained collaboratively to maximize prediction accuracy. In this paper, we first uncover a potential caveat: such a cooperative game could unintentionally introduce a sampling bias during rationale extraction. Specifically, the generator might inadvertently create an incorrect correlation between the selected rationale candidate and the label, even when they are semantically unrelated in the original dataset. Subsequently, we elucidate the origins of this bias using both detailed theoretical analysis and empirical evidence. Our findings suggest a direction for inspecting these correlations through attacks, based on which we further introduce an instruction to prevent the predictor from learning the correlations. Through experiments on six text classification datasets and two graph classification datasets using three network architectures (GRUs, BERT, and GCN), we show that our method significantly outperforms recent rationalization methods.

paragraphs: Some systems explain predictions by first selecting a small part of the input and then asking a predictor to use only that selection. The selector and predictor learn together to improve accuracy. This paper shows how that cooperation can introduce a sampling bias: the selection process may create a relationship between a chosen fragment and a label even when the original data contains no corresponding semantic relationship.

The concern is that a selected rationale can become useful for prediction for the wrong reason. A clean starting dataset does not by itself prevent this problem, because the misleading association can emerge during extraction. The authors investigate the origins of this effect through theoretical analysis and empirical evidence, locating the risk in how the two components cooperate.

They use attacks to inspect these correlations and introduce an instruction intended to prevent the predictor from learning them. Experiments cover six text classification datasets, two graph classification datasets, and GRU, BERT, and GCN architectures. The method significantly outperforms recent rationalization approaches in those evaluations, supporting attention to selection-induced bias when learning explanations.
summary.tldr: Cooperative rationale extraction can create misleading correlations even in clean data, and the paper develops an attack-informed method to counter them.

title: Adversarial Cooperative Rationalization: The Risk of Spurious Correlations in Even Clean Datasets

abstract: The feature maps of vision encoders are fundamental to myriad modern AI tasks, ranging from core perception algorithms (e.g. semantic segmentation, object detection, depth perception, etc.) to modern multimodal understanding in vision-language models (VLMs). Currently, in computer vision, the frontier of general purpose vision backbones is Vision Transformers (ViT), typically trained using contrastive loss (e.g. CLIP). A key problem with most off-the-shelf ViTs, particularly CLIP, is that these models are inflexibly low resolution. Most run at $224 \times 224$px, while the "high-resolution" versions are around $378-448$px, but still inflexible. We introduce a novel method to coherently and cheaply upsample the feature maps of low-resolution vision encoders while picking up on fine-grained details that would otherwise be lost due to resolution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on core perception tasks as well as within agglomerative model training using RADIO as a way of providing richer targets for distillation. Code available at https://github.com/NVlabs/FeatSharp

paragraphs: Vision encoders supply feature maps used in tasks such as segmentation, object detection, depth perception, and vision-language understanding. Many widely used Vision Transformers, especially CLIP models, operate at fixed and relatively low image resolutions. That restriction makes it difficult to retain fine spatial details in the representations passed to downstream systems.

FeatSharp introduces a method for coherently upsampling the feature maps of low-resolution encoders at low computational cost. Its goal is to capture fine details that the original resolution would otherwise lose. The object being improved is the encoder’s feature representation, which makes the approach relevant to multiple tasks that consume those features.

The authors demonstrate effectiveness on core perception tasks and in agglomerative model training using RADIO. In the latter setting, the enhanced features provide richer targets for distillation, the process of training a model to reproduce another representation. These applications show two uses for sharper features: improving representations supplied directly to perception tasks and improving the supervision available when training another model.
summary.tldr: FeatSharp cheaply upsamples vision encoder feature maps to preserve finer details for perception tasks and model distillation.

title: FeatSharp: Your Vision Model Features, Sharper

abstract: We present a constructive universal approximation theorem for learning machines equipped with joint-group-equivariant feature maps, called the joint-equivariant machines, based on the group representation theory. “Constructive” here indicates that the distribution of parameters is given in a closed-form expression known as the ridgelet transform. Joint-group-equivariance encompasses a broad class of feature maps that generalize classical group-equivariance. Particularly, fully-connected networks are not group-equivariant but are joint-group-equivariant. Our main theorem also unifies the universal approximation theorems for both shallow and deep networks. Until this study, the universality of deep networks has been shown in a different manner from the universality of shallow networks, but our results discuss them on common ground. Now we can understand the approximation schemes of various learning machines in a unified manner. As applications, we show the constructive universal approximation properties of four examples: depth-$n$ joint-equivariant machine, depth-$n$ fully-connected network, depth-$n$ group-convolutional network, and a new depth-$2$ network with quadratic forms whose universality has not been known.

This paper develops a constructive version for learning systems whose feature maps satisfy joint-group-equivariance. Constructive means that the result supplies a closed-form expression for the distribution of model parameters, using a mathematical object called the ridgelet transform.

Joint-group-equivariance broadens the symmetry framework beyond classical group-equivariance. In particular, the authors place fully connected networks within this broader class even though they are not group-equivariant in the classical sense. Using group representation theory, the paper brings shallow and deep networks into one approximation framework, connecting results that had previously been established through different arguments.

The authors apply their theorem to arbitrary-depth joint-equivariant machines, fully connected networks, and group-convolutional networks. They also establish constructive universality for a two-layer network built with quadratic forms, whose universality had not previously been known. The contribution is a common mathematical account of approximation across these architectures, including an explicit parameter description that makes the theorem constructive.

title: Deep Ridgelet Transform and Unified Universality Theorem for Deep and Shallow Joint-Group-Equivariant Machines

abstract: We propose a novel prompt design paradigm that challenges conventional wisdom in large language model (LLM) prompting. While conventional wisdom prioritizes well-crafted instructions and demonstrations for in-context learning (ICL), we show that pruning random demonstrations into seemingly incoherent ”gibberish” can remarkably improve performance across diverse tasks. Notably, the ”gibberish” always matches or surpasses state-of-the-art automatic prompt optimization techniques, achieving substantial gains regardless of LLM alignment. Nevertheless, discovering an effective pruning strategy is non-trivial, as existing attribution methods and prompt compression algorithms fail to deliver robust results, let alone human intuition. In terms of this, we propose a self-discover prompt optimization framework, PromptQuine, an evolutionary search framework that automatically searches for the pruning strategy by itself using only low-data regimes. Much like the emergent complexity in nature—such as symbiosis and self-organization—arising in response to resource constraints, our framework evolves and refines unconventional yet highly effective prompts by leveraging only the tokens present within the context. We demonstrate its effectiveness across classification, multi-choice question answering, generation and math reasoning tasks across LLMs, while achieving decent runtime efficiency. We hope our findings can guide mechanistic studies on in-context learning, and provide a call to action, to pave the way for more open-ended search algorithms for more effective LLM prompting.

paragraphs: Prompt design usually emphasizes clear instructions and understandable demonstrations. This paper reports a surprising alternative: selectively pruning random demonstrations can produce apparently incoherent text that improves model performance. Its search draws only on tokens already present in the context, making the existing prompt material the resource from which new prompts evolve.

The evaluation covers classification, multiple-choice answering, generation, and mathematical reasoning across language models, with reported runtime efficiency. These findings suggest that human-readable coherence is not a reliable guide to which demonstrations will help in-context learning. The paper positions this result as motivation for mechanistic investigations and more open-ended prompt search.
summary.tldr: PromptQuine evolves pruned, seemingly incoherent demonstrations that perform strongly across the paper’s language-model evaluations.

title: Evolving Prompts In-Context: An Open-ended, Self-replicating Perspective

abstract: Coverless Image Steganography (CIS) hides information without explicitly modifying a cover image, providing strong imperceptibility and inherent robustness to steganalysis. However, existing CIS methods largely lack robust access control, making it difficult to selectively reveal different hidden contents to different authorized users. Such access control is critical for scalable and privacy-sensitive information hiding in multi-user settings. We propose MIDAS (Multi-Image Diffusion-based Access-controlled Steganography), a training-free diffusion-based CIS framework that enables multi-image hiding with user-specific access control via latent-level fusion. MIDAS introduces a Random Basis mechanism to suppress residual structural information, together with a theoretical analysis of information leakage, and a Latent Vector Fusion module that reshapes aggregated latents to better align with the diffusion process. Experimental results demonstrate that MIDAS consistently outperforms existing training-free CIS baselines in access control functionality, stego image quality and diversity, robustness to noise, and resistance to steganalysis, establishing a practical and scalable approach to access-controlled coverless steganography.

Existing methods, however, often lack robust controls over which hidden contents different users can access. This paper focuses on multi-user settings where several images must be hidden while authorized users receive access only to their designated contents.

Its Random Basis mechanism suppresses residual structural information, and the paper provides a theoretical analysis of information leakage. The contribution addresses both selective disclosure and the quality of the images carrying the hidden information.
summary.tldr: MIDAS combines diffusion-based multi-image hiding with user-specific access control without requiring training.

title: Training-Free Coverless Multi-Image Steganography with Access Control

abstract: Designing genetic circuits, which are biological systems capable of programmed behaviors within living cells, remains a laborious, expert-driven process despite decades of progress in synthetic biology. We introduce GenCircuit-RL, a reinforcement learning framework that trains language models to reason about genetic circuit design through code generation, where models produce Python code using PySBOL to construct circuits in the standardized Synthetic Biology Open Language (SBOL) format. Our approach addresses the challenge of sparse feedback in biological design through hierarchical verification rewards that decompose correctness into five levels, from code execution through structural validity to functional behavior, providing dense learning signal while multiplicative dependencies prevent reward hacking. We contribute SynBio-Reason, a benchmark of approximately 4,753 circuits spanning six canonical circuit types and nine tasks from code repair to de novo design, with held-out biological parts enabling rigorous out-of-distribution evaluation. A four-stage curriculum progressively shifts optimization pressure from basic code generation toward functional correctness, enabling models to acquire compositional reasoning capabilities incrementally. Our framework demonstrates that hierarchical verification combined with curriculum learning enables compact language models to generate functionally correct genetic circuits, including generalization to novel biological parts and rediscovery of canonical designs from synthetic biology literature.

This turns an expert-intensive biological design task into a structured generation problem in which proposed designs can receive feedback at several levels of correctness.

This hierarchy supplies denser feedback than a single final success signal. Multiplicative dependencies between levels are used to prevent reward hacking. A four-stage curriculum gradually shifts training emphasis from producing basic working code toward satisfying functional requirements.

The reported results show compact models producing functionally correct circuits, generalizing to novel parts, and rediscovering canonical designs, supporting the combination of hierarchical verification and progressive training.
summary.tldr: GenCircuit-RL combines layered verification rewards and curriculum learning to train compact language models for genetic-circuit code generation.

title: GenCircuit-RL: Reinforcement Learning from Hierarchical Verification for Genetic Circuit Design

abstract: Accurately modeling the macroscopic dynamics of high-dimensional microscopic systems is of broad interest across the sciences. Many data-driven approaches learn a low-dimensional latent state through an autoencoder trained for pointwise input reconstruction. These methods typically assume a fixed ordering of microscopic degrees of freedom in the input. However, in many settings, such as particle systems, the microscopic state is inherently unordered. This motivates an autoencoder framework that learns permutation-invariant latent representations. To this end, we adopt a permutation-invariant encoder and design the decoder to reconstruct the mass distribution centered at the observed points rather than per-sample reconstruction. We then jointly learn the macroscopic dynamics of the observables together with the latent states. We demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method across a range of microscopic settings, including learning the energy dynamics in interacting particle systems, predicting mixing dynamics in Lennard–Jones fluids, and modeling the stretching dynamics from video data of polymers moving in an elongational force field.

paragraphs: Many physical systems contain numerous microscopic components, while the behavior of interest can be described by a smaller set of macroscopic quantities. Autoencoders can learn compact states for this purpose, but pointwise reconstruction commonly assumes that the microscopic inputs have a fixed ordering. That assumption is unsuitable for inherently unordered systems such as collections of particles.

The proposed framework uses an encoder whose representation is unchanged when the input ordering changes. Its decoder reconstructs a mass distribution centered on the observed points instead of reconstructing each sample in an assigned position. This aligns the reconstruction objective with the unordered nature of the microscopic state. The model jointly learns the latent states and the dynamics of macroscopic observables.

Demonstrations cover energy dynamics in interacting particle systems, mixing in Lennard–Jones fluids, and polymer stretching captured in video under an elongational force field. The authors report effectiveness and robustness across these settings. The approach shows how respecting the symmetry of the input can support learning compact dynamical descriptions across several forms of microscopic data.
summary.tldr: A permutation-invariant autoencoder learns compact physical dynamics by reconstructing distributions instead of ordered microscopic samples.

title: Learning Permutation-invariant Macroscopic Dynamics

abstract: A natural desideratum for generative models is self-correction–detecting and revising low-quality tokens at inference. While Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) have emerged as a promising approach for generative modeling in discrete spaces, their capacity for self-correction remains poorly understood. Prior attempts to incorporate self-correction into MDMs either require overhauling MDM architectures/training or rely on imprecise proxies for token quality, limiting their applicability. Motivated by this, we introduce PRISM–Plug-in Remasking for Inference-time Self-correction of Masked Diffusions–a lightweight, model-agnostic approach that applies to any pretrained MDM. Theoretically, PRISM defines a self-correction loss that provably learns per-token quality scores, without RL or a verifier. These quality scores are computed in the same forward pass with MDM and used to detect low-quality tokens. Empirically, PRISM advances MDM inference across domains and scales: Sudoku; unconditional text (170M); and code with LLaDA (8B). We open-source our codebase in https://github.com/SeunggeunKimkr/PRISM.

paragraphs: A generative model that can identify weak parts of its own output has an opportunity to revise them during inference. Masked diffusion models are promising for this kind of correction, but their ability to assess individual token quality is not well understood. Previous approaches have required substantial model changes or relied on imprecise quality indicators.

PRISM adds a lightweight remasking mechanism to pretrained masked diffusion models. The authors define a self-correction loss and prove that it learns per-token quality scores. Those scores are computed in the same forward pass as the diffusion model and identify low-quality tokens for correction. The approach does not require reinforcement learning or a separate verifier.

The empirical evaluation spans Sudoku, unconditional text generation with a 170-million-parameter model, and code generation with the 8-billion-parameter LLaDA model. The authors report improved inference across these domains and scales. The theoretical result concerns learning token-quality scores; the empirical results demonstrate the practical value of using those scores to guide revision across several types of discrete generation.
summary.tldr: PRISM learns token-quality scores that guide inference-time remasking and self-correction in pretrained masked diffusion models.

title: Fine-Tuning Masked Diffusion for Provable Self-Correction

abstract: Supervised classification has a theoretical optimum, Neural Collapse (NC), yet neither of its two dominant paradigms reaches it in practice. Cross entropy (CE) leaves radial degrees of freedom unconstrained and converges to a degenerate geometry, while supervised contrastive learning (SCL) drives features toward NC during pretraining but discards this structure in a post hoc linear probing phase. We show that both paradigms are different appearances of the same method that contrasts prototypes on the unit hypersphere, and that closing the gap requires fixing each at its point of failure. From the CE side, we propose NTCE and NONL, two normalized losses that import contrastive optimization’s missing ingredients into classifier learning: a large effective negative set and decoupled alignment and uniformity terms. From the SCL side, we prove that SCL’s objective already optimizes throughout training for a principled classifier whose weights are the class mean embeddings, making linear probing both redundant and harmful. Empirically, on four benchmarks including ImageNet-1K, NTCE and NONL surpass CE accuracy, closely approximate NC ($\geq 95%$), and match CE’s converged NC on 4/5 metrics in under $7.5%$ of its iterations, while SCL with fixed prototypes matches linear probing without the hours-long classifier training phase. The learned geometry yields $+5.5%$ mean relative improvement in transfer learning, up to $+8.7%$ under severe class imbalance, and improved robustness to corruptions on ImageNet-C. Our work recasts supervised learning as prototype learning on the hypersphere, with NC reached by design.

From the CE side, we propose NTCE and NONL, two normalized losses that import contrastive optimization’s missing ingredients into classifier learning: a large effective negative set and decoupled alignment and uniformity terms. From the SCL side, we prove that SCL’s objective already optimizes throughout training for a principled classifier whose weights are the class mean embeddings, making linear probing both redundant and harmful. Empirically, on four benchmarks including ImageNet-1K, NTCE and NONL surpass CE accuracy, closely approximate NC ($\geq 95%$), and match CE’s converged NC on 4/5 metrics in under $7.5%$ of its iterations, while SCL with fixed prototypes matches linear probing without the hours-long classifier training phase. The learned geometry yields $+5.5%$ mean relative improvement in transfer learning, up to $+8.7%$ under severe class imbalance, and improved robustness to corruptions on ImageNet-C. Our work recasts supervised learning as prototype learning on the hypersphere, with NC reached by design.

paragraphs: This paper studies the geometry of supervised classification through Neural Collapse, a theoretical optimum for class representations. It argues that cross entropy and supervised contrastive learning both contrast class prototypes on a unit hypersphere, but fail to preserve the desired geometry at different stages of learning.

For cross entropy, the authors introduce two normalized losses, NTCE and NONL. These incorporate a large effective negative set and separate alignment from uniformity. For supervised contrastive learning, they prove that the training objective already optimizes for a classifier whose weights are class mean embeddings. This provides a principled classifier directly from the learned representation, avoiding a later linear-probing stage.

On four benchmarks including ImageNet-1K, the new losses exceed cross-entropy accuracy and closely approximate Neural Collapse. They match cross entropy’s converged behavior on four of five collapse metrics in under 7.5% of its iterations. Fixed-prototype contrastive classification matches linear probing without its additional training phase. The learned geometry also improves transfer, performance under severe class imbalance, and corruption robustness in the reported evaluations, connecting prototype structure to practical classification benefits.
summary.tldr: The paper unifies classification as spherical prototype learning and introduces normalized losses and direct prototype classifiers that improve geometry and empirical performance.

title: Neural Collapse by Design: Learning Class Prototypes on the Hypersphere

abstract: Semi-supervised learning has become a dominant paradigm for reducing annotation costs. However, we argue that the current progress is clouded by a twofold overconfidence problem. Algorithmically, mainstream pseudo-labeling frameworks often conflate prediction confidence with uncertainty, leading to severe confirmation bias. Strategically, since multiple benchmark datasets lack dedicated validation sets, some studies use the test set for validation as well, leading to inflated performance estimates. Subsequent methods, compelled to employ the same strategy to surpass reported SOTA, trigger an arms race of overfitting. This raises concerns that the impressive numerical gains in the community may reflect overfitting rather than genuine progress. Thus, we propose a tri-space calibrated segmentation framework founded on a principled dual-axis reliability assessment engine. It explicitly decouples confidence from uncertainty and uses this signal to detect and correct confirmation bias across feature, probability, and image spaces in a collaborative manner. Across three benchmark datasets, TCSeg consistently delivers strong performance under existing evaluation protocols. More importantly, we advocate that the community report final-checkpoint results under multiple-run protocols, thereby establishing more rigorous benchmarks with a more realistic perspective. Code will be available: github.com/DirkLiii/TCSeg.

paragraphs: The paper identifies two forms of overconfidence in semi-supervised 3D medical image segmentation. First, methods that train on their own predicted labels can mistake confident predictions for reliable ones, reinforcing errors. Second, using test data to choose models can inflate reported performance. The authors argue that repeating this evaluation practice can encourage an escalating cycle of benchmark overfitting.

Their proposed framework, TCSeg, treats confidence and uncertainty as separate dimensions of reliability. It uses this assessment to detect and correct confirmation bias collaboratively across feature representations, predicted probabilities, and image space. The central idea is that a prediction’s apparent certainty should not be the sole basis for deciding how much to trust it during training.

Across three benchmark datasets, TCSeg delivers strong performance under existing evaluation protocols. The authors pair this algorithmic result with a methodological recommendation: report final-checkpoint results across multiple runs. This distinction matters because better scores under current protocols do not, by themselves, resolve concerns about test-set reuse. The paper calls for both better reliability assessment and more rigorous reporting.
summary.tldr: TCSeg separates confidence from uncertainty to reduce pseudo-labeling bias, while the paper calls for evaluation practices less vulnerable to test-set overfitting.

title: Are We Overconfident in Models and Results for Semi-Supervised 3D Medical Image Segmentation?

abstract: Disaggregated serving alleviates memory bottlenecks in Large Language Model (LLM) inference but creates a severe communication bottleneck: transmitting high-dimensional Key-Value (KV) caches often dominates time-to-first-token (TTFT). Moreover, reusing caches across heterogeneous models (e.g., base and fine-tuned variants) causes semantic misalignment that accumulates over layers, degrading generation quality. We propose Semantic Cache Distillation (SCD), a loss-constrained framework that replaces raw KV transmission with compact semantic codes. SCD addresses these challenges via two mechanisms: (1) Reuse, which reconstructs most layers from low-rank subspaces to minimize transfer cost, and (2) Patch, which predicts normalized inputs at sparse transition layers to truncate error propagation. Empirically, SCD delivers up to 2.65 $\times$ TTFT speedup over the oracle consumer prefill and dominates quantization and selective recomputation baselines on the quality–latency Pareto frontier in bandwidth-constrained regimes, while keeping generation quality within 5% F1 of the oracle.

paragraphs: Splitting language-model serving across components can ease memory pressure while making communication the bottleneck. Transferring large key–value caches can dominate the wait for the first output token. Reusing caches between different model variants adds another problem: semantic mismatches can accumulate through successive layers and degrade generation.

Semantic Cache Distillation replaces raw cache transfer with compact semantic codes under a loss constraint. Its Reuse mechanism reconstructs most layers from low-rank subspaces, reducing communication. Its Patch mechanism predicts normalized inputs at a sparse set of transition layers, interrupting error propagation. The two mechanisms jointly address transfer size and accumulated mismatch.

In bandwidth-constrained experiments, SCD achieves up to a 2.65-fold improvement in time to first token relative to oracle consumer prefill, while keeping generation quality within 5% F1 of the oracle. It also dominates quantization and selective recomputation baselines on the reported quality–latency frontier. These results support selective reconstruction and correction as a way to reduce state-transfer costs while controlling the quality loss caused by reuse.
summary.tldr: SCD transfers compact semantic codes and selectively patches reconstructed caches to improve latency while controlling generation-quality loss.

title: Semantic Cache Distillation: Efficient State Transfer via Reuse and Selective Patching

abstract: The performance of pre-trained masked diffusion models is often constrained by their sampling procedure, which makes decisions irreversible and struggles in low-step generation regimes. We introduce a novel sampling algorithm that works with pre-trained models and, after a lightweight fine-tuning of a single layer, significantly improves sample quality and efficiency. Our method reformulates the generation process using a star-shaped paradigm, which inherently allows for error correction. To make this process effective, we augment it with a learnable remasking module that intelligently identifies and revises likely errors. This approach yields a substantial quality boost, particularly when using a small number of sampling steps. We extensively ablate key components of our approach and show its usability in different scenarios. In experiments on text, and code generation, our sampling algorithm outperforms or matches existing methods. Code is available at https://github.com/EgorShibaev/G-Star.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion models can be limited by sampling procedures that make earlier decisions irreversible. This becomes especially troublesome when generation must finish in only a few steps. The paper introduces a sampling method that gives pretrained models a way to revisit likely mistakes and improve the evolving output.

The approach reorganizes generation into a star-shaped process that permits error correction. A learned remasking module identifies decisions that may be wrong and marks them for revision. Adapting the pretrained model requires lightweight fine-tuning of a single layer. The central change therefore concerns how generation proceeds and how opportunities for correction are selected.

Experiments on text and code generation show that the method matches or outperforms existing approaches. The authors report particularly substantial quality gains when using few sampling steps, alongside improvements in efficiency. Component ablations and tests in different scenarios examine the contribution and usability of the design. The results indicate that selective revision can make limited-step masked diffusion generation more effective.
summary.tldr: A star-shaped sampling process and learned remasking let masked diffusion models correct mistakes, especially when generation uses few steps.

title: Guided Star-Shaped Masked Diffusion

abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP have demonstrated remarkable zero-shot generalization, yet remain highly vulnerable to adversarial examples (AEs). While test-time defenses are promising, existing methods fail to provide sufficient robustness against strong attacks and are often hampered by high inference latency and task-specific applicability. To address these limitations, we start by investigating the intrinsic properties of AEs, which reveals that AEs exhibit severe feature inconsistency under progressive frequency attenuation. We further attribute this to the model’s inherent spectral bias. Leveraging this insight, we propose an efficient test-time defense named Contrastive Spectral Rectification (CSR). CSR optimizes a rectification perturbation to realign the input with the natural manifold under a spectral-guided contrastive objective, which is applied input-adaptively. Extensive experiments across 16 classification benchmarks demonstrate that CSR outperforms the SOTA by an average of 18.1% against strong APGD with modest inference overhead. Furthermore, CSR exhibits broad applicability across diverse visual tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/Summu77/CSR.

paragraphs: CLIP can recognize categories without task-specific training, yet adversarial changes to an image can undermine its predictions. This paper studies what happens to adversarial examples as image frequencies are progressively attenuated. It finds pronounced inconsistency in their features and attributes this behavior to the model’s inherent spectral bias.

Contrastive Spectral Rectification uses that observation to defend the model at inference time. For each input, it optimizes a corrective perturbation under a contrastive objective guided by frequency information. The aim is to bring the input back toward the structure of natural images, with the correction adapted to the particular image being processed.

Across 16 classification benchmarks, CSR exceeds the compared state of the art by a reported average of 18.1% against the strong APGD attack, while adding modest inference overhead. The authors also report applicability across different visual tasks. These results suggest that frequency-dependent feature behavior provides a useful defense signal, supporting an input-adaptive correction procedure that balances measured robustness with inference cost.
summary.tldr: CSR uses frequency-guided, input-adaptive corrections to improve CLIP’s adversarial robustness at test time with modest overhead.

title: Contrastive Spectral Rectification: Test-Time Defense towards Zero-shot Adversarial Robustness of CLIP

abstract: While recent autoregressive models have achieved text-to-image generation performance comparable to diffusion models, they significantly struggle with fine-grained semantic alignment. To rigorously evaluate this limitation, we introduce DeltaBench, a benchmark featuring paired prompts with subtle fine-grained differences, which reveals that existing models fail to achieve precise control over visual tokens. To bridge this gap, we propose FocusDiff, a comprehensive framework that enhances alignment by learning from subtle differences in similar text-image pairs. Specifically, we construct FocusDiff-Data, a large-scale dataset of paired samples derived from image editing tasks to capture localized semantic shifts. Furthermore, we introduce Pair-GRPO, an improved reinforcement learning algorithm that extends GRPO to paired samples. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms most prior prominent methods on both DeltaBench and existing benchmarks.

paragraphs: A text-to-image model can produce convincing pictures while still failing to reflect a small but meaningful change in a prompt. This paper investigates that gap in autoregressive image generators, whose overall generation performance has approached diffusion models but whose fine-grained semantic control remains weaker. The focus is whether subtle textual distinctions reliably produce corresponding visual distinctions.

The authors introduce DeltaBench, which evaluates pairs of prompts that differ in small semantic details. They also build FocusDiff-Data from image-editing tasks, creating paired examples that capture localized changes. These paired constructions put the difference between closely related requests at the center of both evaluation and learning.

Their FocusDiff framework includes Pair-GRPO, a reinforcement-learning algorithm that extends GRPO to work with paired samples. The approach trains on subtle differences between similar text-image pairs to improve alignment. Experiments report better performance than most prominent prior methods on DeltaBench and existing benchmarks. The contribution connects a targeted diagnostic, suitable paired training data, and a paired learning objective around the same fine-grained control problem.
summary.tldr: FocusDiff uses paired examples and reinforcement learning to improve image generators' responses to subtle prompt differences.

title: Benchmarking and Improving Fine-Grained Text-to-Image Alignment via Paired Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as planners for cooperative embodied agents, but multi-agent settings amplify inconsistency under partial observability and make explicit communication costly or even unavailable. Many existing approaches rely on online message passing; when communication is removed, agents often fall back to independent local planning that suffers from miscoordination. We introduce Contextual Tacit Communication, a gradient-free protocol that aligns decentralized decisions with a joint LLM value score without explicit message actions. Our method measures context-conditioned value rectifications via residual banding to pinpoint miscoordination actions and amortizes the resulting coordination signals into a retrieval-augmented Tacit Rule Memory that provides prompt-level cooperation rules at execution time. Experiments on VIKI, C-WAH, and TDW-MAT show that our approach improves cooperation performance over baselines while reducing runtime overhead compared with communication-based methods.

paragraphs: Cooperating embodied agents often see only part of their environment. When each uses a language model to plan locally, their choices can conflict. Explicit messages can help coordinate them, but communication may be expensive or unavailable. This paper studies how agents can cooperate without taking explicit messaging actions.

Contextual Tacit Communication uses a joint language-model value score to align decentralized choices. Its gradient-free procedure measures context-dependent value corrections through residual banding, identifying actions associated with miscoordination. It then stores the resulting coordination signals in a retrieval-augmented Tacit Rule Memory.

At execution time, retrieved rules enter the agents’ prompts and guide cooperation. This reuses coordination knowledge without requiring online message exchange for each decision. Experiments on VIKI, C-WAH, and TDW-MAT show improved cooperation over the evaluated baselines and lower runtime overhead than communication-based methods. The findings support converting joint coordination assessments into reusable contextual rules that individual agents can consult when acting under partial observability.
summary.tldr: Contextual Tacit Communication turns joint coordination signals into retrieved prompt rules for cooperation without explicit message actions.

title: Great Minds Think Alike: Contextual Tacit Communication for Decentralized LLM-Agent Cooperation

abstract: We study episodic constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) with linear function approximation, where the goal is to achieve strong regret and constraint violation guarantees without allowing error cancellations. Unlike the existing work, which focuses on either tabular CMDP or model-based reinforcement learning methods. We propose a model-free policy APMPO that achieves near-optimal $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{K})$ strong regret and strong constraint violation with Slater’s condition (or strict feasibility assumption), where $K$ is the total number of episodes. It matches the best-known rates without requiring any prior knowledge of the feasibility gap reported in prior model-based work for tabular CMDPs. Besides, APMPO achieves $\widetilde{O}(K^{\frac{3}{4}})$ strong regret and $\widetilde{O}(K^\frac{3}{4})$ strong constraint violation without Slater’s condition. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first sublinear result of CMDP w.r.t. the strong metrics without Slater’s condition. APMPO achieves these results by a novel and adaptive design of a violation-aware penalty and learning rates to balance the strong regret and constraint violation, which is quite different from the (regularized) primal-dual methods imposing constraints via dual penalty in the literature. The experiments show APMPO significantly outperforms the strong baselines, which justify our design and theoretical performance.

paragraphs: Constrained reinforcement learning must improve reward while respecting constraints. This paper studies episodic problems with linear function approximation using strong measures of regret and constraint violation, which prevent favorable errors from canceling unfavorable ones. Its model-free method, APMPO, aims to control both measures without learning a full environment model.

Under Slater’s condition, meaning strict feasibility, APMPO achieves near-optimal bounds that grow as the square root of the number of episodes, up to logarithmic factors. It does not require prior knowledge of the feasibility gap. Without strict feasibility, both bounds grow as K to the three-quarter power, again up to logarithmic factors. These weaker bounds remain sublinear, so the corresponding per-episode quantities decline as training grows.

The method uses an adaptive violation-aware penalty and adaptive learning rates to balance reward shortfall against constraint violations. This differs from imposing constraints through the dual penalties used in primal-dual approaches. Experiments report substantial improvements over strong baselines. The theoretical contribution is especially notable for retaining sublinear guarantees under the strong metrics even when the strict-feasibility assumption is removed.
summary.tldr: APMPO provides sublinear strong regret and constraint-violation guarantees, with near-optimal rates under strict feasibility and weaker rates without it.

title: Towards Achieving Optimal Strong Regret and Constraint Violation via Computationally Efficient Model-free RL

abstract: Cross-domain offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to learn a policy in the target domain with a limited target domain dataset and a source domain dataset that exhibits a dynamics shift. Training directly on the original source dataset typically leads to performance collapse. Recent studies perform data filtering from the perspective of dynamics alignment or value alignment to enable efficient policy transfer. However, these studies are typically validated on single-domain or single-behavior-policy source datasets. In this work, we explore a more general heterogeneous cross-domain offline RL setting, where the source datasets may be collected from multiple source domains by diverse behavior policies. We first uncover a critical yet overlooked issue in this setting: value misassignment. Empirically and theoretically, we demonstrate that value misassignment can undermine value alignment, mislead data filtering toward selecting suboptimal samples, and loosen the suboptimality gap, thereby degrading the agent’s performance. To address this issue, we propose V2A, which integrates dynamics alignment, value alignment, and value assignment. V2A first employs temporally-consistent modality representation learning to extract dynamics modalities from the source dataset, followed by modality-aware advantage learning to rectify value alignment. Finally, it adopts a data filtering paradigm to selectively share source data for policy learning. Empirical results show that V2A significantly outperforms strong baseline methods under general heterogeneous cross-domain offline RL settings.
