paragraphs: Cross-domain offline reinforcement learning uses source experience to supplement limited target-domain data. Differences in environment dynamics can make direct transfer harmful. The paper considers a broader setting in which source data comes from several domains and behavior policies, making it harder to decide which experience is useful for the target.

The authors identify value misassignment as a critical problem in this heterogeneous setting. Their empirical and theoretical analysis shows that assigning value incorrectly can undermine value alignment, make filtering favor suboptimal samples, and weaken the suboptimality bound. A filtering method can therefore make poor choices even when it is explicitly trying to retain high-value experience.

V2A combines dynamics alignment, value alignment, and value assignment. It learns temporally consistent representations to distinguish dynamics modalities, uses modality-aware advantage learning to correct value alignment, and then filters source data for policy learning. Experiments report substantial gains over strong baselines in heterogeneous cross-domain settings. The contribution makes the dynamics context of a value estimate part of the transfer decision, helping determine which source experience should actually be shared.
summary.tldr: V2A improves heterogeneous offline transfer by correcting value assignment before filtering source experience for target-domain learning.

title: Unifying Value Alignment and Assignment in Cross-Domain Offline Reinforcement Learning with Heterogeneous Datasets

abstract: Geographic data is fundamentally local. Disease outbreaks cluster in population centers, ecological patterns emerge along coastlines, and economic activity concentrates within country borders. Machine learning models that encode geographic location, however, distribute representational capacity uniformly across the globe, struggling at the fine-grained resolutions localized applications require. We propose a geographic location encoder built from spherical Slepian functions that concentrates representational capacity inside a region-of-interest and scales to high resolutions without extensive computational demands. For settings requiring global context, we present a hybrid Slepian-Spherical Harmonic encoder that efficiently bridges the tradeoff between local-global performance, while retaining desirable properties such as pole-safety and spherical-surface-distance preservation. Across five tasks spanning classification, regression, and image-augmented prediction, Slepian encodings outperform baselines and retain performance advantages across a wide variety of neural network architectures.

paragraphs: Many geographic prediction tasks care about fine detail within a particular region. An encoder that spreads its representational capacity uniformly around the planet may allocate too little detail to that area. This paper proposes a location representation built from spherical Slepian functions, concentrating capacity inside a chosen region of interest.

The approach is designed to support high spatial resolution without extensive computational demands. For applications that also need information outside the target region, the authors introduce a hybrid encoder combining Slepian functions with spherical harmonics. This provides a way to balance local detail and global context while retaining pole-safety and preservation of distances along the spherical surface.

The evaluation spans five tasks covering classification, regression, and prediction augmented with images. Slepian encodings outperform the tested baselines, and their advantages persist across a broad range of neural network architectures. The findings indicate that the geographic representation itself can improve performance: allocating capacity where the task needs spatial detail can help multiple kinds of downstream models.
summary.tldr: Slepian-based location encoders concentrate geographic detail in a target region and outperform tested alternatives across five prediction tasks.

title: Localized, High-resolution Geographic Representations with Slepian Functions

abstract: Understanding memorization in generative models remains challenging, with implications for copyright and privacy. Beyond verbatim reproduction, models can encode subtler traces of their training data that never surface in their outputs yet remain exploitable. We refer to these measurable asymmetries as the membership signal, and we study this regime for Flow Matching, which are increasingly used in deployed generative systems. We analyze the linear interpolation path $X_\lambda = (1-\lambda)X_0 + \lambda X_1$ that defines standard Flow Matching training. We show that a gap exists between the reconstruction of train and test data that follows a bell-shaped curve over $\lambda$, which accumulates during training, while the validation metrics remain stable. The signal has a maximum whose location we derive in closed form under Gaussian assumptions. We validate these predictions on both audio and images and show that the bell-shaped structure is universal, while the peak prediction holds when our assumptions are satisfied. As a proof of concept, we exploit this specific $\lambda$-resolved structure to perform a Membership Inference Attack, distinguishing members of the training set from non-members.

paragraphs: A generative model can reveal whether an example was in its training data without reproducing that example in its outputs. This paper studies such membership signals in flow matching. It examines reconstruction behavior along the linear interpolation path used in training, rather than looking only at final generated samples.

The authors find that the reconstruction gap between training and test examples traces a bell-shaped curve along this path. The gap accumulates during training even while validation metrics remain stable. A proof-of-concept membership-inference attack exploits this location-dependent signal to distinguish training examples from nonmembers. The findings show how apparently stable validation behavior can coexist with increasing traces of training membership, and why examining the interpolation path reveals information that output reproduction alone would miss.
summary.tldr: Flow-matching reconstruction errors expose a bell-shaped membership signal along the training interpolation path that can support membership-inference attacks.

title: Where Flow Matching Leaks: Characterising the Membership Signals Along the Interpolation Path

abstract: Despite their capabilities, large foundation models (LFMs) remain susceptible to adversarial manipulation. Current defenses predominantly rely on the “locality hypothesis", suppressing isolated neurons or features. However, harmful semantics act as distributed, cross-layer circuits, rendering such localized interventions brittle and detrimental to utility. To bridge this gap, we propose TraceRouter, a path-level framework that traces and disconnects the causal propagation circuits of illicit semantics. TraceRouter operates in three stages: (1) it pinpoints a sensitive onset layer by analyzing attention divergence; (2) it leverages sparse autoencoders (SAEs) and differential activation analysis to disentangle and isolate malicious features; and (3) it maps these features to downstream causal pathways via feature influence scores (FIS) derived from zero-out interventions. By selectively suppressing these causal chains, TraceRouter physically severs the flow of harmful information while leaving orthogonal computation routes intact. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TraceRouter significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving a superior trade-off between adversarial robustness and general utility. Our code will be publicly released. WARNING: This paper contains unsafe model responses.

summary.tldr: TraceRouter traces and suppresses cross-layer pathways carrying harmful information, improving the reported balance between robustness and utility.

title: TraceRouter: Robust Safety for Large Foundation Models via Path-Level Intervention

abstract: Despite their practical success, it remains unclear why Mixture of Experts (MoE) models can outperform dense networks beyond sheer parameter scaling. We study an iso-parameter regime where inputs exhibit latent modular structure but are corrupted by feature noise, a proxy for noisy internal activations. We show that sparse expert activation acts as a noise filter: compared to a dense estimator, MoEs achieve lower generalization error under feature noise, improved robustness to perturbations, and faster convergence speed. Empirical results on synthetic data and real-world language tasks corroborate the theoretical insights, demonstrating consistent robustness and efficiency gains from sparse modular computation.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether mixtures of experts can outperform dense networks for reasons beyond having more parameters. It studies models with equal parameter counts in a setting where inputs have an underlying modular structure but their features are corrupted by noise. The feature noise serves as a stand-in for noisy internal activations.

The analysis identifies sparse expert activation as a noise-filtering mechanism. Under the studied setting, activating a limited selection of experts yields lower generalization error than a dense estimator, stronger resistance to perturbations, and faster convergence. The explanation connects the benefit to selective modular computation, while the equal-parameter comparison separates it from a simple increase in model size.

Experiments on synthetic data and real-world language tasks corroborate these theoretical findings, reporting consistent gains in robustness and efficiency. The paper therefore offers a structural explanation for expert-model advantages under feature noise. Its theoretical setting includes latent modularity in the inputs, which is central to understanding the scope of the proposed explanation.
summary.tldr: With equal parameter counts and latent modular inputs, sparse expert activation filters feature noise and improves robustness and convergence.

title: Robustness of Mixtures of Experts to Feature Noise

abstract: While Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) offer a flexible, arbitrary-order alternative to the autoregressive paradigm, their non-causal nature precludes standard KV caching, forcing costly hidden state recomputation at every decoding step. Existing caching approaches reduce this cost by selective hidden state updates; however, they are still limited by (i) computationally costly token-wise update identification heuristics and (ii) rigid, uniform budget allocation that fails to account for heterogeneous hidden- tate dynamics. To address these challenges, we present SPA-Cache that jointly optimizes update identification and budget allocation. First, we derive a low-dimensional singular proxy that enables the identification of update-critical tokens in a low-dimensional subspace, substantially reducing the overhead of update identification. Second, motivated by the layer-wise heterogeneity in hidden state dynamics, we introduce an adaptive strategy that allocates fewer updates to stable layers without degrading generation quality. Together, these contributions significantly improve the efficiency of DLMs, yielding up to an $8\times$ throughput improvement over vanilla models decoding and a $2$-$4\times$ speedup over existing caching baselines.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can generate in arbitrary order, but their non-causal operation prevents standard key-value caching. Recomputing hidden states at each decoding step is expensive. Existing caching methods selectively update states, yet deciding which tokens need updates can itself be costly, and uniform update budgets ignore differences between layers.

SPA-Cache tackles both decisions together. A low-dimensional singular proxy identifies tokens whose hidden states most need updating, reducing the cost of that selection process. An adaptive allocation strategy then gives fewer updates to stable layers. This uses the observed variation in hidden-state dynamics to direct computation toward parts of the model that need it more.

The paper reports up to an eightfold throughput improvement over vanilla decoding and speedups of two to four times over existing caching baselines. Its adaptive layer allocation is described as preserving generation quality. The contribution shows that effective caching depends on both choosing updates cheaply and allocating them according to how differently the model’s layers evolve.
summary.tldr: SPA-Cache accelerates diffusion language models with cheap token-update selection and adaptive update budgets across layers.

title: Singular Proxies for Adaptive Caching in Diffusion Language Models

abstract: Listwise reranking is a critical yet costly component in vision-centric retrieval and multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (M-RAG) over long documents. Although recent VLM-based rerankers achieve strong accuracy, they are often impractical due to long visual-token inputs and autoregressive decoding, resulting in high latency. We propose ZipRerank, a very efficient listwise multimodal reranker that directly addresses both bottlenecks: it shortens the input via query-image early interaction and eliminates multi-step generation by scoring all candidates in a single forward pass. ZipRerank is trained with a two-stage recipe: listwise pretraining on large-scale text reranking data rendered as images, followed by multimodal finetuning with VLM-teacher supervision and a soft-ranking objective to handle noisy rankings. Extensive experiments on the MMDocIR benchmark demonstrate that ZipRerank matches or surpasses state-of-the-art multimodal rerankers while reducing LLM inference latency by up to an order of magnitude, making it well-suited for latency-sensitive real-world systems. Source code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ZipRerank.

Vision-language rerankers can be accurate but slow because document images create long visual-token inputs and ranking through autoregressive generation takes multiple decoding steps. The paper addresses both sources of latency.

The model uses early interaction between the query and image to shorten its input. It then scores all candidates in one forward pass, removing the need for multi-step generation. On MMDocIR, ZipRerank matches or surpasses state-of-the-art multimodal rerankers while reducing language-model inference latency by up to an order of magnitude. The results support combining shorter inputs and direct candidate scoring to retain ranking quality while making this retrieval component more practical for latency-sensitive systems.
summary.tldr: ZipRerank shortens visual inputs and scores all candidates in one pass, cutting reranking inference latency by up to an order of magnitude.

title: Very Efficient Listwise Multimodal Reranking for Long Documents

abstract: Compositional generalization, the ability to recognize familiar parts in novel contexts, is a defining property of intelligent systems, yet modern models, despite massive training sets, see only a tiny fraction of the combinatorial input space. We ask what structure representations must have to support generalization to unseen combinations. We formalize three desiderata (divisibility, transferability, stability) and show they impose necessary geometric constraints under standard training: representations must decompose linearly into per-concept components, orthogonal across concepts. This grounds the Linear Representation Hypothesis as a necessary consequence of compositional generalization, and yields dimension bounds linking the number of composable concepts to embedding geometry. Empirically, across CLIP, SigLIP, and DINO, we find partial linear factorization with low-rank near-orthogonal per-concept factors, and the degree of this structure correlates with compositional generalization on unseen combinations. As models continue to scale, these conditions predict the geometry they may converge to. Code: https://github.com/oshapio/necessary-compositionality

paragraphs: Recognizing familiar concepts in unfamiliar combinations requires more than remembering previously seen inputs. This paper asks what geometry an embedding must have to support that capability. It formalizes three requirements—divisibility, transferability, and stability—and studies the constraints they impose on representations under standard training.

The theoretical result is that satisfying these requirements necessitates a linear decomposition into components for individual concepts, with different concepts represented orthogonally. In geometric terms, concept contributions must combine additively while occupying perpendicular directions. This provides a conditional foundation for the Linear Representation Hypothesis and yields bounds connecting embedding dimension with the number of concepts that can be composed.

Experiments on CLIP, SigLIP, and DINO find partial versions of this structure: concept factors are low-rank and nearly orthogonal. Stronger evidence of this geometry correlates with better generalization to unseen combinations. The empirical result supports the theoretical picture without establishing that these models fully satisfy its requirements. Together, the findings identify representation structure associated with compositional capability and describe geometry that larger models may approach as they scale.
summary.tldr: Under three formal requirements and standard training, compositional generalization requires linear concept components that are orthogonal across concepts.

title: Compositional Generalization Requires Linear, Orthogonal Representations in Vision Embedding Models

abstract: Dynamic graph learning, which focuses on modeling the merging, vanishing, and reconnection of nodes and edges, is crucial for real-world applications. In dynamic graphs, node neighborhoods often exhibit diverse and time-evolving topologies, including hierarchical, grid-like, and cyclic patterns. Existing methods typically embed graphs into a single curvature space, which limits the quality of node representations when the embedding geometry is not aligned well with the local graph topology. In this paper, we propose DyGMoCE, a Dynamic Graph Transformer with a Mixture of Curvature-aware Experts, which efficiently embeds each node at every timestamp into an adaptive curvature space. Specifically, DyGMoCE incorporates a mixture-of-experts framework to both the attention and feed-forward modules, where each expert operates on a Riemannian manifold with a distinct curvature. Then, motivated by the geometric continuity across the experts, we introduce a routing mechanism with a ranking constraint. To improve efficiency, we design a fast Riemannian attention module for DyGMoCE, achieving an average speedup of 27.5% and memory reduction of 52.6%. Notably, the fast Riemannian attention module is broadly applicable to Transformer models with sequence inputs. Extensive experimental results show that DyGMoCE significantly outperforms other state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: A changing graph can contain hierarchical, grid-like, and cyclic neighborhoods at the same time. Their shapes can also change as nodes and connections appear or disappear. DyGMoCE addresses the mismatch that arises when all these structures must be represented in a space with one fixed curvature.

The model adds curvature-aware experts to both the attention and feed-forward parts of a dynamic graph Transformer. summary.tldr: DyGMoCE adapts representation curvature to changing graph neighborhoods and introduces faster, more memory-efficient Riemannian attention.

title: Fast Mixture of Curvature-Aware Experts for Diverse and Dynamic Graph Topologies

abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by verifying candidate tokens from a draft model against a larger target model. Recent "judge” decoding boosts this process by relaxing verification criteria by accepting draft tokens that may exhibit minor discrepancies from target model output, but existing methods are restricted by their reliance on human annotations or tasks with verifiable ground truths, limiting generalizability across diverse NLP tasks. We propose SelfJudge, which trains judge verifiers via self-supervision of the target model. Our method measures semantic preservation by assessing whether token-substituted responses preserve the meaning of original responses, enabling automatic verifier training across diverse NLP tasks. Our experiments show SelfJudge achieves superior inference-accuracy trade-offs than judge decoding baselines, offering a broadly applicable solution for faster LLM inference.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding speeds up language-model generation by having a draft model propose tokens for a larger target model to verify. Judge decoding relaxes this verification, allowing minor differences from the target's output. However, existing judge-training methods depend on human annotations or tasks with verifiable answers, restricting where they can be applied.

SelfJudge trains these verifiers through self-supervision from the target model. It evaluates whether responses with substituted tokens preserve the meaning of the original responses. This semantic-preservation signal supplies automatic training information for the judge, allowing verifier training across diverse natural-language tasks without relying on the same task-specific sources of supervision.

Experiments report better inference–accuracy trade-offs than judge-decoding baselines. The significance is that a judge can learn which token differences are acceptable from signals supplied by the target model itself. The resulting approach broadens the applicability of relaxed verification while retaining accuracy as part of the evaluation, rather than treating generation speed as the only objective.
summary.tldr: SelfJudge trains speculative-decoding verifiers from the target model's own semantic-preservation signals, improving inference–accuracy trade-offs.

title: SelfJudge: Faster Speculative Decoding via Self-Supervised Judge Verification

abstract: How can we use AI to discover a new state of the art for a scientific problem? Prior work in test-time scaling, such as AlphaEvolve, performs search by prompting a frozen LLM. We perform reinforcement learning at test time, so the LLM can continue to train, but now with experience specific to the test problem. This form of continual learning is quite special, because its goal is to produce one great solution rather than many good ones on average, and to solve this very problem rather than generalize to other problems. Therefore, our learning objective and search subroutine are designed to prioritize the most promising solutions. We call this method Test-Time Training to Discover (TTT-Discover). Following prior work, we focus on problems with continuous rewards. We report results for every problem we attempted, across mathematics, GPU kernel engineering, algorithm design, and biology. TTT-Discover sets the new state of the art in almost all of them: (i) Erdős’ minimum overlap problem and an autocorrelation inequality; (ii) a GPUMode kernel competition (up to 2$\times$ faster than prior art); (iii) past AtCoder algorithm competitions; and (iv) denoising problem in single-cell analysis. Our solutions are reviewed by experts or the organizers. All our results are achieved with an open model, OpenAI gpt-oss-120b, and can be reproduced with our publicly available code, in contrast to previous best results that required closed frontier models. Our test-time training runs are performed using Tinker, an API by Thinking Machines, with a cost of only a few hundred dollars per problem.

title: Learning to Discover at Test Time

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning has become a key technique for enhancing large language models (LLMs) on reasoning-intensive tasks, motivating its extension to vision language models (VLMs). While RL-tuned VLMs improve on visual reasoning benchmarks, they remain vulnerable to weak visual grounding, hallucinations, and over-reliance on textual cues. We show that simple, controlled textual perturbations—misleading captions or incorrect chain-of-thought (CoT) traces—cause substantial drops in robustness, and that these effects are more pronounced when CoT consistency is taken into account across open-source multimodal reasoning models. In contrast, closed models exhibit similar failure modes but maintain markedly greater robustness and reasoning consistency, suggesting that the gap reflects a shortcoming in current RL fine-tuning methods rather than an inherent limitation of the task. To better understand these vulnerabilities, we further analyze RL fine-tuning dynamics and uncover an accuracy–faithfulness trade-off: fine-tuning raises benchmark accuracy, but can simultaneously erode the reliability of the accompanying CoT and its robustness to contextual shifts. Although adversarial augmentation improves robustness, it does not by itself prevent faithfulness drift. Incorporating a faithfulness-aware reward can restore alignment between answers and reasoning, but when paired with augmentation, training risks collapsing onto shortcut strategies. Together, these findings highlight the limitations of accuracy-only evaluations and motivate training and assessment protocols that jointly emphasize correctness, robustness, and consistency in visually grounded reasoning.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning fine-tuning can improve visual reasoning scores while leaving models susceptible to misleading text. This paper tests controlled perturbations such as incorrect captions and erroneous reasoning traces. These cause substantial robustness drops, with weaknesses becoming more pronounced when evaluation also considers consistency of the model's chain of thought.

Open-source multimodal reasoning models show particularly strong vulnerabilities. summary.tldr: RL fine-tuning can improve visual reasoning accuracy while weakening reasoning faithfulness and robustness to misleading textual context.

title: On Robustness and Chain-of-Thought Consistency of RL-Finetuned VLMs

abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) often exhibit severe instability during Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) training, limiting the effectiveness of reinforcement learning for improving reasoning capabilities. In dLLMs, the importance ratios used by GRPO are derived from finite-sample estimates rather than exact likelihoods, making them inherently noisy. In this paper, we show that GRPO is highly sensitive to this noise, which drives training instability. Through theoretical analysis and empirical evidence, we identify a self-reinforcing instability loop in which noisy importance ratios induce gradient spikes and policy drift, further amplifying future importance ratio estimation variance. To address this issue, we propose StableDRL, a novel reinforcement learning framework for dLLMs. StableDRL stabilizes training via (i) unconditional clipping to suppress outlier-induced gradient spikes, and (ii) self-normalization to constrain gradients within the convex hull of per-sample updates. We further extend StableDRL to block-wise diffusion models via a staircase attention mechanism. StableDRL is the first method that enables stable, full-parameter reinforcement learning for dLLMs. It achieves the state-of-the-art performance, outperforming prior best full-attention baselines by 6% on MATH500 and block-diffusion baselines by 25.6% on AIME.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can become severely unstable when trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization. This paper traces the problem to importance ratios computed from finite-sample likelihood estimates. Their noise can trigger large gradient spikes and policy drift, which then increase the variance of later ratio estimates, creating a self-reinforcing instability loop.

StableDRL addresses that loop through two mechanisms. Unconditional clipping suppresses spikes caused by outliers, while self-normalization constrains the combined gradient to the convex hull of individual sample updates. These comparisons connect the stability intervention to stronger reasoning performance in the evaluated settings, rather than treating stable optimization as an isolated outcome.
summary.tldr: StableDRL controls noisy importance-ratio updates to stabilize reinforcement learning and improve evaluated diffusion-language-model reasoning performance.

In this paper, we present anestimator of replicability of an experiment that is efficient. paragraphs: A classifier comparison can produce a different conclusion when the same data is randomized differently. This paper studies replicability in that specific sense: the probability that an experimental outcome repeats under another randomization. It treats the stability of the experimental conclusion as something that can be estimated and compared across evaluation procedures.

The authors present an unbiased estimator with the lowest variance among estimators formed as linear combinations of experimental outcomes on a given dataset. That qualification defines the scope of the optimality result. The estimator provides a principled tool for studying how reliably an experiment’s conclusion survives changes in data randomization.

Empirical comparisons show that both sampling schemes and hypothesis tests affect replicability. The results suggest avoiding sign tests because of low replicability; rank-sum tests perform better. Among the studied combinations, sorted-runs sampling with a t-test offers the most desirable balance of Type I error, Type II error, and replicability. These findings concern the evaluation procedure as well as the classifiers being evaluated.
summary.tldr: The paper estimates how reliably classifier experiments repeat and shows that sampling and hypothesis-test choices affect that reliability.

title: Estimating replicability of classifier learning experiments

abstract: Many learning applications are characterized by high dimensions. Usually not all of these dimensions are relevant and some are redundant. There are two main approaches to reduce dimensionality: feature selection and feature transformation. When one wishes to keep the original meaning of the features, feature selection is desired. Feature selection and transformation are typically presented separately. In this paper, we introduce a general approach for converting transformation-based methods to feature selection methods through L_1/L_infty regularization. Instead of solving feature selection as a discrete optimization, we relax and formulate the problem as a continuous optimization problem. An additional advantage of our formulation is that our optimization criterion optimizes for feature relevance and redundancy removal automatically. Here, we illustrate how our approach can be utilized to convert linear discriminant analysis (LDA) and the dimensionality reduction version of the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) to two new feature selection algorithms. Experiments show that our new feature selection methods out-perform related state-of-the-art feature selection approaches.

paragraphs: Dimensionality reduction can either construct new features or select a subset of the existing ones. Selection is useful when the original features need to retain their meaning. This paper connects the two approaches by showing how methods designed to transform features can be converted into methods that choose original features.

The conversion uses L1/L-infinity regularization and replaces a discrete selection problem with a continuous optimization formulation. Its objective accounts for both relevance and redundancy, so it seeks features that carry useful information without simply retaining repeated information. This makes feature selection part of the optimization criterion rather than a separate filtering step.

The authors demonstrate the framework by deriving selection algorithms from linear discriminant analysis and a dimensionality-reduction version of the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion. Their experiments report better performance than related state-of-the-art feature-selection approaches. The broader contribution is a reusable connection between transformation objectives and interpretable feature subsets, illustrated through these two concrete conversions and their empirical results.
summary.tldr: A continuous regularized formulation converts dimensionality-reduction methods into feature selectors that jointly address relevance and redundancy.

title: From Transformation-Based Dimensionality Reduction to Feature Selection

abstract: Many policy search algorithms minimize the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence to a certain target distribution in order to fit their policy. The commonly used KL-divergence forces the resulting policy to be 'reward-attracted'. The policy tries to reproduce all positively rewarded experience while negative experience is neglected. However, the KL-divergence is not symmetric and we can also minimize the the reversed KL-divergence, which is typically used in variational inference. The policy now becomes 'cost-averse'. It tries to avoid reproducing any negatively-rewarded experience while maximizing exploration. Due to this 'cost-averseness' of the policy, Variational Inference for Policy Search (VIP) has several interesting properties. It requires no kernel-bandwith nor exploration rate, such settings are determined automatically by the inference. The algorithm meets the performance of state-of-the-art methods while being applicable to simultaneously learning in multiple situations. We concentrate on using VIP for policy search in robotics. We apply our algorithm to learn dynamic counterbalancing of different kinds of pushes with a human-like 4-link robot.

paragraphs: Many policy-search algorithms fit a policy by minimizing Kullback-Leibler divergence to a target distribution. This paper emphasizes that the divergence is asymmetric: reversing its direction changes the behavior encouraged by learning. The usual direction attracts the policy toward positively rewarded experiences while neglecting negative experiences, whereas the reversed direction encourages avoidance of negatively rewarded behavior.

The proposed method, Variational Inference for Policy Search, uses this reversed divergence. Its cost-averse policy seeks to avoid reproducing negative experiences while maximizing exploration. The inference also determines settings that would otherwise require an exploration rate or kernel bandwidth, removing the need to specify those quantities separately.

The authors report performance matching state-of-the-art methods and the ability to learn in multiple situations simultaneously. Their robotics application trains a human-like four-link robot to dynamically counterbalance different kinds of pushes. This illustrates the paper's central motivation: changing the distribution-fitting objective can support policy learning across varying situations while automatically determining aspects of exploration.
summary.tldr: Reversing KL divergence produces a cost-averse policy-search method that determines exploration settings automatically and learns across multiple situations.

title: Variational Inference for Policy Search in changing situations

abstract: We study surrogate losses in the context of cost-sensitive classification with example-dependent costs, a problem also known as regression level set estimation. We give sufficient conditions on the surrogate loss for the existence of a surrogate regret bound. Such bounds imply that as the surrogate risk tends to its optimal value, so too does the expected misclassification cost. Our sufficient conditions encompass example-dependent versions of the hinge, exponential, and other common losses. These results provide theoretical justification for some previously proposed surrogate-based algorithms, and suggests others that have not yet been developed.

We give sufficient conditions on the surrogate loss for the existence of a surrogate regret bound. Such bounds imply that as the surrogate risk tends to its optimal value, so too does the expected misclassification cost. Our sufficient conditions encompass example-dependent versions of the hinge, exponential, and other common losses. These results provide theoretical justification for some previously proposed surrogate-based algorithms, and suggests others that have not yet been developed.

paragraphs: In cost-sensitive classification, errors can carry different costs, and here those costs may also depend on the individual example. The paper studies surrogate losses used to learn classifiers for this setting, also described as regression level-set estimation. The central question is whether optimizing the surrogate reliably advances the actual cost-sensitive objective.

The authors give sufficient conditions for a surrogate regret bound to exist. Such a bound connects the gap from optimal surrogate risk to the gap from optimal expected misclassification cost. Consequently, as the surrogate risk approaches its optimum, the expected classification cost also approaches its optimum under the stated conditions.

The sufficient conditions cover example-dependent versions of familiar losses, including hinge and exponential losses. This provides theoretical justification for some algorithms that had already been proposed and points toward other possible algorithms. The result is a guarantee connecting two optimization objectives; its sufficient conditions establish when that connection holds without claiming they are the only conditions under which it could hold.
summary.tldr: Sufficient conditions connect surrogate optimization to optimal classification cost when error costs depend on individual examples.

title: Surrogate losses and regret bounds for cost-sensitive classification with example-dependent costs

abstract: We present a flexible formulation for variable selection in multi-task regression to allow for discrepancies in the estimated sparsity patterns accross the multiple tasks, while leveraging the common structure among them. Our approach is based on an intuitive decomposition of the regression coefficients into a product between a component that is common to all tasks and another component that captures task-specificity. This decomposition yields the Multi-level Lasso objective that can be solved efficiently via alternating optimization. The analysis of the “orthonormal design” case reveals some interesting insights on the nature of the shrinkage performed by our method, compared to that of related work. Theoretical guarantees are provided on the consistency of Multi-level Lasso. Simulations and empirical study of micro-array data further demonstrate the value of our framework.

Our approach is based on an intuitive decomposition of the regression coefficients into a product between a component that is common to all tasks and another component that captures task-specificity. This decomposition yields the Multi-level Lasso objective that can be solved efficiently via alternating optimization. The analysis of the “orthonormal design” case reveals some interesting insights on the nature of the shrinkage performed by our method, compared to that of related work. Theoretical guarantees are provided on the consistency of Multi-level Lasso. Simulations and empirical study of micro-array data further demonstrate the value of our framework.

paragraphs: Related regression tasks can benefit from shared information, but they need not use exactly the same variables. This paper introduces Multi-level Lasso to select variables across tasks while allowing their sparsity patterns to differ. The aim is to use common structure without forcing every task to have an identical set of nonzero coefficients.

The method expresses regression coefficients as a product of two components. One component is shared by all tasks, while the other captures task-specific behavior. This decomposition produces an objective that can be solved efficiently through alternating optimization. It gives shared and individual structure explicit roles in determining the fitted coefficients.

The authors analyze the special case of an orthonormal design to explain how the method shrinks coefficients compared with related approaches. They also provide theoretical consistency guarantees and evaluate the framework through simulations and a microarray-data study. Together, these contributions support a flexible approach to sparse multitask regression, with both mathematical analysis and empirical evidence for its value.
summary.tldr: Multi-level Lasso multiplies shared and task-specific coefficient components to select variables flexibly across related regression tasks.

title: Multi-level Lasso for Sparse Multi-task Regression
